{@i "Bow-long"} {@b (Bo's dragon)}

The blizzard had rolled in pretty hard and we were pushin' through the snow to find some shelter. We decided to move into a denser part of the forest–to get a bit of cover from that piercin' wind. Seems we weren't the only ones with that idea. We came across a herd of lumberin' hadrosaur-lookin' dinosaurs. They were kinda small for that group and were spendin' most of their time on their hind legs, scrapin' away the snow in search of fresh growth. They weren't keen on us takin' up their warm spot in the forest and were honkin' loudly.
{@i Bolong} is one of the most basal members of the Hadrosauroidea, the group that includes the duck-billed dinosaurs, and is a relatively small member of it.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Bolong} was a relatively small hardrosauroid with an estimated length of 13 ft. and weighed approximately 440 lb. Although it shared many of the same features as other members of Hadrosauroidea, such as a beaked snout, robust hindlimbs, much lighter forelimbs, and a long thick tail, {@i Bolong} had much stockier proportions than its relatives. As the earliest branching hadrosauroid, it had features similar to the closely related iguanodontians including the first digit on each forelimb being modified into a thumb spike.

Like all hadrosauroids, {@i Bolong} was a herbivore and, given its low profile, likely fed near to the ground. It had large robust teeth and a modified jaw, specialised for chewing. This, combined with stomach contents, shows that {@i Bolong} was able to eat hard plants and even decomposing wood.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Hadrosauroids are frequently portrayed as relatively harmless animals that could only flee from danger. However, any modern large herbivore can be extremely dangerous, either because it is naturally aggressive or because it will use its bulk to defend itself. Hadrosauroids had thick, powerful tails which could strike attackers and {@i Bolong} possessed a thumb spike which could be used to fight predators (or other {@i Bolong}). Most hadrosauroids are also thought to have been communal animals, who were likely involved and protective parents, similar to modern cows.
We suggest {@i Bolong} be played as an apparently peaceful grazing animal, but with both the capacity for extreme aggression (especially if protecting young) and sudden panic, fleeing en-mass.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Hadrosauroids are members of the iguanodontians, a highly successful group of dinosaurs that arose in the Middle Jurassic and thrived until the end Cretaceous extinction. They were a varied group, containing animals such as {@creature Iguanodon|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@book The Rest of the Alphabet|PartneredDDDoD|7}) and the famous "duck-billed" hadrosaurs, as well as small bipedal animals like {@i Dryosaurus}.

{@i Bolong} provides a better understanding of this group's distribution during the Early Cretaceous. It's presence in China clarifies that a land connection between Asia and western North America + Europe was already established before or during the Barremian (middle of the Early Cretaceous), allowing us to better reconstruct ancient geography.

entries.name: Walking
entries: There has been some debate over whether {@i Bolong} walked on four legs all the time (obligate quadruped) or was capable of walking on two legs as well (facultative biped). Its front legs were relatively short and appear less able to support its body weight compared to other hadrosauroids, yet the foot was short and stocky, similar to those of true quadrupeds. Interestingly the younger animals had proportionally longer limbs, similar to their four-legged relatives. Perhaps juveniles walked on all fours before becoming more bipedal as heavier adults.

{@i "CAR-CHAR-OH-DON-TOE-SORE-US"} {@b (shark tooth reptile)}

There are some beasts that really do straddle the line between animal and monster. We heard it first–the thunderin' footsteps and gurglin' deep growls. We could feel the sounds deep in our chests. Cowerin' in the undergrowth, we used some subtle magic to mask our scent and a few members of the party whispered prayers to their deities. When we finally glimpsed it through the bushes, we had to hold back our gasps. The towerin' creature was among the peak of predatory perfection. A massive bulk and its maw was encrusted with dried blood–soaked in fact. It must have had a rippin' bite like no other.
{@i Carcharodontosaurus} was a Cretaceous (99-94 million years ago) theropod dinosaur and one of the largest theropods in the fossil record.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Carcharodontosaurus} was an extremely large animal, comparable in size to {@creature Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex|PartneredDDDoD|Tyrannosaurus rex} (see {@book Ancient Tyrannosaurus rex|PartneredDDDoD|8|Ancient Tyrannosaurus} ). It had an enlarged skull which was over 5 ft. long with jaws full of serrated knife-like teeth. Its eyes were positioned laterally, giving it an excellent range of vision, but compromising its binocular eyesight slightly.

While it shared its environment with another large carnivore, {@creature Spinosaurus|PartneredDDDoD}, it is likely that these animals were niche partitioned. This means that they relied on different resources for survival and probably did not directly compete with each other for food. This was partially because {@i Carcharodontosaurus} was not a permanent resident of the Bahariya environment, and may have spent more time hunting in the dryer scrubland surrounding the mangroves.

{@i Carcharodontosaurus} was likely a generalist hunter, meaning that it fed on anything it could bring down or scavenge. Evidence suggests it was capable of lifting animals or chunks of meat weighing up to 1750 lb. Potential prey from the Bahariya Formation included immature sauropods, hadrosaurs, other theropods, reptiles, and washed-up fish.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: As a large carnivore, {@i Carcharodontosaurus} would have spent most of the day resting, and less time searching for food. Given its size, it would not have been able to hide from prey, and likely relied on chasing down slower-moving animals. We recommend that it be run as a pursuit hunter, which will chase prey over a long distance. When not hunting or resting it should be curious of, but not automatically hostile to, players if given a wide berth.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Carcharodontosaurus} was a member of the Carcharodontosauridae. This was a sub-group of the Allosauroidea, the group that includes {@creature Allosaurus|XMM} (see {@book Pledger's Custom Dinosaurs|PartneredDDDoD|8|Big Al}). Carcharodontosaurids were medium-to-large sized theropods which included many giant species such as {@i Carcharodontosaurus}, {@creature Concavenator|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@book The Rest of the Alphabet|PartneredDDDoD|7|Concavenator}), {@i Giganotosaurus}, {@i Acrocanthosaurus} and {@i Meraxes}. They have been found globally in the Early-Middle Cretaceous, frequently occupying the role of arch-predators, and are considered a highly-successful group.

{@i "Car-no-tore-us"} {@b (meat-eating bull)} Chosen by Ahappypsycho

Some predatory dinosaurs hunt largely by smell and carno was one such beastie. It pursued us for four days, followin' the scent trail we left. Thankfully, we were able to out manoeuvre it. More than once we crossed a river, and circled round to observe it. We watched it lose, then re-pick up our trail several times. Must have been very hungry to chase us for so long. I guess it picked up the trail of somethin' easier to track when it stopped followin' us though.

{@i Carnotaurus sastrei} is the most famous member of the unusual Abelisauridae, a group of medium-sized theropods. {@i Carnotaurus sastrei} is known from the La Colonia Formation (71-69 million years ago) and has distinctive brow horns, giving it a bull-like appearance.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Carnotaurus sastrei} was medium-sized for an abelisaurid, at 26 ft. long and weighing approximately 1.5-2 tonnes. It had relatively long and strong legs which would have allowed for short bursts of sprinting. It also had highly reduced arms, so much so that the elbow joint no longer worked. Its arms could be rotated at the shoulder but couldn't bend like other theropods, and it also had 4 tiny fingers which may have lacked claws. Its head was boxy, with a tall and narrow skull but shallow lower jaw, and topped with a pair of prominent keratin-covered brow horns that protruded sideways.

{@i Carnotaurus sastrei} was built for short, explosive bursts of speed, making it an excellent pursuit hunter, running down prey. It was also able to bite rapidly, allowing it to quickly snap at escaping victims. {@i Carnotaurus sastrei} likely hunted prey smaller than itself, but it may also have predated upon medium-sized (juvenile) sauropods, bringing them down through rapid slashing bites. It is thought to have been a woodland or open plains predator.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Carnotaurus sastrei} would likely have stalked prey by getting within sprinting distance and then charging. It had an exceptional sense of smell, with a large olfactory lobe, but relatively low frequency hearing. It may also have hunted in pairs or small groups, meaning that prey would be charged by multiple {@i Carnotaurus sastrei}. Its horns were likely primarily used for intraspecific (same species) competition, displaying to, and even fighting with, other {@i Carnotaurus sastrei}.

We recommend that {@i Carnotaurus sastrei} be played as an ambush and pursuit hunter. It should track prey with its powerful sense of smell, sneak up as close as possible, then charge and pursue if the prey flees. It can be present in small groups (2 or 3 animals), socialising with each other. Like most large carnivores, {@i Carnotaurus sastrei} would have spent much of its time resting, so it would not be uncommon to encounter a small group sleeping together for most of the day.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Abelisaurs were an unusual group of theropods, with boxy skulls adorned with horns or bosses, and highly reduced arms. {@i Carnotaurus sastrei} was therefore fairly typical for the group. They first appeared in the Jurassic and were reasonably successful, surviving until the end-Cretaceous extinction. They are mostly known from the Southern Hemisphere in Africa, South America, India, and Madagascar, although there is some evidence that they may have been present in Europe too.

{@i "Sent-trow-sore-us"} {@b (Pointed reptile)}

Some herbivores are much more aggressive than others. We had setup a small, fixed camp on the edges of a large forest, hoping to eventually establish a permanent settlement later. The area was perfect–clear flat shrubland with a small stream for fresh water. After a week of work, one afternoon we were alerted to an approachin' herd of ceratops. They were bearin' down on us at speed, hootin' and honkin'. Within moments, a bull had charged through our camp, trampling four tents and injurin' two labourers. Evidently, this was their clearin' and they weren't happy to share.

{@i Centrosaurus} is a member of the horned dinosaurs (Ceratopsidae) from the Late Cretaceous (75 million years ago) of Canada and a smaller relative of the famous {@i Triceratops}. Its fossils have been discovered in colossal numbers within the Dinosaur Park Formation.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Centrosaurus} was a medium sized ceratopsid, measuring approximately 18 ft. long and weighing up to 2.5 tonnes. Its most distinctive feature was its skull, which bore the typical ceratopsian parrot-like beak and broad neck frill. This frill was ringed by small bones along its edge (epioccipitals) and the highest four were curved into crescent moon shapes. It had three horns, with two being small brow horns, and the third an enormous nasal horn. These horns were covered in a keratinous sheath that may have ended in a sharp point.

{@i Centrosaurus}, like all horned dinosaurs, had a fundamentally herbivorous diet. With a powerful beak and a shearing bite, it was well suited for snipping off tough plant material, browsing on ferns or stripping branches of their leaves. {@i Centrosaurus} lived in the temperate forests surrounding the swampland of the Dinosaur Park Formation of Cretaceous North America, browsing the shrubbery alongside a wide variety of other dinosaurs including ankylosaurs, other ceratopsians, many small theropods, and large tyrannosaurs.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Centrosaurus} lived in sizable herds and may have taken part in large seasonal migrations. Living in herds would have provided protection and increased the availability of reproductive partners. Like many other ceratopsians, while the horns would have been excellent defensive weapons they were also used for display and intraspecific (same species) squabbles. Like many ceratopsids (excluding {@i Triceratops}), {@i Centrosaurus}' frill was relatively thin and would not have provided defence against the powerful bite of a tyrannosaur and was primarily for display.

We suggest that {@i Centrosaurus} be played as a social animal, moving in groups. They should be {@variantrule Hostile [Attitude]|XPHB|Hostile} to an approaching party, but should not immediately attack. Instead, threat displays and false charges should be made to attempt to drive intruders away before a fight begins.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Centrosaurus} is a member of the Ceratopsidae, one of the most successful groups of Cretaceous dinosaurs and well-known for their impressive horns and large frills. Originating in Asia, this group spread throughout Asia and North America with a couple of fragments reported from Europe. Broadly speaking, the group has been divided along the lines of their frill and horn morphology (although there are exceptions). Animals with short frills, short brow horns and long nose horns belong to the Centrosaurinae (e.g., {@i Centrosaurus}) and those with long frills, long brow horns and short nose horns were in Chasmosaurinae (e.g., {@i Triceratops}).

Ceratopsids horns and frills can have a lot of variation within a single genus, sometimes leading scientists to misinterpret a variant as a different genus or species. {@i Centrosaurus} was part of a famous taxonomic (naming) debate, whereby some scientists proposed that its fossils were actually from a genus erected in the 1800s called Monoclonius, and did not warrant their own genus name (called a junior synonym). Eventually a consensus emerged, that the two were indeed the same genus, however the original material used to describe Monoclonius was insufficient, rendering the name invalid. We now exclusively use {@i Centrosaurus} to describe this animal.

{@i "Con-cah-ven-ah-tor"} {@b (Concave hunter)}

It took us forty minutes to realise that we were bein' hunted. By that point, an encounter was inevitable. We setup a defensive position to stand our ground and braced ourselves for battle. Before long, we were bein' circled by three meat-eatin' dinosaurs. Although your typical theropods with wicked claws and sharp teeth, these ones also had a strange lil' hump over their hips. Didn't have the time to ponder what those might be for though, as moments after I spotted 'em, they charged to attack all at once.

{@i Concavenator} is a small carcharodontosaurid from the Early Cretaceous (130 million years old) Las Hoyas fossil site in Spain and is a relative of the African giant {@creature Carcharodontosaurus|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@book The Bahariya Formation|PartneredDDDoD|4|Carcharodontosaurus}).

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Concavenator} was relatively small for a carcharodontosaurid, at most 20 ft. long and weighing about 700 lb. It had elongate three clawed forelimbs, a robust but elongate skull, and a distinctive "hump" situated above its pelvis. This hump is created by elongated vertebral spines, creating a tall concave structure. While similar structures are seen in {@creature Spinosaurus|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@book The Bahariya Formation|PartneredDDDoD|4|Spinosaurus}) and some other carcharodontosaurids, they form large sails made of numerous vertebrae. {@i Concavenator} is unique in that it utilises only two vertebrae to create a small hump and its function remains uncertain. It has been suggested to be a form of display, a method of heat regulation, and even analogous to a camel hump. Of these, a display structure seems the most plausible.

When the fossil was first discovered, the authors noticed a series of strange knobs on its forearm. They suggested that these were anchoring points for quills, similar to the tail of {@creature Psittacosaurus|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@book The Yixian Formation|PartneredDDDoD|3|Psittacosaurus}). However, further analysis revealed that the bone was deformed by taphonomy (the processes of fossilisation) and these were actually normal muscle attachment points.

{@i Concavenator} was a carnivorous dinosaur and while less massive than its relatives, is still the largest theropod known from the Las Hoyas site. This site formed around a lake which would have been a water source for many species including iguanodontians, other smaller theropods, mammals and reptiles, and {@i Concavenator} was the arch-predator of this locality.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Concavenator} would have been a light, agile predator capable of running down prey. Like other carcharodontosaurids, it may have lived in small groups and used the hump on its back as a means of signaling to other {@i Concavenator}. This might be sexual signaling, warnings of danger, or even intimidation displays.

We recommend that {@i Concavenator} be played as a large social carnivore–similar to a lion, resting long hours, highly communicative, and very agile when hunting. It should see all humanoids up to Large in size as prey and might be drawn to settlements to hunt livestock or pick off unwary travelers.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: While carchodontosaurids are best known for being giants, many of the earlier animals were much smaller. These smaller animals are known from Europe and South America and likely evolved reduced sizes to survive on much smaller prey. This would allow them to occupy a different niche to larger predators, avoiding direct competition.

{@i "Krah-toe-a-vis"} {@b (Crato bird)}

Among the sun-scorched branches and chirpin' of crickets, we saw a small flash of vivid colour accompanied by a wonderful chorus of squarkin'. We stopped for a moment to see whether we could identify what it was. Once we spotted it, we glimpsed the most beautiful bird I've ever seen. It was performin' some sorta strange dancin' display in the treetops, hoppin' from branch to branch. It was absolutely hypnotic to watch.
{@i Cratoavis} is an enantiornithian, a group of birds (avialans) from the Early Cretaceous that shared many similarities with modern birds, but were their own distinctive group.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Cratoavis} looks quite similar to a modern bird. It stands out from its living cousins by having small peg-like teeth and short claws on its wings, giving it a characteristic 'prehistoric' appearance. Enantiornithians occupied a variety of ecological niches, but {@i Cratoavis} was likely an insectivore feeding on small insects it caught in trees or on the ground. It may have also opportunistically fed on fruits, berries, or even carrion, but peg/needle-like teeth are usually associated with eating insects.
{@i Cratoavis} had modified tail feathers that formed a twinned set of elongate feather vanes. These were undoubtedly a signalling device and were probably used in elaborate mating displays.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Cratoavis} bears such a strong similarity to modern birds that it is reasonable to expect it to behave in a similar fashion. Given its small size, it was likely a relatively vulnerable animal and would have been extremely wary of being approached by potential predators. We recommend that {@i Cratoavis} retreat when approached but possess curiosity about anything novel in its environment. Parties are highly unlikely to be attacked by {@i Cratoavis} unless they knowingly or unknowingly damage their nests.

entries.name: Exceptional Preservation
entries: When people think of fossils, they frequently think of large complete skeletons, isolated bones or partial fragments. Soft tissue like muscles, skin, feathers etc. are assumed to have degraded long before fossilisation can occur, yet there are numerous cases of exceptionally well-preserved fossils showing soft tissues. {@i Cratoavis}' fossil is one such example. Not only is the specimen fully articulated (joints still connected) and almost entirely complete, it also preserves exquisite impressions of its feathers and other soft tissues.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Cratoavis} belongs to the group Enantiornithes. This is a group of feathered theropods that looked very similar to modern birds, but retained primitive features like teeth and wing claws. They were an extremely successful group originating in the Early Cretaceous, with 80 species spread across every continent, bar Antartica, before dying out at the end-Cretaceous extinction. Despite their success, we are still a bit uncertain as to their relationships. While they are universally placed in Avialae (the group including modern birds and their closest relatives such as {@i Archaeopteryx} or {@creature Balaur|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@book Hațeg Island|PartneredDDDoD|5|Balaur})), others go further and identify them as primitive members of the "true birds" Aves.

Zhang, F., Kearns, S.L., Orr, P.J., Benton, M.J., Zhou, Z., Johnson, D., Xu, X. and Wang, X., 2010. Fossilized melanosomes and the colour of Cretaceous dinosaurs and birds. {@i Nature}, {@b 463(7284)}, 1075-1078.
{@i "Dye-no-keir-rus"} {@b (horrible hand)}

In the fetid swamp, we had the misfortune of havin' to wade through some pretty foul water. This was made all the more unpleasant by a huge oily, fuzzy, hump-backed theropod dinosaur that waded through the water. Thankfully, it was a herbivore, so there didn't appear to be any immediate danger of becomin' lunch. That said, it had some very mighty lookin' claws and could no doubt rend a person in two fairly easily. For that reason, and the smell, we kept our distance.

{@i Deinocheirus} is a giant ornithomimosaur from the Late Cretaceous (70 million years old) Nemegt Formation of Mongolia. A relative of Gallimimus, Ornithomimus, and Struthiomimus, it is both the largest and most bizarre member of its family.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Deinocheirus} was an enormous ornithomimosaur, a group of otherwise ostrich-like theropods. It was at least 36 ft. long and weighed up to 5 tonnes when fully grown, putting it in the same size category as giant carnivorous theropods like {@creature Carcharodontosaurus|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@book The Bahariya Formation|PartneredDDDoD|4|Carcharodontosaurus}) or {@creature Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex|PartneredDDDoD|Tyrannosaurus} (see {@book Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex|PartneredDDDoD|8|Ancient Tyrannosaurus}). Its arms were long with extremely large, but blunt, hooked claws. The vertebrae in the centre of its back had fused spines that stuck up, giving the animal a highly distinctive hump or sail (though much smaller than animals like {@creature Spinosaurus|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@book The Bahariya Formation|PartneredDDDoD|4|Spinosaurus})). Its face was long and narrow with a toothless snout that flared sideways at the tip, giving its jaws a shovel like appearance. Like other ornithomimosaurs, it likely had a full body covering of feathers, and possibly a broad fan of feathers on the end of its tail.

While a theropod, {@i Deinocheirus} was not the stereotypical carnivore. Its blunt hooked claws were well adapted for digging or grasping, allowing it to pull at plants or excavate soil while looking for invertebrates. Its stomach contained gastroliths (stones used to crush plants), as well as fish scales. Its jaw possessed anchor points for a powerful tongue that may have been long and possibly quite mobile. The Nemegt Formation of Mongolia is constituted of mudstone and sandstone sediments from a mixture of fluvial (river), alluvial (floodplain), paludal (marsh), and lacustrine (lake) settings. This unusual morphology, diet, and habitat leads us to think that {@i Deinocheirus} was a specialist wader, moving through wet or swampy environments, browsing on soft water plants and snapping up unwary fish.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Deinocheirus}' brain was relatively small and less complex than other ornithomimosaurs, suggesting a more sedate and less involved lifestyle. It may have been a solitary giant, feeding in wetland environments. An adult {@i Deinocheirus} would have been slow and would have had to stand its ground if attacked. Large predators like Tarbosaurus stalked the same regions and, while very large itself, these comparably sized animals may have predated upon {@i Deinocheirus}. While its claws were blunt, they were also powerful and a potent defensive weapon.

We suggest that {@i Deinocheirus} be played as a slow-moving oblivious herbivore, wading through wetlands or lumbering through forests. It should be placid if ignored but extremely {@variantrule Hostile [Attitude]|XPHB|Hostile} if threatened, butchering threats within reach, although rarely pursuing fleeing targets. Yet, if treated with caution, {@i Deinocheirus} might be an easily appeased animal and excellent wetland mount.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Deinocheirus} was first described in 1970 by Osmólska and Roniewicz, after a giant pair of forelimbs and shoulder girdle were discovered in Cretaceous sediments from Mongolia. These huge forelimbs were suspected to be from a massive predatory theropod dinosaur, given their vicious claws. However, the rest of the animal remained a mystery for 44 years and in that time various hypotheses were presented, including the suggestion that it was a giant tree-climbing animal. It wasn't until 2014, when most of the rest of the holotype and several other specimens were discovered, that the truly bizarre nature of this dinosaur was revealed.

Ornithomimosauria was a diverse group of medium to huge sized ostrich-like theropods. They were very distinct from other theropods, as they were toothless, had long arms, long necks, long legs, and feet with short claws. They are an exclusively Cretaceous group, but were quite successful, occurring throughout Lauraisa (North America, Europe, and Asia) and survived until the end-Cretaceous extinction.

entries.name: References
entries: Bell, P.R., Currie, P.J., and Lee, Y.N. 2012. Tyrannosaur feeding traces on {@i Deinocheirus} (Theropoda:?Ornithomimosauria) remains from the Nemegt Formation (Late Cretaceous), Mongolia. {@i Cretaceous Research}, {@b 37}, 186-190.

Kobayashi, Y., Lee, H.J., Godefroit, P., Escuillié, F.O., and Chinzorig, T. 2014. Resolving the long-standing enigmas of a giant ornithomimosaur {@i Deinocheirus mirificus}. {@i Nature}, {@b 515(7526)}, 257-260.

Owocki, K., Kremer, B., Cotte, M., and Bocherens, H. 2020. Diet preferences and climate inferred from oxygen and carbon isotopes of tooth enamel of {@i Tarbosaurus bataar} (Nemegt Formation, Upper Cretaceous, Mongolia). {@i Palaeogeography, Palaeoclimatology, Palaeoecology}, {@b 537}, 109190.
{@i "Die-no-soo-cus"} {@b (Terrible Crocodile)}

Most of us who adventure are familiar with crocs, big'uns too. But this... this one was somethin' else. A gargantuan croc, far bigger than any other I've ever seen. Thankfully, we came upon it while it was baskin', rather than huntin'. It was so big that it was barely interested in us. I reckon it could take down even the biggest of dinosaurs with ease. Certainly wouldn't want to be on the receiving end of a bite from it. The heaviest plate armour wouldn't even make a difference.

{@i Deinosuchus} is from the Late Cretaceous (82 million years ago) of North America and is a giant relative of modern alligators. It was a highly successful animal that occurred on both sides of the Western Interior Sea.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Deinosuchus} is thought to have reached a maximum size of approximately 33 ft. and weighed around 2.5 tonnes, although some may have been larger. Aside from its size, it was very similar to a modern alligator, albeit with a slightly more bulbous snout. Like its modern relatives, {@i Deinosuchus} had extremely powerful jaws which are estimated to have had a bite similar in strength to {@creature Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex|PartneredDDDoD|Tyrannosaurus} (see {@book Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex|PartneredDDDoD|8|Ancient Tyrannosaurus}). The estimated strength of this bite varies hugely between different studies, from as low as 2 tonnes and as high as 20 tonnes in force but, even at the low end this would be devastating against most animals.

{@i Deinosuchus} is known from multiple fossil localities along both sides of the Western Interior Sea. This was a huge inland sea that formed in the Cretaceous and divided what would become North America in two. Like modern alligators, {@i Deinosuchus} was a semi-aquatic ambush predator, slowly moving in muddy water before striking suddenly at unsuspecting prey. Based on bite marks in numerous fossils, we know that it fed on a range of prey from turtles to large dinosaurs.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: The similarities {@i Deinosuchus} shares with modern alligators suggests that it behaved similarly. Alligators are powerful, patient predators who can live alone or in large groups. When in groups, they regularly fight with each other. Given its size, {@i Deinosuchus} probably only formed groups of a dozen or so individuals at maximum. Many likely suffered horrific injuries from their fights that would have been debilitating for other animals, but {@i Deinosuchus}' remarkable resilience and exceptional immune system would have allowed them to continue largely unphased.

We suggest that {@i Deinosuchus} be played as an animal that rarely moves and prefers to either bask in the sun or lie motionless in water, with just its nostrils and eyes peeking out. They should also have no fear of attacking anything that comes within striking range (excluding monsters like the {@creature Tarrasque|XMM} or Ancient Dragons). We suggest that this power and resilience could cause {@i Deinosuchus} to be worshiped as a deity by pre-industrial cultures.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Deinosuchus} was one of the early members of Crocodilia, the only surviving group of crocodylomorphs today. Crocodiles, gharials and alligators are frequently called "living fossils" as they have changed little over many millions of years. However, they represent just a fraction of the various crocodylomorph species that existed. Appearing in the Late Triassic, the group included a huge variety of animals from dinosaur-like small predators, to oceanic animals that had lost the ability to come on land, and even armoured herbivores.

entries.name: References
entries: Baker, C.J., Frère, C.H., Franklin, C.E., Campbell, H.A., Irwin, T.R., and Dwyer, R.G. 2023. Long-term tracking reveals a dynamic crocodylian social system. {@i Animal Behaviour}, {@b 199}, 59-78.

Cossette, A.P., and Brochu, C.A. 2020. A systematic review of the giant alligatoroid {@i Deinosuchus} from the Campanian of North America and its implications for the relationships at the root of Crocodylia. {@i Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology}, {@b 40}, e1767638.
Schwimmer, D.R. 2002. {@i King of the Crocodylians: The Paleobiology of Deinosuchus}. Indiana University press, pp. 220.
Siroski, P.A., and Soledad, M.B.M. 2020. Review of the Recent Knowledge on the Crocodilian Immune System. {@i South American Journal of Herpetology}, {@b 18}, 68-77.
{@i "Dye-lof-oh-sore-us"} {@b (Twin crested reptile)} Chosen by Steven Law

We had been hackin' our way through the dense, hot swamp for several hours now. Everythin' we had encountered had been small enough to just spook away, but that was about to change. A horrible hissin' sound creeped out of the heavy foliage to me left, then a dual-crested gnarl-toothed head poked out at eye-level to me. I fell back, gaspin' in shock as the head began to rise. As it did, a large gangly theropod stepped out, towerin' over me. I thought I was a gonner for sure. It lunged towards me lightnin' fast, but our paladin threw herself between us. Its teeth made a horrid screechin' sound as they glanced across her plate. The rest of our party shortly followed, ready for the fight. Thank the gods they were.

{@i Dilophosaurus} was a large theropod from the Early Jurassic (193 million years ago) of North America. Believed for many years to be a delicate scavenger, recent research suggests it was in fact a robust and powerful arch-predator.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Dilophosaurus} was one of the largest theropod dinosaurs of the Early Jurassic, measuring 23 ft. long and weighing almost half a tonne. Its skull was big for its body size, but also relatively light, and had a pair of tall dorsal arched crests that would have been covered in keratin in life. At the front of its upper jaw was a divot separating the front and back teeth, creating a distinctive notch, similar to that of {@creature Garjainia|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@book The Rest of the Alphabet|PartneredDDDoD|7|Garjainia}). Its jaws were well muscled, and it probably had a powerful bite. The forelimbs had four fingers, with the fourth finger being vestigial (reduced to the point of non-function). Overall, the forelimbs were quite strong but with limited forward motion. Its legs were powerfully built, with a large femur, which suggests it was a fast runner.

{@i Dilophosaurus} possessed the large, pointed teeth of a carnivore specialised in tackling big prey. The Kayenta Formation, where the first specimen was found, represents an arid environment with sparse rivers running through it that would have concentrated prey animals. {@i Dilophosaurus} probably stalked these watering holes, feeding on sauropodomorphs (early relatives of sauropods), early mammal-like animals, armored dinosaurs, heterodontosaurs (small bipedal dinosaurs), smaller theropods, and various reptiles. This hypothesis is supported by the presence of {@i Dilophosaurus} bite marks on the skeletons of sauropodomorphs.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Early research on {@i Dilophosaurus} suggested that it was a relatively delicate animal with a weak bite that would struggle to capture large prey, and it was considered a scavenger for many years. This image of {@i Dilophosaurus} as a weaker animal bled into its portrayal in popular media, particularly in Jurassic Park, where its size is diminished and it spits venom to compensate for its fragility (not to mention the entirely fictional frill). However, further research has revealed that {@i Dilophosaurus} was large, powerful, fast, and capable of overpowering struggling prey. Its flexible fingers and strong forelimbs are adapted to grasp moving targets, reducing the risk of breakage. Healed injuries found on {@i Dilophosaurus} also indicate that it was a hardy animal, able to shrug off serious wounds.

We suggest that {@i Dilophosaurus} be played as an aggressive solitary predator, willing to hunt prey larger than itself. It should sneak as close as possible, then charge its prey with open jaws. Once in range, {@i Dilophosaurus} should grapple prey with its robust forelimbs and bite down for the kill. It would have no qualms about hunting humanoids, even when in groups. When not hunting, it can use its crests as a means of display either to threaten a rival or attract a mate.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Dilophosaurus} has uncertain relationships and has shifted placement between the taxonomic groups Megalosauridae, Coelophysoidea, and Dilophosauridae. The latter was erected for {@i Dilophosaurus}, but some authors have placed the Antarctic Cryolophosaurus and/or the African Dracovenator in it as well. Recent research suggests that Dilophosauridae does not accurately represent real relationships, as it is based on highly variable traits like crests. Whether further support for Dilophosauridae can be found remains to be seen, but it is currently placed within the much larger group Neotheropoda, which includes all theropods related to both the Triassic theropod Coelophysis and modern birds.

entries.name: References
entries: Marsh, A.D., and Rowe, T.B. 2020. A comprehensive anatomical and phylogenetic evaluation of {@i Dilophosaurus wetherilli} (Dinosauria, Theropoda) with descriptions of new specimens from the Kayenta Formation of northern Arizona. {@i Journal of Paleontology}, {@b 94(S78)}, 1-103.

Senter, P.J., and Sullivan, C. 2019. Forelimbs of the theropod dinosaur {@i Dilophosaurus wetherilli}: range of motion, influence of paleopathology and soft tissues, and description of a distal carpal bone. {@i Palaeontologia Electronica}, {@b 22(2)}, 1-19.
Welles, S.P. 1970. Dilophosaurus (Reptilia: Saurischia), a new name for a dinosaur. {@i Journal of Paleontology}, {@b 44(5)}, 989.
{@i "Err-eat-throw-soo-cus"} {@b (Red crocodile)}

Travelin' through the desert, we had had three nights of restless campin'. The sounds of huge bellowin' creatures filled every night, making sleep difficult and worrisome. On the dawn of the fourth day, we had the misfortune to bein' awoken by one of the beasts tryin' to drag away our paladin. She, weirdly, sleeps in her armour and we had mocked her for it before. That night it likely saved her though. The thin' was huge and bizarre lookin'. It had a gigantic head with a fearsome bite, but smaller body–almost comical. As we struck at it, it thrashed from side to side, and opened its maw to bare its teeth–thankfully droppin' our friend.

{@i Erythrosuchus} was a giant erythrosuchid from the Middle Triassic (245 million years ago) of South Africa (Beaufort Group). A close relative of {@creature Garjainia|PartneredDDDoD}, it was the largest and most powerful predator in its ecosystem.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Erythrosuchus} was, unsurprisingly, an erythrosuchid, a group of four-legged land predators, and was the largest of the group at about 16 ft. long. Its skull was enormous relative to its body, with extremely robust jaws and teeth. Its neck was short and powerful, meaning it could both bite very hard and forcibly thrash prey. Its body was typical of reptiles for the time, with robust limbs and a short tail. Like later archosaurs (the ancestors of dinosaurs), its pelvis allowed for an erect stance, so it stood upright rather than sprawling like many other reptiles.

{@i Erythrosuchus} was the largest carnivore in the Beaufort group, which was laid down in a semi-arid environment with seasonal rains. It is thought to have been the arch-predator of this area, feeding on a wide variety of prey such as early synapsids (mammal-like reptiles), amphibians, and reptiles. It likely specialised in tackling medium-large sized dicynodonts, the squat herbivorous synapsids that were extremely abundant at the time.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Very little information is known about the behaviour of erythrosuchids, with little to no research into their likely interactions or hunting strategies. As they were almost certainly arch predators, we suggest they would have behaved similarly to modern carnivores. This meant that much of the day was spent resting to avoid wasting energy. {@i Erythrosuchus} was too bulky to run down prey and likely ambushed it instead, wrestling anything it caught with its powerful jaws.

We recommend {@i Erythrosuchus} be played as a slow but persistent predator that is highly dangerous if close, but otherwise lazy if resting or given a safe margin by a party. Like many animals in an arid environment, it should be most active in the evening, night, and dawn to avoid the blistering midday heat. This makes it the ideal creature to ambush a resting party.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Erythrosuchids were members of the Archosauriformes, the group which gave rise to the true archosaurs like pterosaurs, crocodiles, and dinosaurs. Like many archosaurs, they had an erect gait and rapid growth, suggesting that they were warm-blooded (endothermic). If this is true, this, along with other evidence from early archosaurs, suggests that being warm-blooded was a basal (primitive) condition for archosauriformes.

entries.name: References
entries: Benton, M.J., 2021. The origin of endothermy in synapsids and archosaurs and arms races in the Triassic. {@i Gondwana Research}, {@b 100}, pp.261-289.
Broom, R. 1905. Notice of some new reptiles from the Karoo Beds of South Africa. {@i Records of the Albany Museum}, {@b 1}, 331-337.
Ezcurra, M.D., Butler, R.J., and Gower, D.J. 2013. 'Proterosuchia': the origin and early history of Archosauriformes. {@i Geological Society, London, Special Publications}, {@b 379(1)}, 9-33.

Hancox, P.J., Neveling, J., and Rubidge, B.S. 2020. Biostratigraphy of the Cynognathus Assemblage Zone (Beaufort Group, Karoo Supergroup), South Africa. {@i South African Journal of Geology}, {@b 123(2)}, 217-238.
Parrish, J.M. 1992. Phylogeny of the Erythrosuchidae (Reptilia: Archosauriformes). {@i Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology}, {@b 12(1)}, 93-102.
{@i "Fal-kah-take-lee"} {@b (Small scythe)}

The mornin' chorus in this region was much more vibrant than most areas. It didn't take long for us to find out why, since the culprit was such a beautiful beastie. A stunnin', vividly-patterned bird with a long curved beak. {@variantrule Friendly [Attitude]|XPHB|Friendly} thin'–seemed to have a fondness of fruits if I recall.

{@i Falcatakely} was a bird-like theropod from the Cretaceous (65-70 million years ago) of Madagascar. It was a relative of {@creature Cratoavis|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@book The Crato Formation|PartneredDDDoD|6|Cratoavis}) and was about the size of a raven. It possessed an unusual beak and appears to be another example of a specialised animal evolving on an isolated island.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Falcatakely} was a small animal with a wingspan of about 3 ft. that was outwardly very similar to a modern bird, albeit with clawed fingers and a toothed beak. It had a large beak-like snout, similar to a toucan, with small teeth in the front of its mouth (premaxilla). This toucan-like appearance has led scientists to hypothesise that {@i Falcatakely} shared a similar fruit-eating (frugivorous) lifestyle, while perhaps also eating insects and small vertebrate prey.

{@i Falcatakely} is from the Maevarano Formation, which was laid down in a seasonally wet/arid environment with shallow rivers and abundant flood plains in northern Madagascar. By this point in time Madagascar was already isolated from the mainland and {@i Falcatakely} may be an example of specialised adaptations in this island isolation.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Little is known about {@i Falcatakely}'s behaviour, but it is reasonable to presume that it shared similarities to toucans. It may have been social, forming breeding pairs that roosted within hollows in trees. We recommend that {@i Falcatakely} be played in much the same manner as you would a normal bird, meaning it will be skittish of players who disturb it, but loyal if tamed or hand-reared.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Enantiornitheans have a complicated phylogeny and there is still debate over whether they are true birds. This is a common problem in the wider Avialae, the theropod group leading to birds, as much of them share the presence of complex feathers, wings, and beaks. Currently, there isn't a consensus on which features can be considered truly "bird"-like, and so {@i Falcatakely}'s position in the tree of life is unlikely to be resolved until further analyses are complete.

entries.name: References
entries: Chiappe, L. M. 2009. Downsized Dinosaurs: The Evolutionary Transition to Modern Birds. {@i Evolution: Education and Outreach}, {@b 2(2)}, 248-256.
O'Connor, J.K., and Chiappe, L.M. 2011. A revision of enantiornithine (Aves: Ornithothoraces) skull morphology. {@i Journal of Systematic Palaeontology}, {@b 9(1)}, 135-157.

O'Connor, P.M., Turner, A.H., Groenke, J.R., Felice, R.N., Rogers, R.R., Krause, D.W., and Rahantarisoa, L.J. 2020. Late Cretaceous bird from Madagascar reveals unique development of beaks. {@i Nature}, {@b 588}, 272-276.
{@i "Gar-jar-nee-ah"} {@b (Swift roar?)}

When we first saw these lil' blighters, we thought they'd be unbothersome. But don't let their size fool ya. They've got a mean bite. Our Ranger approached one of 'em and before we knew it, it was latched onto his arm. Can't much fire a bow with one hand now. Funny at first, then we saw three more scurrying out of the brush to join the frenzy. Wouldn't be long before they'd disarm all of us!

{@i Garjainia} is an early erythrosuchid, a group of quadrupedal carnivores from the Early Triassic (249-237 million years ago) of Russia and Africa. It walked with a raised gait and had an enormous head, making it an unusual looking animal.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Garjainia} was a medium sized predator for the Triassic, measuring approximately 8 ft. long. It had a reptilian body structure that was typical for the era, except for two key features. Its legs were beneath its body giving it an erect gait, rather than a sprawling one, and its head was enormous, making up about a quarter of its total body length. Its skull was huge with a long and robust jaws, and a characteristic notch towards the front of the upper jaw, similar to {@creature Spinosaurus|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@book The Bahariya Formation|PartneredDDDoD|4|Spinosaurus}). Its teeth were long, fang-like, and partially fused to the jaw. Usually vertebrate teeth are either fused (ankylothedocont) or unfused (thecodont), and so {@i Garjainia} represents an unusual middle-ground.

Originally thought to have been semi-aquatic due to their dense bones, recent studies indicate that {@i Garjainia} was a capable terrestrial animal and its bone density was a result of its short robust stature. Its strong jaws and robust teeth indicate that it was capable of overpowering large struggling prey. It shared its environment with a wide variety of other animals including amphibians, a variety of synapsids (mammal-like reptiles), and other erythrosuchids, many of which were larger than itself. Although able to tackle large animals, it may have been hunted by bigger erythrosuchids like {@creature Erythrosuchus|PartneredDDDoD}.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Erythrosuchid behaviour is poorly understood, but we know that they grew relatively fast and may have been endothermic (warm-blooded). {@i Garjainia} was clearly built for strength, rather than speed and was probably an ambush predator, lying in wait until prey was close enough for a rapid strike. Some species possessed bony bumps on the side of their heads, which may have been used for display or fights for dominance rights.

We suggest that {@i Garjainia} be played similar to a Komodo Dragon; a powerful animal that slowly stalks the undergrowth and occasionally charges large prey. It may aggregate in groups, simultaneously attacking to bring down huge prey, essentially forming a swarm. While a single {@i Garjainia} may be a reasonable threat, a swarm is a significant one, able to mob and disable party members.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: As an erythrosuchid, {@i Garjainia} is part of the Archosauriformes, placing it in the sibling group to crocodiles, dinosaurs, and pterosaurs. The Erythrosuchidae were unusual high-gait lizard-like animals that ranged from dog- to cow-sized. They are known from Europe, Africa, India, and China, where they were major predators in their ecosystems.

entries.name: References
entries: Ezcurra, M., Gower, D., Sennikov, A., and Butler, R. 2019. The osteology of the holotype of the early erythrosuchid {@i Garjainia prima} Ochev, 1958 (Diapsida: Archosauromorpha) from the upper Lower Triassic of European Russia. {@i Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society}, {@b 185(3)}, 717-783.

Gower, D.J., Hancox, J.P., Botha-Brink, J., Sennikov, A.G., and Butler, R.J. 2014. A New Species of {@i Garjainia} Ochev, 1958 (Diapsida: Archosauriformes: Erythrosuchidae) from the Early Triassic of South Africa. {@i PLOS ONE}, {@b 9(11)}, e111154.
Ochev V.G. 1958. Новые данные о псевдозухиях СССР ["New data concerning the pseudosuchians of the USSR"]. {@i Doklady AN SSSR}, {@b 123}, 749-751.
{@i "Gi-raf-ah-tie-tan"} {@b (Giraffe giant)}

The heat had been gettin' to us pretty bad and we'd start'd to run low on water. Headin' down to the coast seemed like a good idea at the time. There, we could boil some of the salt water and condense out somethin' fresh to drink. At first, we couldn't make out the gigantic forms on the horizon. The blarin' sun hazin' our view. When we got a bit closer, we saw em—towerin' sauropods traipsin' through the waves to keep cool and scavengin' what few plants grew on the coast. Aproachin' was a bad decision. They was pretty defensive of their feedin' patch and boy, those things can't half give ya a whack when they wanna.

{@i Giraffatitan} is a giant brachiosaurid sauropod from the Late Jurassic (145 million years ago) Tendaguru Formation of Tanzania. A larger relative of the American Brachiosaurus, it was considered the biggest land animal until fossils of the giant titanosaurs, like {@creature Paralititan|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@book The Bahariya Formation|PartneredDDDoD|4|Paralititan}), were discovered.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Giraffatitan} is known from incomplete remains, leading to several estimations of its size. The most recent analyses suggest it was around 85 ft. long and weighed 45 tonnes. This may seem exceptionally heavy, but is much less than another animal of the same size would be. This is because sauropods had weight reduction adaptations, such as hollow air sac-filled bones (pneumatisation). It had a very tall shoulders, elevating the front of its body and sloping its back. Its tail was relatively short for a sauropod, but its neck was very long, held erect and tipped by a blunt snouted skull that had a tall bony arch on its forehead.

{@i Giraffatitan} was a herbivorous animal with peg-like teeth that it used to strip tall conifer trees of leaves. It was not a permanent resident of the Tendaguru Formation, which was a tidal flat environment, as its upright posture meant it was a high browser. Instead, it must have lived in a forested area and may have visited the tidal flats in times of drought or while migrating elsewhere.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Due to its size, {@i Giraffatitan} would have been a slow-moving animal, travelling in groups from place to place, stripping the greenery from the tallest trees. An adult {@i Giraffatitan} would have been safe from all but the largest of predators, although young {@i Giraffatitan} may have been quite vulnerable. Currently, there is no evidence of any predators in the Tendaguru Formation large enough to threaten an adult {@i Giraffatitan}. However, its biggest threat was probably other {@i Giraffatitan} as it may have undertaken intraspecific (same species) fighting.

We recommend {@i Giraffatitan} be largely dismissive of most smaller animals, so long as they are not perceived as a threat to their young. Parties should be able to get relatively close to adults without disturbing them, as they slowly travel across the landscape looking for food. {@i Giraffatitan} are too slow to chase or charge opponents and will instead stand their ground, crushing enemies within reach.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Brachiosaurids were among the largest dinosaurs ever to live. They arose in the Late Jurassic (160 million years ago) and survived into the Late Cretaceous (93 million years ago). Initially very successful, they spread to every continent bar Antarctica and Australia before becoming restricted to North America in the Early Cretaceous.

entries.name: Periscope Up
entries: Sauropods were such massive animals that early palaeontologists wondered how they could possibly support their massive weight on land. Most fossils were found in sites that represented wetlands, coasts, and riverbeds and some palaeontologists argued that they must have been semi-aquatic. They suggested that their long necks and tall forelimbs were adaptations to wading in deep water, keeping their heads at the surface like a giant snorkel. This hypothesis has now been extensively disproven, as pressure at that depth would have collapsed their lungs, and their hollow bones would have made them very buoyant, causing them to float and then topple over. We now know that they were terrestrial animals of the forests and plains, and their abundance in watery environments in the fossil record is a preservational bias.

{@i "Hats-egg-op-tear-ix"} {@b (Hațeg basin wing)}

We were told that it wasn't safe to explore these islands, but we didn't care for the stories. We should'a listened... We figured that the biggest critters would be towards the centre of the islands, and it'd be safe to skirt the edges. But after only a few hours walkin' along the coastline that hypothesis was flattened. The beast descended from the sky faster than any dragon I've ever seen and with more lethal ferocity than the nastiest rex. It downed two members of our crew on impact, snatched up one of our guides and took straight back off. I saw it swallow the poor sod whole. The entire attack took seconds and in just as much time we were all scrabblin' for the treeline as it circled above. We should'a listened.

{@i Hatzegopteryx} is a member of the Azhdarchidae, the giant, long-necked pterosaurs. It is one of the largest and heaviest flying animals known and is a close relative of the famous giant pterosaur {@creature Quetzalcoatlus|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@book The Rest of the Alphabet|PartneredDDDoD|7|Quetzalcoatlus}).

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Hatzegopteryx} was an enormous pterosaur, with a wingspan estimated to be between 33 and 39 ft. It was also extremely heavy for a flying animal, weighing somewhere in the range of 440-550 lb., at least 10 times heavier than the heaviest flying birds alive today. Like other azhdarchid pterosaurs, it had long limbs and was very tall when standing, with forelimbs longer than its hindlimbs, giving it a sloping back. Its neck was elongated in comparison to most pterosaurs, but it was shorter and stockier than other azhdarchids. Its skull was massive, perhaps 5 ft. long, but again more robustly built than animals like {@creature Quetzalcoatlus|PartneredDDDoD}.

{@i Hatzegopteryx} stood at about the height of a giraffe and towered above the (often) dwarfed fauna of the Hațeg Island. As it could fly, it was not affected by the resource limitations of the island and did not undergo insular dwarfism, making it the largest carnivore present by far. Azhdarchids were once assumed to be fish specialists that skim or dip fed, however the consensus now is that they were largely terrestrial animals that spent most of their time walking on the ground, hunting like giant storks. {@i Hatzegopteryx} would stalk the undergrowth, catching prey and killing it with its powerful beak. Its prey would have included any animal small enough for it to grab and swallow whole, but it may also have been able to skewer and pull apart slightly larger prey and carrion.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: As the dominant predator on the island, {@i Hatzegopteryx} would have had little to fear from other animals once fully grown. It was likely a relatively solitary animal that nested on the ground and may have had at least some level of parental care, although to what degree is still speculative. Combat between {@i Hatzegopteryx} may have involved striking each other with their jaws or side-on blows using their powerful necks.

We recommend that {@i Hatzegopteryx} be played as an animal with little fear that would be highly curious of new creatures or objects in its territory. It would not hesitate to strike potential prey, including most humanoids. When faced with a party, it may choose to snatch and swallow a single target, before simply flying away. This makes it a particularly lethal threat to players. It can be portrayed moving in a bobbing, ungainly fashion (perhaps similar to a marabou stork).

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Azhdarchid pterosaurs are a diverse group, with members ranging from relatively small animals (10 ft. wingspans) to giants like {@creature Quetzalcoatlus|PartneredDDDoD} and {@creature Hatzegopteryx|PartneredDDDoD} (>33 ft. wingspans). The group first arose around the middle of the Cretaceous and survived right up until the end-Cretaceous extinction. In this time, they spread globally and azhdarchids (or possible azhdarchids) are known from every continent except Antarctica.

{@i "Ig-wan-oh-don"} {@b (iguana tooth)}

One of the more common dinosaurs we encountered was those large ornithopods, {@i Iguanodon}. Easily recognisable by their large thumb spikes and grumpy attitude, they were a staple prey for all of the big predators in this area but rarely moved alone. If you wanted to pick a fight with one, you'd usually end up outnumbered. Fine if you're a big predatory dinosaur, less fine if you're a lil' adventurer. Despite their moderate size compared to other dinosaurs, these thin's were still pretty dangerous when they heft their weight around.

{@i Iguanodon} is an iguanodontian ornithischian dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous (126-120 million years ago) of Europe. The second dinosaur to be described and named; it is the most famous example of how our understanding of dinosaurs has changed over time.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Iguanodon} was a large ornithopod, measuring up to 36 ft. long and weighing 4-5 tonnes. Like hadrosaurs, it had long robust hindlimbs and shorter forelimbs. It was capable of running on two legs but spent most of its time on all fours. One of its most distinctive features was a thumb-like spike modified from the first digit on each forelimb. When first discovered in 1830, this thumb spike was mistakenly assumed to be a nasal horn. That interpretation was ubiquitous and was even incorporated into the life-sized sculptures of {@i Iguanodon} at Crystal Palace, which still stand today. Since its identification as a thumb spike, the function of this structure has been debated. Most researchers now agree that it was used for combat, probably more often against other {@i Iguanodon} rather than predators.

{@i Iguanodon} takes its namesake from its teeth, which are superficially similar to modern iguanas. Its head was large, elongated, and tipped with a well-developed beak. Its slightly broad snout suggests that it may have been a generalist herbivore and, like {@creature Bolong|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@book The Yixian Formation|PartneredDDDoD|3|Bolong}), was capable of chewing. Its diet may have included conifers, ferns, cycads, and early flowering plants, and it could effectively process tough plant material by chewing it.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Iguanodon} has been found in mass mortality assemblages (bones of many individuals found in one spot). It's thought that these assemblages were formed either during a flash flood or while a group was crossing a river. In any case, these indicate that {@i Iguanodon} moved in large herds, similar to bison or zebra.

We suggest that {@i Iguanodon} be played as a highly social animal, moving in large herds constantly courting, squabbling, and vocalising. When disturbed or threatened, a herd should stampede away, running on two legs. Only individuals who end up isolated or those who can't keep up should turn to fight their attackers. The stampeding mass of {@i Iguanodon} should be a danger in and of itself, trampling smaller creatures. We also suggest that {@i Iguanodon} migrates in these herds, following a well-established route and even possibly grouping with other species. These mass migrations can be followed by predators that will pick off weaker animals.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Iguanodon} has a complex phylogenetic history. Traditionally, it was considered a member of the Iguanodontidae, a group of iguanodontians which were the sister group to the hadrosaurs. However, that became a 'wastebasket group', meaning that similar animals with poorly known phylogenetic relationships were 'dumped' in there without much evidence.

A series of reviews starting in the 2000s argued that many animals thought to belong to this family were part of the Hadrosauroidea (hadrosaurs and their relatives). Currently, Iguanodontidae is not a well-supported group and researchers are not in agreement if it exists or if {@i Iguanodon} should simply be seen as a basal iguanodontian, related to but outside of Hadrosauroidea.

{@i "Jur-rah-ven-ah-tor"} {@b (Jura mountains hunter)}

The third night that we camped along the riverbank, I was on first watch. After a few hours, I could feel myself noddin' off, so wandered down to the river's edge to splash myself with some water. It were deathly quiet, bar the chirpin' of crickets. As I crouched down into the water, I saw the shine of a tiny pair of eyes off in the reeds a few feet ahead. It was some kind of small theropod pluckin' minnows out of the water. I took a step forward to try and get a closer look, but the slosh of me foot spooked it, and it darted off into the night.

{@i Juravenator} was a very small theropod dinosaur from the Late Jurassic Francoinian Jura (151 million years ago) of Germany. The holotype (diagnostic specimen) is based on a juvenile, meaning that we have a limited understanding of its adult form.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: The only fossil of {@i Juravenator} is an exceptionally well-preserved tiny immature individual at just 30 inches long. It was a bipedal theropod with unusually large eyes. These could suggest that it was nocturnal but might also simply be a result of its immaturity, as many young animals have relatively large eyes (neoteny). {@i Juravenator} had a mouth full of sharp teeth and almost certainly fed on small animals like insects, fish, and other smaller vertebrates. Alternatively, an adult may have fed it.

{@i Juravenator} was first interpreted as a scaly animal, as a patch of preserved skin on the tail appeared featherless with scales. However, further research including high-resolution CT scans showed that this skin actually had a thin covering of feathers, although it may have been sparser than in other feathered theropods. Newer research also reinterpreted these scales as a by-product of fat decay, suggesting that the animal had a fatty skin layer. Another recent study argued instead that these were indeed scales and were similar to the sensory scales of crocodiles, suggesting a semi-aquatic wading lifestyle (although this is not well supported by the rest of the anatomy). Ultimately, research is ongoing and many questions still remain unanswered about {@i Juravenator}.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: The limited information available for {@i Juravenator} and the myriad interpretations of its fossil leave a lot of room for speculation about how this animal behaved. Here we take a mixed approach, including several elements from the studies mentioned above.

We suggest playing a baby {@i Juravenator} as a highly skittish creature that is largely non-hostile and prefers to flee from danger. It may be attracted to the light of a campfire or the smell of food, and could be relatively easy to befriend if fed. The behaviour of an adult {@i Juravenator} is unknown, but perhaps it could be a more aggressive predator.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: As the only specimen of {@i Juravenator} is a juvenile, its phylogenetic placement is particularly difficult. Originally, {@i Juravenator} was considered a compsognathid, closely related to the small theropod Compsognathus from Germany. However, it has since then been re-placed multiple times, including in Maniraptora (see {@book Velociraptor|PartneredDDDoD|7|Velociraptor}) and even Megalosauroidea (see {@book Megalosaurus|PartneredDDDoD|7|Megalosaurus}). The anatomy of animals usually changes as they mature, and we can only estimate what an adult {@i Juravenator} may have looked like, let alone firmly establish its place in the tree of life.

{@i "Kent-trow-sore-us"} {@b (prickle reptile)}

Over the rollin' hills and rocky shrubland, we spied some medium-sized spikey-armoured dinosaurs. They was pretty calm 'n largely uninterested in us, but we kept our distance nonetheless. The front half of 'em was covered with broad plates standin' on end, but the back half and tail had massive bony spikes. Can't imagine a big predator would fancy chompin' on that–seems like a pretty good deterrent.

{@i Kentrosaurus} is a relatively small stegosaur from the Late Jurassic (165 million years ago) Tendaguru Formation of Tanzania. A close relative of Gigantspinosaurus and the famous Stegosaurus, it is well known for having a mix of defensive plates and spines along its back.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Kentrosaurus} was approximately 15 ft. long and weighed up to 1.5 tonnes, making it relatively small for a stegosaur. Its morphology was typical for the group with a robust body, long tail, low shoulders, tall hips, a small head with a sharp keratinous beak, and large osteoderms (bones embedded in its skin). It had a huge backwards pointing spike on each shoulder, and two parallel rows of osteoderms along its back that transition from plates to large spikes after the 7th pair, and a double pair of spikes on the end of its tail (thagomizers).

{@i Kentrosaurus}' narrow and pointed beak suggests that it was a selective herbivore, picking out lush plant growth at ground level. This would have allowed it to feed without competing with other much taller herbivores from the Tendaguru Formation, such as {@creature Giraffatitan|PartneredDDDoD}. Some stegosaurs are known to have swallowed pebbles (gastroliths) that aided in breaking up plant material and {@i Kentrosaurus} probably did as well, allowing it to consume tougher stems.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Kentrosaurus}' armaments pose many questions; were they for social display or combat, and how could animals like this mate? The latter is hypothesised to have required extremely elongate male genitalia, however, the former can be investigated mechanically. There is strong evidence that {@i Kentrosaurus}' tail was a functional weapon as it was powerfully muscled, could be swung rapidly, and was capable of wide motions in a 180-degree arc. This, combined with its formidable defences, suggests that these weapons were used for intraspecific (same species) fighting, and there is evidence that {@i Kentrosaurus} lived in herds. Nevertheless, these tails were still used to defend it from attackers, as thagomizer wounds (from a different stegosaur) have been identified in some Allosaurus.

We suggest {@i Kentrosaurus} be portrayed as a gregarious (grouping) animal, moving in small herds between feeding spots. When encountered by a party, they should be alert but not necessarily aggressive, with the dominant animal making its presence clear and visible. Once a party gets too close, the herd will probably move away, relying on their defences to protect them, and only stand and fight if continually harassed.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Kentrosaurus} is a member of the Stegosauridae, a family which includes Stegosaurus and Gigantspinosaurus. Stegosauridae is part of the larger group Thyreophora, which alongside stegosaurs includes the ankylosaurs such as {@creature Zuul|PartneredDDDoD} and other related animals like {@creature Scelidosaurus|PartneredDDDoD}. All members are herbivores and have bony weaponry or armour embedded in their skin. The Thyreophora arose in the Early Jurassic (200 million years ago) and were highly successful, colonising every continent until the end-Cretaceous extinction.

{@i "Clo-bi-oh-don"} {@b (Cage tooth)}

This whole area was filled with lil' fish-snatching pterosaurs. They kept their distance from us–I guess they're used to being plucked off of the ground by small predators. Still, beautiful creatures to see flyin' and fascinatin' to observe perchin' on rocks. They fed by flyin' low over the water and quickly dippin' their heads in, nabbin' unaware fish. Nifty stuff.
{@i Klobiodon} is a Jurassic (166 million years old) European pterosaur found in the Taynton Limestone Formation.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Klobiodon} is only known from an isolated jaw, but we can make reasonable deductions about its morphology, as it is very similar to {@i Rhamphorynchus}, albeit larger with a wingspan of at least 6.5 ft. Its wings would have been long and thin with a broadly similar silhouette to a gull, and it likely had a long tail tipped by a triangular vane. {@i Klobiodon}'s most distinctive feature was a set of robust protruding spike-like teeth that were longer towards the tip of the jaw. These formed an interlocking cage that helped grab slippery wriggling prey (often called a "fish trap").

The Taynton Limestone Formation was laid down in a coastal environment with influence from both fresh and saltwater. This resulted in a diverse assemblage of wildlife including insects, ammonites, numerous fish, early mammals, crocodiles, dinosaurs, turtles, and, of course, pterosaurs.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Klobiodon} was a near-shore hunter, eating fish, squid, and other surface-dwelling aquatic prey. Groups would likely congregate around the edges of seas, lagoons, and estuaries to nest or socialise. They would have been skittish if {@status surprised|XPHB} but may have been willing to mob threats that entered their territory.

We recommend {@i Klobiodon} be played in a similar manner to modern herring gulls, albeit much larger and with a much more vicious bite. Small numbers of {@i Klobiodon} can be easily dispersed, but large groups may mob intruding players to drive them away from nesting grounds or to steal food. When incorporating its magical rules, parties in near-shore environments run the risk of wandering into a camouflaged flock.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Klobiodon} was part of the Rhamphorhynchidae group, which were an extremely successful group of pterosaurs that arose in the Middle Jurassic (160 million years ago) and survived until the Late Jurassic (148 million years ago). They spread across Laurasia (the modern Northern Hemisphere), with some additional new material recently found in South America.

{@i "Coo-lin-dah-drome-e-us"} {@b (Kulinda runner)}

One of the thin's I love most about our journeys is when we catch a glimpse of an animal and it doesn't know we're watchin' it. We get to see thin's that no one else has ever seen. We spotted one lil' group of ornithopod dinosaurs in a small forest clearin', preparin' to make nests. They were kickin' back the leaf litter and usin' their lil' beaks to pick up the remainin' leaves. Covered in soft downy fuzz, they were the cutest lil' critters you could imagine, peepin' away at each other as they squabbled for space.

{@i Kulindadromeus} is a small bipedal neornithiscian (a diverse clade of ornithiscian dinosaurs) from the Middle Jurassic (166-168 million years ago) Ukureyskaya Formation of Russia. {@i Kulindadromeus} is an important species as it shows the earliest evidence for filaments in a non-theropod dinosaur.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Kulindadromeus} was fairly typical for early neornithischians as it walked on two legs and had short forelimbs. It was relatively small at 3-5 ft. long and weighed about 4.5 lb. It had a toothless snout with a keratinous sheath, giving it a short beak, and a reduced number of teeth at the back of its mouth. It was herbivorous and likely fed on ferns, although may have supplemented its diet with insects. {@i Kulindadromeus} possessed a combination of scales on its arms, underbelly, legs and tail, and feather-like filaments across the rest of its body. These were the earliest possible feather-like structures identified in a non-theropod dinosaur.

{@i Kulindadromeus} was found in the Ukureyskaya Formation of Russia, which was deposited in a freshwater lake environment with a nearby volcano. The formation contains numerous fossils of plants and insects, but does not have a large vertebrate assemblage. Little is known about the other dinosaurs from this environment beyond sparse evidence of an unknown medium sized theropod and unidentified ornithischians.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Kulindadromeus} would have likely behaved similarly to many small herbivores. It would have been quite skittish, constantly checking for potential predators. Little is known about how social it was, but small and medium herbivores tend to live in groups for safety.

We recommend playing {@i Kulindadromeus} as an alert animal that will flee if startled. If a group flees, they should scatter in different directions rather than as a unit. It may also be rather curious and, if unthreatened, may approach the edges of camps in search of discarded food.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Kulindadromeus} was a primitive neornithischian. This was a varied group that appeared in the Early-Middle Jurassic (166-168 million years ago) and included a variety of dinosaurs from the bipedal, tusked heterodontosaurs, to giant "duck-billed" hadrosaurs, and horned ceratopsians. The group was so successful that by the Late Cretaceous they were the most common and diverse herbivorous dinosaurs.

{@i "Lep-toe-neck-tees"} {@b (Slender Swimmer)}

After a couple days at sea, I'd become restless in the night and decided to sit up on deck for a few hours. The calm breeze blowin' and rockin' boat was pretty soothin'. I noticed the sound of rollin' splashes starboard and decided to take a peek. The waters were dully lit by bioluminescent jellies and in the murk, I could see several large dolphin-like shapes dartin' between the shadows and occasionally snappin' up a jelly or two. They were ichthyosaurs, feedin' in the moonlight and unbothered by our presence.

{@i Leptonectes} is an ichthyosaurid from the Late Triassic to Early Jurassic (205-185 million years ago) of Europe. It was a fairly typical ichthyosaur, but is one of a handful of taxa that have specimens preserved with unborn embryos still within the mothers.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Leptonectes} was a medium to large sized (10-20 ft. in length) ichthyosaur, which are a group of fully-aquatic marine reptiles. Its morphology was typical of ichthyosaurs, with a fusiform (spindle-like) body, triangular dorsal fin, four paddle-like limbs, a crescent-shaped tail, and extremely elongated slender jaws. {@i Leptonectes}' jaws were lined with uniform conical pointy teeth and its mouth curved downwards at the back, which gave the animal a frowning appearance. Its highly modified forelimbs were large and broad paddles, while the hind paddles were much smaller. Its tail bent sharply downwards at the tip, forming the bottom half of a crescent shape, with the upper half formed by a soft tissue fluke. Overall, {@i Leptonectes} would have had a similar profile to a large dolphin or shark.

Different ichthyosaur species exploited niche partitioning, whereby concurrent organisms utilise different resources (or the same resources in different ways) which prevented or reduced competition, increasing survivability. Some fed on fish, turtles, ammonites, and possibly even birds, whereas others like {@i Leptonectes} may have specialised in soft bodied organisms like jellyfish and squid. This is suggested by their stomach contents and the shape of their teeth. In all cases, the ichthyosaurs were marine animals and could not leave the water.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: If {@i Leptonectes} was a specialist in hunting squid, octopuses, and jellyfish, it may have been most active at night when these animals most frequently visit the upper water column to feed. Little is known about the social behaviour of ichthyosaurs, but we can make some inferences based on the number and size of their preserved unborn embryos. A specimen described in 2012 was found with two relatively large embryos, whereas other species of ichthyosaur have been found with up to ten smaller ones. Assuming that no embryos are missing, it's possible that {@i Leptonectes} followed a similar strategy as the {@creature Bahariyan Polycotylid|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@book The Bahariya Formation|PartneredDDDoD|4|Bahariyan Polycotylid}), investing more time into fewer infants in order to increase their individual chances of survival.

We suggest that {@i Leptonectes} be played as a semi-solitary animal, with females living alongside their young and potentially forming small maternity pods. They should be quick to attack potential threats and may be curious if a party enters their territory on a boat. As they may be more active at night, this means players run a greater risk of unknowingly encountering them in low light. Males should be more solitary but also more sedate, only becoming dangerous if they feel their space has been invaded or their food source disturbed.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Leptonectes} is a member of the Ichthyosauridae. This is an exceptionally successful group of marine reptiles that arose in the Late Triassic and diversified rapidly. While the classic ichthyosaur is dolphin-like in appearance, they had a variety of forms and included the largest aquatic reptiles known. The group survived multiple extinction events and remained diverse up until the Cretaceous, where they are thought to have been pushed to extinction by rapid environmental change.
