{@i "Loo-doh-dack-tal-us"} {@b (play finger)}

We finally had a chance to take a decent rest near the lakeside. It was a beautiful day, so I took me pencil'n'pad out to sketch the view and some of the dartin' pterosaurs. They were soaring just above the water, dippin' their heads in as they go to snatch up fish. Those long pointed teeth look like the perfect fit for it. I was half-way through me sketch when a few of 'em took interest. One of the blighters snatched the pencil right out of my hands! Flew off and dropped it in the lake when it realised it couldn't eat it, the bastard. Good thing I always keep spares.
{@i Ludodactylus} is a relatively large anhanguerid pterosaur, slightly bigger than {@creature Tupandactylus|PartneredDDDoD}.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Ludodactylus} was a large pterosaur with a wingspan of approximately 13 ft. Like other anhanguerids, it possessed low convex crests on its upper and lower jaws, but uniquely, it also had a tall Pteranodon-like crest jutting out of the back of its skull, making its head highly ornamented.

Anhanguerids are well known to be piscivorous (fish-eating), and {@i Ludodactylus} had elongate teeth that formed a "fish trap" cage at the end of its snout, an adaptation to trap fleeing slippery prey. It would likely have hunted by flying low over the water's surface, plucking fish on the wing, or perhaps wading through shallows with its snout dipped in the water, waiting for fish to come too close.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Ludodactylus} would have primarily been associated with water and are unlikely to have travelled far inland, unless following a large river system or migrating to new coastal regions. Large oceanic pterosaurs have been known to form sizable colonies and it is possible that {@i Ludodactylus} also formed nesting colonies.

An individual {@i Ludodactylus} should be hesitant to approach players unless drawn by food, in which case it is likely to become more aggressive. Groups of {@i Ludodactylus} may mob players in a similar manner to modern herring gulls (albeit much, much bigger). They lacked the tools to hunt and devour anything other than Tiny prey, so would not try to hunt Small or larger party members. Nevertheless, they were certainly capable of delivering an extremely nasty bite. If a party encounters a colony, particularly one that is nesting, the animals should be much more aggressive. They would threaten intruders with raucous calls and displays before attacking, with individuals dive-bombing enemies from above with teeth or, worse, vomit and faeces.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: As mentioned above, {@i Ludodactylus} is an anhanguerid pterosaur, which are a group that are typically characterised by crests on their snouts and had a global distribution in the Early-Late Cretaceous. They are part of the larger pterosaur family Ornithocheiroidia, which includes the toothless Pteranodonia (like {@i Pteranodon}). Ornithocheiroidia (like {@i Ornithocheirus}) are distant relatives of the giant azhdarchids (such as {@creature Quetzalcoatlus|PartneredDDDoD}, in {@book The Rest of the Alphabet|PartneredDDDoD|7|Quetzalcoatlus}).

entries.name: Moments in Time
entries: We usually develop our interpretations of the lives of extinct animals by examining and interpreting their fossils. These interpretations can vary depending on current evidence or researchers' differing opinions. However, sometimes we find "smoking gun" evidence, where exceptional fossils preserve an interaction irrefutably. {@i Ludodactylus} shows one such "smoking gun", with the original specimen fossilised with a frayed yucca tree leaf protruding through its jaws. This animal clearly died from this injury, as the leaf pierced through its mouth, preventing it from feeding and likely causing an infection. The frayed edge indicates that the animal tried to dislodge the leaf by scraping it against the ground. It probably snatched the leaf out of the water thinking it was a fish, a misjudgement that modern seabirds still make today.

entries: Frey, E., Martill, D.M., and Buchy, M.C. 2003. A new crested ornithocheirid from the Lower Cretaceous of northeastern Brazil and the unusual death of an unusual pterosaur. Geological Society, London, Special Publications, 217(1), 55-63.
Isles, T.E., 2009. The socio-sexual behaviour of extant archosaurs: implications for understanding dinosaur behaviour. Historical Biology, 21(3-4), 139-214.

Veldmeijer, A.J., Signore, M., and Bucci, E., 2007. Predator-prey interaction of Brazilian Cretaceous toothed pterosaurs: a case example. In Elewa, A.M.T. (Ed.). Predation in Organisms. Springer, Berlin, Heidelberg, 295-308.
Witton, M.P. 2018. Pterosaurs in Mesozoic food webs: a review of fossil evidence. Geological Society, London, Special Publications, 455(1), 7-23.
"MAG-YAHR-OH-SORE-US" {@b (MAGYAR REPTILE)}

As we pushed through the undergrowth, keepin' outa sight of the sky, we encountered dozens of strange island species, includin' many that were miniature versions of their mainland cousins. One of the most strikin' examples we came across were some titanosaurs. Hidden between the trees were lumberin' longnecks, usually towerin' over the treeline–but these ones were about the size of a horse, albeit much longer. Pretty calm thin's really. I guess they didn't have many land-based predators botherin' 'em in the forest.

{@i Magyarosaurus} was an exceptionally small titanosaur, a group famous for including the largest land animals ever to live. It is a dramatic example of the effect of living in a restricted environment, as it is one of the smallest sauropods discovered.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Magyarosaurus} was not only a modestly-sized dinosaur in general, but one of the smallest sauropods. It was tiny in comparison to its giant relatives like {@creature Paralititan|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@book The Bahariya Formation|PartneredDDDoD|4|Paralititan}), at a measly 20 ft. long and about 1 tonne in weight. It was so small that initially all remains were assumed to have been from juveniles, however research in 2010 provided strong evidence that the animals were indeed simply tiny adults (at least by sauropod standards). This makes {@i Magyarosaurus} one of the most compelling examples of insular dwarfism among the Hațeg Island fauna.

As with all sauropods, one of {@i Magyarosaurus}' most distinctive features was its long neck. The function and posture of these necks has been the subject of debate for many years. Current consensus supports the idea that sauropods held their necks aloft, allowing them to feed higher than other herbivores, or swung their necks low over a wide area, allowing them to browse on low lying plants without moving. While small, {@i Magyarosaurus} likely specialised in stripping leaves from tall trees and would still have been able to feed at a much higher level than competing hadrosaurs, ankylosaurs, or rhabdodonts.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Although tiny, it is likely that {@i Magyarosaurus} behaved much like other titanosaurs. It would have lived in a herd, constantly moving to find new food. While it lacked the sheer strength of its relatives, an adult {@i Magyarosaurus} would still have been difficult for any ground predator on the island to tackle as it was still a large animal, and had a hide studded with osteoderms (bony structures in the skin). Juveniles were able to feed themselves from hatching, but would have been exceptionally vulnerable to predation, given their relatively slow speed. They may have relied on camouflage to hide from predators, keeping to dense undergrowth. It is almost certain that the giant azhdarchid pterosaur {@creature Hatzegopteryx|PartneredDDDoD} hunted these hatchlings.

We suggest that {@i Magyarosaurus} be played as an animal always slowly on the move and rarely found alone. While not much heavier than a large cow, it is still a powerful animal that could easily injure or kill humanoids. In comparison to other sauropods, it should be more wary and more aware of its surroundings, yet its island isolation should make it less cautious of unfamiliar threats. Like {@creature Zalmoxes|PartneredDDDoD}, we suggest {@i Magyarosaurus} would fit well into the role of agricultural livestock.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Magyarosaurus} is a titanosaur, a group known for its giants like Argentinosaurus and {@creature Paralititan|PartneredDDDoD}. {@i Magyarosaurus} is part of a subfamily of small to medium sized animals called the Saltasauridae. The saltasaurs were a successful group with a near global biogeographical range.

entries.name: References
entries: Csiki, Z. 1999. New evidence of armoured titanosaurids in the Late Cretaceous. {@i Magyarosaurus dacus} from the Hateg Basin (Romania). {@i ORYCTOS}, {@b 2}, 93-99.

{@i "Mass-toe-don-sore-us"} {@b (nipple tooth reptile)}

The swamps are a particularly dangerous place to venture. Not only are they slow to wade through, but many nasty predators hide in the murky waters. One of the scarier ones is a giant amphibian that lies in wait, fully submerged and totally indistinguishable from the mud its squalorin' in. Those who have the misfortune to step too close are met with an explosion of tusked fury–water flyin' everywhere. Ambushes like this were painfully common and we lost a few good adventurers over the course of the weeks spent there.

{@i Mastodonsaurus} is an enormous amphibian from the Middle Triassic (245 million years ago) of Europe. It was one of the largest amphibians in the fossil record and superficially looked like a cross between a frog and a crocodile.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Mastodonsaurus} was huge for an amphibian, measuring up to 20 ft. long. It had an elongate body with a powerful tail and reduced, sprawling limbs. It had a very large triangular-shaped head, measuring 5 ft. long in the largest adults. Its eyes were on the top of its skull, rather than the side, and its jaws were lined with a double row of sharp conical teeth, as well as two tusks on the lower jaw that stuck out through holes in the upper jaw.

{@i Mastodonsaurus} was a powerful aquatic carnivore and, based on the position of its eyes, likely ambushed prey from below. Given its size, it probably ate a variety of other animals, presumably anything small enough for it to swallow. This idea is supported by tooth marks on other amphibian fossils that appear to be from {@i Mastodonsaurus}, although these could be the result of scavenging. Bite marks on {@i Mastodonsaurus} itself suggest that it was predated upon by large terrestrial carnivores, perhaps while trapped in a drying-up pool.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Mastodonsaurus} likely spent much of its time unmoving at the bottom of rivers, swamps, and pools of water, hiding in wait beneath mud. When prey came within range, it would rush forward with its mouth agape, sucking the prey towards it. {@i Mastodonsaurus} would then snap down, piercing the prey with its teeth and tusks. If a terrestrial animal was drinking on the waters edge, it may have slowly moved into position before rushing it and attempting to drag it back into the water. It's unlikely {@i Mastodonsaurus} was a social animal and they probably lived solitary lives, apart from coming together to mate. It would have spent as little time on land as possible, only leaving the water to move to new hunting grounds or find a mate.

We suggest {@i Mastodonsaurus} be played essentially as a crocodile-like animal, willing to lie in wait for prey for hours or even days. While able to attack creatures on land, it should be cautious of leaving the water and will quickly retreat after lunging out at prey. It should be solitary, although a party may encounter multiple {@i Mastodonsaurus} along a given river or waterway, evenly spaced in their own territories.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Mastodonsaurus} is a member of the Mastodonsauridae, a group of large seemingly piscivorous (fish-feeding) amphibians, many of which had prominent tusks. They were a successful group surviving from the Middle Triassic (250 million years ago) until the border of the Jurassic (199 million years ago). Mastodonsaurids were part of a wider order of amphibians called the Temnospondyli. These were giant amphibious carnivores with a global range that appeared in the Middle Triassic (220 million years ago) and persisted for 100 million years, up until the Early Cretaceous (120 million years ago).

entries.name: References
entries: Moser, M., and Schoch, R. 2007. Revision of the type material and nomenclature of {@i Mastodonsaurus giganteus} (Jaeger)(Temnospondyli) from the Middle Triassic of Germany. {@i Palaeontology}, {@b 50(5)}, 1245-1266.

Schoch, R.R., Seegis, D. and Mujal, E., 2022. The Middle Triassic vertebrate deposits of Kupferzell (Germany): Palaeoenvironmental evolution of complex ecosystems. {@i Palaeogeography, Palaeoclimatology, Palaeoecology}, {@b 603}, 111181.
Witzmann, F., and Gassner, T. 2008. Metoposaurid and mastodonsaurid stereospondyls from the Triassic–Jurassic boundary of Portugal. {@i Alcheringa}, {@b 32(1)}, 37-51.
{@i "Meg-ah-low-sore-us"} {@b (Great reptile)}

This is a beast that I'd read lots about in the ancient libraries of my university–the first dinosaur fossil ever described by scientists. When we first sighted it, I was all giddy with excitement. But, nothin' prepared me for how magnificent and deadly it was. It attacked without warnin' and unleashed a flurry of claws, teeth, kicks, and tail swipes. We were able to fend it off with some cold steel, but our cleric had a hearty job of healin' us up afterwards.

{@i Megalosaurus} was a medium sized theropod from the Middle Jurassic (166 million years ago) Taynton Limestone and Chipping Norton formations of England. {@i Megalosaurus} is one of the most famous dinosaurs as it was the first taxon to be formally described.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Megalosaurus}' fossils are incomplete, but it is thought to have been approximately 30 ft. long and weighed between 1.5–2 tonnes. While smaller than later giant theropods, it was still one of the largest carnivorous dinosaurs of the Jurassic. Overall, it was a robust animal, with thick legs and short powerful forelimbs. It had a robust skull that was relatively low and long, filled with curved blade-like teeth.

As the biggest and heaviest carnivore known from the Middle Jurassic of England, {@i Megalosaurus} may have been the arch-predator of its habitat. Its heavy build suggests that it was perhaps analogous to tyrannosaurs, overpowering prey rather than engaging in fast chases. The Taynton Limestone and Chipping Norton formations were both deposited in sub-tropical lagoons, conditions that attract a variety of animals, all of which would have been potential prey for {@i Megalosaurus}. However, it may also have fed on fish or aquatic reptiles pulled from the lagoon.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Based on the shape of its jugal (cheek bone), {@i Megalosaurus}' eyes were probably on the sides of its head, similar to {@creature Big Al|PartneredDDDoD|Allosaurus} (see {@book Big Al in Pledgers' Custom Dinosaurs|PartneredDDDoD|8|Big Al}). This suggests that it chased prey down over relatively long distances, rather than ambushing over short distances. Ambushing requires binocular vision for bursts of speed, but chasing allows a predator to determine distance by swinging its head. Like most large carnivores, it would have also been an opportunistic scavenger, using its size to bully other carnivores away from a carcass.

We suggest {@i Megalosaurus} be played as a patient animal that patrols a territory. It could patrol a watering hole and take advantage of desperate, dehydrated animals trying to drink, charging them. However, large modern land predators spend most of their time resting, and {@i Megalosaurus} almost certainly did the same. It is more likely that a party will encounter a dozing {@i Megalosaurus} than an actively hunting one, although it will take the opportunity to strike if someone wanders too close.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Megalosaurus} was one of the largest members of the Megalosauridae. This was a group of small-medium sized theropods with relatively low but elongated skulls that are primarily known from Europe, with some occurrences in the Americas and Africa. Interestingly, within the larger group Megalosauroidea, their closest relatives appear to be the highly derived and unusual spinosaurids like {@creature Spinosaurus|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@book The Bahariya Formation|PartneredDDDoD|4|Spinosaurus}). Most megalosaurs are from Jurassic formations, although some did survive into the Late Cretaceous (93 million years ago).

entries.name: The First of Many
entries: The first record of {@i Megalosaurus} was the end of an isolated fragmentary femur (sadly now lost) described in 1763 by Brookes. He gave it the comedic name of Scrotum humanum due to its unfortunate shape. Later in the 1700s, a partial jaw was discovered that was eventually named {@i Megalosaurus} by William Buckland in 1824. It was considered to be some kind of lizard or crocodile and in 1842 Richard Owen erected the group Dinosauria to house it, {@book Iguanodon|PartneredDDDoD|7|Iguanodon}, and {@i Hylaeosaurus}. While {@i Megalosaurus} would ultimately be eclipsed by the more spectacular dinosaurs of the American fossil rush, it remains one of the most historically important taxa and sculptures of its original reconstruction still stand in The Crystal Palace, London.

entries.name: References

Buckland, W. 1824. XXI.—Notice on the {@i Megalosaurus} or great Fossil Lizard of Stonesfield. {@i Transactions of the Geological Society of London}, {@b 1(2)}, 390-396.

Howlett, E.A., Kennedy, W.J., Powell, H.P., and Torrens, H.S. 2017. New light on the history of {@i Megalosaurus}, the great lizard of Stonesfield. {@i Archives of Natural History}, {@b 44(1)}, 82-102.
{@i "My-crow-wrap-tor"} {@b (Small plunderer)}

The ancient forest 'round us was filled with the chirpin' and squawkin' of various dinosaurs, radiatin' from the trees above. Among the foliage, I glimpsed the shimmerin' of iridescent feathers streakin' through the sky. A tiny, but brilliant, four-winged dinosaur soared down from above, landin' on a branch just a few feet away. Remarkable!

{@i Microraptor} is a small, highly specialised member of the Dromaeosauridae. Its most distinctive feature was its well-developed flight feathers on all four limbs, making it the first four-winged dinosaur known. This trait may be present in other dromaeosaurs, but {@i Microraptor} was the first animal with unequivocal evidence of four wings.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Microraptor} was extremely small, one of the smallest non-avian theropods at only 2.5 ft. long, weighing only 1-3 lb., and with a wingspan of about 3 ft. Its long tail ended in a feathery fan, and it possessed long flight feathers on both its forelimbs and hindlimbs. Studies into dinosaur colour suggest that it might have been black with an iridescent sheen like modern starlings.

{@i Microraptor} was a predatory arboreal (tree dwelling) animal, hunting in dense forests. It could fly, although not particularly well by modern bird standards. It likely darted from tree to tree, jumping from one and flapping somewhat awkwardly or gliding to another.

{@i Microraptor} had a non-specialized carnivorous diet, eating whatever it could find. This included insects, small lizards, small mammals, birds, other non-avian dinosaurs, and fish. It is known to have swallowed small prey whole, likely dropping down from branches above, surprising prey.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: The four wings of {@i Microraptor} likely made it a clumsy walker. It spent the vast majority of its time in trees, gliding and flying from branch to branch. It should rarely leave the trees but can be seen by players hunting in the canopy. As a dromaeosaur, {@i Microraptor} was probably relatively intelligent for its size.

We recommend playing this creature as an inquisitive hunter that may follow a party, taking advantage of them distracting prey. This may lead a particularly curious {@i Microraptor} to become relatively docile around the party and may allow an opportunity for a wily party member to tame it.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Microraptor} was a dromaeosaurid but was not closely related to the more famous {@creature Velociraptor|PartneredDDDoD} or {@creature Utahraptor|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@book The Rest of the Alphabet|PartneredDDDoD|7}). Instead, it was part of a group of smaller dromaeosaurs currently only known from China. Many of these animals had a similar morphology to {@i Microraptor} and it has been suggested they may also have been able to fly or glide.

entries.name: Fossil Fakes
entries: When the first {@i Microraptor} fossil was discovered between 1997-1999, it was illegally smuggled out of China and amalgamated into a chimera. This is a practice that some unscrupulous fossil dealers undertake to try to increase the value of their fossils. Chimeras and improper fossil collecting methods not only risk the loss of valuable scientific information, but they also give private collectors (even those who act legally and morally) a bad reputation.

The original specimen, informally called "Archaeoraptor", attracted a lot of media attention for its excellent preservation, but controversy quickly arose due to the illegal handling of the fossil and its suspicious 'cobbled-together' appearance. When finally examined, it became apparent that the fossil was actually three distinct animals that were each a new species. The tail-end was eventually described as the remarkable {@i Microraptor}.

Hone, D.W., Dececchi, A.T., Sullivan, C., Xing, X. and Larsson, H.C. 2022. Generalist diet of {@i Microraptor zhaoianus} included mammals. {@i Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology}, e2144337.

O'Connor, J., Zhou, Z., and Xu, X. 2011. Additional specimen of {@i Microraptor} provides unique evidence of dinosaurs preying on birds. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America, 108(49), 19662-19665.
Xing, X., Zhinghe, Z., Xiaolin, W., Xuewen, K., Fucheng, Z., and Xiangke, D. 2003. Four-winged dinosaurs from China. {@i Nature}. {@b 421(6921)}, 335-340.
{@i "Mm-nya-ma-wah-mm-too-ka"} {@b (beast of the Mtuka river drainage)}

Among our travels we had seen myriad behaviours of various dinosaurs, includin' complex matin' rituals. None were so excitin' as these huge sauropods. They pranced around each other with uncharacteristic grace in a wonderful' ballet that had no doubt been practiced hundreds of times. When we encounter such a thin', we stay to watch but ensure never to interfere. That policy gifted us their complete matin' ritual and it was well worth our patience.

{@i Mnyamawamtuka} is an Early Cretaceous (110 million years ago) titanosaur from the Galula Formation in Tanzania. Known from a single immature specimen, it is an important fossil for understanding sauropod diversification.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: The {@i Mnyamawamtuka} fossil is from a relatively small sauropod, 25 ft. long and weighing about 1.5 tonnes. Like all sauropods, it had hollow bones filled with air sacs (pneumatisation) that greatly reduced its weight and gave it unidirectional breathing (air flowing through the lungs and air sacs in one direction). As the bones weren't completely fused when the animal died, it is likely it was immature. In many ways it was a typical titanosaur with large columnar limbs, shovel-like teeth, and a long neck and tail. The middle vertebrae in the tail had an unusual heart-shaped cross-section and it is speculated to have had bony osteoderms (bones embedded in the skin) dotting its hide.

Titanosaurs were all herbivores and, based on its teeth, {@i Mnyamawamtuka} likely had a similar diet to its relatives. This would have included ferns, conifers, cycads, and early grasses. It may have competed with other sauropods for food, as they are one of the few dinosaurs known from the Galula Formation, although their apparent abundance is likely a result of biases in this site's type of fossilisation.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Little is known of {@i Mnyamawamtuka} and its behaviour, but based on other studies we suggest it behaved in a similar fashion to its larger relatives like {@creature Paralititan|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@book The Bahariya Formation|PartneredDDDoD|4|Paralititan}), with young animals growing up separately from adults before joining a herd when large enough to avoid being trampled. As the specimen we have is from an immature animal, we can't be certain of the maximum size that this animal reached.

We suggest taking a fairly conservative approach when playing {@i Mnyamawamtuka} by making it relatively peaceful when unchallenged, but aggressive if threatened. Adults should roam open spaces constantly feeding, whereas juveniles should congregate in larger numbers within the safety of dense forests. Given the high diversity of early titanosaurs, feel free to alter or add behaviour based on any adaptations given to {@i Mnyamawamtuka}.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Mnyamawamtuka} is a titanosaur sauropod, one of the most successful groups of Cretaceous herbivores. The earliest member of this group (Ninjatitan) arose 140 million years ago in South America, and within 30 million years the group had a global population and were highly diverse. By the Late Cretaceous, they had become the last surviving sauropods and continued to thrive until the end-Cretaceous extinction event.

entries.name: References

Gorscak, E., and O'Connor, P.M. 2019. A new African titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur from the middle Cretaceous Galula Formation (Mtuka Member), Rukwa Rift Basin, southwestern Tanzania. {@i PLoS One}, {@b 2(14)}, e0211412.
Prasad, V., Strömberg, C.A.E., Alimohammadian, H., and Sahni, A. 2005. {@i Dinosaur Coprolites and the Early Evolution of Grasses and Grazers. Science}, {@b 310(5751)}, 1177-1180.
{@i "Moe-sah-sore-us"} {@b (Meuse river reptile)}

Sailin' on the ancient sea ain't without its dangers. All the usual monsters still haunt the deep oceans, but there's also some pretty mean reptiles that swim the surfaces too. Durin' one stormy night, we sighted a huge one breach–its slick body glistening in the moonlight. It seemed completely unphased by the bad weather and was probably scoutin' us out–figurin' out what our ship was and whether it could eat us. If someone had fallen in, I'm sure they wouldn't have stood a chance.

{@i Mosasaurus} is a large aquatic reptile from the Late Cretaceous (80 million years ago) and inhabited oceans across the world. A member of the squamates (snakes and lizards), it is one of the largest aquatic predators in the fossil record.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Mosasaurus} was undeniably huge but, due to a lack of complete specimens, our size estimates vary dramatically from 36 - 56 ft. in length, with a potential maximum weight of 11 tonnes. Its body was elongate, broader towards the front and tapered from the middle. Its tail ended in an asymmetrical fluke, with a longer lower boned fin and a smaller soft-tissue upper fin. Its skull was long and large, accounting for 1/7th of the total body length. It had large conical teeth and a second set of palatal teeth on the roof of its mouth. {@i Mosasaurus}' limbs were adapted into swimming paddles, although without the extreme skeletal modifications seen in plesiosaurs. Its nostrils were set on the top of the skull like a dolphin and, as with all marine reptiles, it breathed air.

{@i Mosasaurus} was carnivorous and likely had a wide diet. Based on stomach contents, we know that small mosasaurs ate fish, but bite marks and isotopic analyses demonstrate that {@i Mosasaurus} was an apex carnivore feeding on turtles, plesiosaurs, fish, nautiloids, and other smaller mosasaurs. It is known to have inhabited the North American Western Interior Sea, the European Tethys ocean, and waters around Antarctica.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Mosasaurus} probably hunted close to the surface, perhaps using countershading (dark on top, light on the bottom) as camouflage before rushing prey from underneath. They likely gave birth to live young and, based on low numbers of babies birthed (k-selected), may have had some form of parenting behaviour. However, infants would have been able to swim and feed shortly after birth. While it is highly unlikely these predators lived in social groups, there is strong evidence of intraspecific (same species) combat. Several specimens have been found with bite wounds from other {@i Mosasaurus}, some of which have healed and others that were likely fatal. These may have been caused by territorial fighting or cannibalism.

We suggest that {@i Mosasaurus} be played as a largely solitary predator with strong territorial instincts. It will not tolerate any intruders into its territory, with the exception of its own young offspring. It should live in relatively deep waters and be most dangerous to parties in small-medium sized boats that have the same silhouette as {@i Mosasaurus}' prey from underneath. When hunting, its countershading will camouflage it and its presence may only be revealed by the panicked disappearance of smaller marine life. If a boat is viewed as a territorial threat, players might be warned by the sight or sound of a {@i Mosasaurus} slapping the surface of the water with its paddle.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Mosasaurids are the last of the Mosasauroidea, a group of specialised squamate reptiles that adapted for permanent life in the water. Mosasaurids were extremely successful, appearing 100 million years ago and becoming the dominant oceanic predators in the Late Cretaceous, outcompeting ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs. They spread throughout the world's oceans and survived up until the end-Cretaceous extinction.

There is ongoing debate about where in Squamata the mosasaurids sit, with them usually being placed as either the sister group to snakes or monitor lizards. However, there now appears to be increasing consensus that they are more closely related to snakes.

{@i "No-toe-oh-sore-us"} {@b (false reptile)}

The beach was a raucous place. Along the rocks and shingle there were dozens of large four-flippered reptiles baskin'. They were makin' loud low grumbles that echoed off the cliffs. I reckon they were complain' to each other about the lack of space on the best rocks and some were pushin' and shovin'. They were cumbersome on land, but the ones out at sea were rollin' with the waves with ease, usin' their protrudin' teeth to snatch fish.
{@i Nothosaurus} was a large semi-aquatic reptile from the Middle Triassic (240-210 million years ago). It was a sauropterygian, just like its distant relatives, the aquatic plesiosaurs.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Nothosaurus} was a highly successful carnivorous animal found in shallow ocean deposits in many countries, including in the Netherlands, Germany, and China. It had a low, rounded body with short limbs and an elongate neck. Its toes were elongated with webbing between them, turning its feet into pseudo-paddles. Its skull was wide and low, with long jaws full of sharp, needle-like teeth. {@i Nothosaurus} varied in length between 13-22 ft., meaning the largest individuals were bigger than modern great white sharks.

{@i Nothosaurus} lived in open water and so shared its environment with a wide variety of animals including fish, cephalopods, and other marine reptiles. Its teeth were sharp, circular in cross-section, and needle-like, making them excellent at grabbing slippery fish, or soft bodied animals like cephalopods and jellyfish. Given their large size, other smaller marine reptiles were also potential prey. Fossil trackways also indicate {@i Nothosaurus} may have swum low over sandy bottoms, stirring them up in search of hiding prey.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Nothosaurus} was likely a near-shore predator, hunting in shallow seas and coming onto the land to rest and possibly mate. While it possessed functional legs, they were not well adapted to life out of the water and it would have been clumsy on land. While in water, it would have been a swift and dangerous predator. Like ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs, several species of {@i Nothosaurus} gave birth to live young (likely in water), although the number of offspring and subsequent level of parental care is unknown.

We suggest that {@i Nothosaurus} should act quite differently depending on whether it is on land or in water. On land it should be defensive, making threatening calls and displays at a party that gets too close. In water it should be a much more direct threat, willing to stalk or strike without fear. Players near the surface of the water should be especially vulnerable as attacking prey from underneath is a common strategy used by aquatic predators.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Nothosaurus} was the largest member of the Nothosauridae. This group arose in the Middle Triassic (247 million years ago) and spread globally before becoming extinct in the Late Triassic (210 million years ago). The group was quite conservative in their morphology, with most members sharing similar traits. They were the sibling group to the Pachypleurosaura, which were smaller, more primitive, and less well adapted for the ocean. Together, these two groups were close relatives of the Plesiosaura, an incredibly successful group of marine reptiles that would dominate the oceanic environment of the Mesozoic. Combined, these three families were part of a larger group, the Sauropterygia.

{@i "Nick-toe-sore-us"} {@b (Night reptile)}

Sometimes you see somethin' that makes you double-take. While hikin' up a cliff, we spotted a small group of pterosaurs circling below. They were using the air currents to gain altitude. It took 'em a few minutes to rise, but as they passed us, we saw that they had the strangest huge Y-shaped crests protrudin' from the backs of their heads. How the hell they could fly with such unwieldly ornamentation is beyond me, but they were!

{@i Nyctosaurus} was a medium sized pterosaur from the Late Cretaceous Niobara Formation (86-83 million years ago). It was a relative of the much larger Pteranodon, and had a highly distinctive crest and wing morphology.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Nyctosaurus} was medium sized with a wingspan of approximately 6.5 ft. Its wings were extremely long relative to its body size, which would have given it a very upright posture when standing on the ground. Unlike the majority of pterosaurs, it had lost almost all of its fingers, only retaining the hyper-elongated wing finger, and that was also composed of only three bones rather than the usual four. Its jaws were long and toothless, and it had an unusual head crest composed of a short base with one long bar extending upwards, and another pointing backwards. These bars were up to 3 ft. in length on some individuals and were superficially antler-like.

{@i Nyctosaurus} is found exclusively in the Niobrara Formation, which is comprised of Late Cretaceous chalky rock formed along the edge of the Western Interior Sea, a stretch of shallow water that divided North America in two. This was a highly productive shallow seaway, brimming with life. In this setting, {@i Nyctosaurus} is seen as an analogue to the modern albatross, spending much of its time soaring over open ocean. This, combined with the strong similarity to the piscivorous (fish-eating) Pteranodon, suggests that it fed on the same food, catching fish on-the-wing as it flew low over water. Alternatively, it could have had the ability to plunge into the water like a modern Gannet. {@i Nyctosaurus} probably ate a wide diversity of fish, but may have consumed soft bodied invertebrates like squid or jellyfish as well.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Nyctosaurus}' extremely long wings and lack of fingers would have made it one of the more awkward and ungainly pterosaurs on land. It likely spent a short amount of its life on the ground, either when nesting or resting, and spent the majority of its time soaring. It may even have rested on-the-wing.

We recommend that {@i Nyctosaurus} be played in a manner befitting modern sea birds. It should prefer to remain in the air when possible and take any opportunity to snatch an easy meal, whether this is an unwary fish or the discarded remains of a party member's dinner. It should be cautious about being approached, retreating but never truly being driven off. If defending a nesting site, several {@i Nyctosaurus} should mob intruders. Its crest will largely be used for communication with other {@i Nyctosaurus}.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Nyctosaurus} was the most well-known member of the small family Nyctosauridae, with only two other taxa in the group. Members of this group have been found in Africa, North America, and South America, suggesting that they were fairly widespread. Nyctosauridae were exclusively from the Late Cretaceous and were related to the more well-known Pteranodontidae.

{@i "Oh-vih-rap-tor"} {@b (egg plunderer)}

We had started to run low on rations while trekkin' through the badlands. We had made sure we had surplus water, but food was the problem. After a few more hours of walkin' with growlin' stomachs, we encountered a series of nests guarded by honkin' squawkin' beaked gangly theropods. There was a wealth of eggs, but I knew we'd be in for a fierce fight to get 'em. Still, hunger pushes a man to do dangerous thin's.

{@i Oviraptor} is a small Late Cretaceous (75-71 million years ago) theropod from the Djadochta Formation of Mongolia and several other localities. Its egg-thieving name is the result of a misinterpretation of a remarkable fossil.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Oviraptor} was a small theropod at about 5 ft. long, with well-developed feathered plumage, a toothless beaked jaw, and a crest on the middle of its skull. Its legs and arms were quite long for its size with elongated fingers and large claws. By contrast, its tail was quite short for a theropod and ended in a pygostyle (the vertebrae were fused together), an adaptation that has been extended to the entire tail in modern birds.

{@i Oviraptor} is known from a number of formations in Mongolia which shared an arid/semi-arid environment with seasonal rains and rivers. While they do occur in wetlands, higher numbers are found in more desert-like environments. This seems to correspond with the size of other dinosaurs present, with {@i Oviraptor} being more common in arid formations with generally smaller dinosaurs. It is thought to have been an omnivore, hunting small prey while also feeding on low lying vegetation.

The original {@i Oviraptor} specimen (holotype) discovered in 1923 was a partial skeleton found lying on top of a nest of eggs. These eggs were initially misidentified as Protoceratops eggs and {@i Oviraptor}'s unusual mouth morphology led scientists to presume that it was a specialist egg feeder. This image of {@i Oviraptor} as an egg thief took hold in both scientific and non-scientific media as the defining aspect of the animal. Later CT scans revealed that the eggs in fact belonged to {@i Oviraptor}, and the fossil actually represented a protective parent shielding its nest from a colossal sandstorm.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Oviraptor} was probably an opportunistic feeder, foraging for anything that it could devour and snatching up small prey items, rather than actively hunting. It was a protective parent that guarded its nest with its life and almost certainly formed mated pairs. Multiple pairs then probably lived in small flocks, in a similar manner to many modern social birds.

We recommend {@i Oviraptor} be played as a highly social creature, with loud and expressive communication between its own species. It should readily flee from threats unless it is guarding a nest, where it should be exceptionally aggressive.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Oviraptor} is the most well-known member of the Oviraptoridae. These were generally small theropods with toothless jaws covered in keratin, often sporting a head crest that varied in shape from species to species. They were common in the arid environments of the Late Cretaceous, throughout what is now the Gobi Desert.

{@i "PAH-RA-LEE-TIE-TAN"} {@b (Tidal giant)}

The whole time we were wadin' through the river delta, we could see towerin' sauropods in the distance. They were flankin' the edges of the delta mostly, feedin' on the lush vegetation without venturin' too close to the muddy waters. I reckoned they could easily stride through the water and walk on the sand, but gettin' caught in the wrong patch of mud could be lethal. Still, their long necks gave 'em ample reach to feed–archin' over the waterways. Funny really, they seemed unbothered by most of the big predators. I guessed they could pack a punch if somethin' got too close.
{@i Paralititan stromeri} (Stromer's Tidal Giant) was a large member of the Titanosauria, a group of sauropods which included the largest known land animals to ever live.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Paralititan} is a relatively poorly known sauropod despite its discovery dating back to 1912. Recorded by German palaentologist Ernst Stromer, the original material was among the large fossil collection destroyed in World War II. It was not until 2000 when a team of palaeontologists discovered new material. Initially, it was estimated to weigh approximately 65 tonnes with a projected length of 85 ft. although it has been estimated to have been as light as 33 tonnes. While neither estimate would make it a match for the very largest titanosaurs, it was considerably bigger than any other animal known from the Bahariya Formation.

Like all sauropods, {@i Paralititan} was a herbivore. Due to its enormous size, it must have been a non-selective feeder. This means it was not choosy about what it ate, ingesting whatever plant matter (including early grasses) it could without any sort of preference.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Paralititan}'s sheer size gave it enormous strength and healthy adults would have been safe from most predators. However, like for modern elephants, some predators (such as {@creature Carcharodontosaurus|PartneredDDDoD}) would have been a potential threat if attacking in numbers, and especially to younger animals. Sauropods are frequently portrayed as being gentle giants. However, for many of them this is likely far from the truth, as modern large herbivores can be extremely aggressive and territorial (e.g., rhinos and buffalo). While sauropods may not have hunted for food, it is very possible that they would have met anything large enough to be a potential threat with a violent response.

Like most sauropods, {@i Paralititan} was not an involved parent. Juveniles grew rapidly and were capable of feeding without care (precocial). However, there is strong evidence that hatchlings of various ages grouped together for safety.

We recommend {@i Paralititan} be played as a gregarious animal, moving in herds while constantly feeding. Unfamiliar party members may spook them, resulting in unpredictable and aggressive behaviour, such as mock charges, displays of strength, or all-out attacks. When unthreatened they should be relatively calm animals.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Titanosaurs were an unusual group of animals which arose in the Early Cretaceous to become the dominant sauropod across the world and survived up the end Cretaceous extinction. They were members of the Macronaria, a group of long limbed large and skulled sauropods including {@i Brachiosaurus} and {@creature Giraffatitan|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@book The Rest of the Alphabet|PartneredDDDoD|7|Giraffatitan}). Like brachiosaurs, their forelimbs were elongated, giving them a tall-chested giraffe-like profile. Titanosaurs possessed short, blocky reduced toes; with most of the foot being made up of the metacarpals (knuckle bones). In some species the toes were completely absent.

{@i "Si-tac-oh-sore-us"} {@b (Parrot reptile)}

Occasionally, the doldrum of the cold forest would be broken by loud cherpin'. The first time this happened, we moved on quickly to avoid whatever was makin' that racket. The second time, we hung around to see what it was. Turns out it was a huge swarm of quilled, beaked, ceratopsians. There was one big 'un, and dozens of lil' 'uns. They didn't half make a racket, cryin' at the big one for attention as they scurried to keep up. Like a mumma duck and her hatchlin's, 'cept no single mumma laid that many eggs for sure!

{@i Psittacosaurus} is a basal member of the Ceratopsia (horned dinosaurs) and is known from many Early Cretaceous localities, including several from Mongolia, China, Russia, and Thailand. Due to the high number of exceptionally preserved fossils of {@i Psittacosaurus}, it is one of the best understood dinosaurs.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Psittacosaurus} was a 6.5 ft. long bipedal herbivore that lacked the true horn and frills of its more derived ceratopsain relatives. It had a broad head with cheek bones that flared out into triangular keratin-covered points. Exceptionally preserved specimens have retained the entire exterior of this animal, revealing colour patterned scaly skin, a series of long quills running down the upper surface of its tail, and even a cloaca with dark pigmentation.

{@i Psittacosaurus} was a herbivorous animal, able to scissor off tough leaves with its beak. This, combined with grinding teeth and its short stature, strongly indicates that it was an undergrowth-feeder, devouring fresh plant growth. Wear marks on young {@i Psittacosaurus} teeth indicate that they were precocial and could feed themselves immediately after hatching.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Psittacosaurus} are known to be highly social and gregarious (grouping together), even beyond basic nesting behaviour. They formed large herds of dozens to hundreds of individuals and, despite the young being able to feed themselves, they were still protected by numerous adults. Eggs were laid in clutches of up to 30, and the young formed creche groups made up of individuals of a variety of ages. It is even possible that parental duties may have been shared among the herd to lessen the load.

We recommend that {@i Psittacosaurus} be played as a dinosaurian equivalent to sheep, gathering in huge herds with some individuals maintaining a lookout. Upon spotting a threat, they should be more prone to fleeing, using their numbers to confuse their attackers. They should only stand and fight in desperate situations when unable to flee.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Psittacosaurus} was the most basal member of the Ceratopsia, the horned dinosaurs. This group includes a huge variety of dinosaurs ranging from small bipeds (like {@i Psittacosaurus}) to large-headed quadrupeds in the Leptoceratopsids, and the classic horned giants like {@creature Centrosaurus|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@book The Rest of the Alphabet|PartneredDDDoD|7}). The group enjoyed great success, surviving right up to the end-Cretaceous extinction.

entries.name: Biostratigraphy
entries: {@i Psittacosaurus} was an exceptionally successful animal. They inhabited huge swathes of Asia in vast herds and persisted for at least 24 million years. This means that their fossils occur in such large numbers across such vast areas and timescales that we are able to use them to reliably date rock formations, based on the species of {@i Psittacosaurus} present (see Biostratigraphy notes in {@book Introduction|PartneredDDDoD|0|Deep Time and the Geological Timescale}). This is almost unheard of for vertebrates and highlights just how successful {@i Psittacosaurus} was.

{@i "Tear-oh-dow-strow"} {@b (wing from the south)}

Not all of our adventures were bombastic fights of life'n'death. Some days we really were just able to enjoy the sights. One warm evenin', while the sun was settin', we were relaxin' on a lakeside. We watched a flock of a dozen pterosaurs wadin' just off the shore. They had heads like upturned hairbrushes and were filterin' the water through their bristle-like teeth. With each slosh, they pulled small invertebrates out of the silt and gobbled 'em down. The sound of the water lappin' as they fed was so soothin', it almost put me to sleep right then and there.
{@i Pterodaustro} is a pterosaur from the Early Cretaceous (105 million years ago) Lagarcito Formation of Argentina. It has a distinctive and bizarre comb of tightly packed elongated teeth.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Pterodaustro} was a medium-sized pterosaur with a 10 ft. wingspan and weighed around 20 lbs. It had relatively robust limbs, large feet, and a long tail for its group, although much shorter than earlier long-tailed pterosaurs. {@i Pterodaustro}'s most distinctive feature was its head, which was very elongate, with most of that length being the curved jaws. Its lower jaw had over a thousand exceptionally thin, tall, blunt, and densely packed teeth that were 0.04 in. (1 mm) wide and 1.5 in. tall. These teeth formed a distinctive bristly comb superficially similar to the baleen of whales or the beak filaments of flamingos and are so unusual that they form the basis for interpreting {@i Pterodaustro}'s ecology.

{@i Pterodaustro} is considered to be a filter-feeding animal and it almost certainly gulped water, pushed it through its fine teeth, and swallowed whole any small invertebrates, fish, plankton, or plant fragments that remained. These would then be broken down in its stomach by small stones (gastroliths). Filter-feeding has been suggested for other closely related pterosaurs, but {@i Pterodaustro} possesses the most obvious and specialised adaptations for it.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Pterodaustro} is usually depicted as the pterosaur analogue for modern flamingos. Its strong legs and wide feet would have allowed it to wade through shallow water comfortably or perhaps even swim. Research on {@i Pterodaustro}'s eggs indicate that its hatchlings were precocial (able to be independent) and probably had little parental care. This adaptation allowed {@i Pterodaustro} to evolve its cumbersome feeding apparatus, which would have otherwise prevented parental care in other lineages.

We suggest that {@i Pterodaustro} live in large flocks that settle in lakes and marshlands to feed. Each flock should have sentries: individuals who periodically scan the horizon for potential threats. When startled, the flock should simultaneously launch into the air, fleeing and confusing predators. As they swallow stones, {@i Pterodaustro} might accidentally ingest small gems washed out into lakes by local rivers. This makes them a high-value target for hunters, and {@i Pterodaustro} will be very wary of humanoids.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Pterodaustro} is a member of the Ctenochasmatoidea. This is a group of pterosaurs that arose in the Late Jurassic (152 million years ago), survived until the Early Cretaceous (105 million years ago), and includes the famous Pterodactylus. The group was reasonably successful, with fossils found on most continents. Basal animals like Pterodactylus were more generalist carnivores but the group became more specialist wading or aquatic feeders in later forms. One of the most derived subgroups, the Ctenochasmatidae (which includes {@i Pterodaustro}) became the most heavily specialised filter feeders.

{@i "Quet-zal-coh-ah-ta-lus"} {@b (after the Aztec god Quetzacoatl)}

Few thin's compare to the monumental sight of a full-grown Quetz soarin' above. While sailin' along the coast we had the opportunity to witness their annual migration, with several spotted each day. Their huge blade-like wings let 'em glide effortlessly over the waters, as they made their way to their inland nestin' grounds. Biggest flyin' thin' I ever saw. We caught the sight of a couple more many hundreds of feet up too–tiny shapes that lost all sense of scale in the endless sky.

{@i Quetzalcoatlus} was a giant azhdarchid pterosaur from the Late Cretaceous (68-66 million years ago) of North America. Well known for being one of the largest flying animals, it stood tall enough to look a {@i Tyrannosaurus} in the eye.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Quetzalcoatlus} is among the tallest azdarchid pterosaurs, reaching a height of at least 10 ft. at the shoulder and 16 ft. at the head while standing. Its wings were much broader than other pterosaurs like {@creature Nyctosaurus|PartneredDDDoD} or {@creature Rhamphorhynchus|PartneredDDDoD} and, when fully outstretched, could span over 30 ft. across. Like other azdarchids, {@i Quetzalcoatlus} was well adapted for terrestrial movement, with sturdy legs and forearms. Its neck was very long and muscular, topped with an elongate toothless skull that had a hard keratinous beak and bony crest on the top. While not as heavily built as {@creature Hatzegopteryx|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@book Hațeg Island|PartneredDDDoD|5|Hatzegopteryx}), it was still one of the heaviest ever flying animals at over 400 lb. in weight.

{@i Quetzalcoatlus} is known from the Javelina Formation in Texas, North America. This Late Cretaceous Formation was deposited in a rich floodplain with nearby rivers and lakes. It is thought that these were situated far inland, with surrounding subtropical forests. {@i Quetzalcoatlus} was certainly capable of flying great distances and probably inhabited many environments, but would have favoured areas where there was room for it to take off and land. It did this via the 'quad-launch' method, propelling itself into the air using all four limbs, rather than taking a running start like some large birds.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Much of the behaviour of {@i Quetzalcoatlus} is still unknown, but some evidence suggests that the largest ones were solitary. It may have flown long distances to move between feeding sites, but otherwise spent most of its life walking along the ground, searching for prey. {@i Quetzalcoatlus} was previously thought to have been a specialised skim-feeder, but biomechanical analysis demonstrated that this was impossible. It is now thought to have hunted like a Indian hornbill, searching for smaller creatures while walking.

{@i Quetzalcoatlus}' size and proportions meant that it could not incubate its eggs by sitting on them, and instead likely buried them in warm rotting plant matter. Larger pterosaurs seem to have been less precocial than smaller ones, and hatchlings were probably fed and protected by a watchful adult.

We recommend that {@i Quetzalcoatlus} be played as a confident predator, stalking the landscape in search of prey. It may have been indiscriminate in its attempts to eat creatures smaller than itself, similar to a pelican, or curious of novel objects. While Medium-sized party members would likely be on the upper limit of prey, {@i Quetzalcoatlus} should still be a major predatory threat. As it was probably solitary, adult {@i Quetzalcoatlus} should view each other as direct competition and may prioritise fighting each other over hunting prey, so long as they aren't courting.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Quetzalcoatlus} is the tallest member of the Azdarchidae. This is a group of medium-to-giant sized pterosaurs that occurred globally during the Cretaceous. They are generally characterised by their strongly-elongated neckbones and their long limbs, believed to be well adapted for a walking lifestyle. They are all toothless, with some having {@item spear|XPHB}-like beaks. Their closest relatives are the Chaoyangopterids, a group of smaller pterosaurs that are thought to have lived similar lifestyles.

{@i "Ram-for-ring-cus"} {@b (beak snout)}

These tiny lil' pterosaurs are such a pain. They're highly inquisitive and have a nasty habit of snatchin' stuff right out of your hands. I guess they're used to grabbin' food, since they sometimes swallow the stuff without even thinkin'. Reminds me of herring gulls back in our time. Difference is, herring gulls ain't armed with dozens of protrudin' teeth! The hatchlin's of this species are gregarious–they find safety in numbers and bunch up into swarms. They get pretty hungry too and anyone carryin' food tends to get mobbed pretty quick. For somethin' so small, they can be quite fearsome in numbers. Almost like lil' angry flyin' piranhas.

{@i Rhamphorhynchus} was a medium sized rhamphorhynchid pterosaur from the Late Jurassic (150 million years ago) of Germany and Britain. It is one of the most famous Jurassic pterosaurs and has been found in huge numbers from famous sites like the Solnhofen Limestone Formation.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Rhamphorhynchus} was a medium-sized pterosaur, with the largest individuals reaching a wingspan of 6 ft. It had a jaw full of large, pointed, spaced teeth that interlocked when closed, forming a "fish trap", in the same manner as {@creature Klobiodon|PartneredDDDoD} and {@creature Ludodactylus|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@book The Crato Formation|PartneredDDDoD|6|Ludodactylus}). It had a very small body for its wingspan, giving it a broad profile, while also having a long thin tail that ended in a triangular vane.

Like several other rhamphorhyncids, {@i Rhamphorhynchus} was an oceanic predator, flying over the sea and plucking prey from the water below. This is corroborated by its abundance in the Solnhofen Limestone Formation, which was deposited in a tropical coastal environment, with some freshwater influence. It probably hunted both near- and off-shore, plucking up fish and squid that were near the surface or being pursued by marine predators from below.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Based on the large number of specimens found, it's likely that {@i Rhamphorhynchus} was common along the Late Jurassic coasts and may have congregated in groups, forming shore-line colonies. Pterosaur hatchlings were precocial, meaning they could feed and climb from the moment they hatched. In fact, unlike modern birds, it seems that hatchlings may also have been able to fly very soon after hatching. This raises the question of what, if any, parental care existed for {@i Rhamphorhynchus}. Perhaps adults gathered to breed, but quickly moved on once the eggs were hatched, with little direct care for their young.

We suggest playing {@i Rhamphorhynchus} in a similar fashion to a gull. It should be an alert animal that is willing to snatch food wherever it can. It should also be an animal quick to adjust to player interaction and may become relatively friendly over time, especially if routinely fed. However, entering a creche or nesting area should result in a mobbing by angry adults or a swarm of juveniles.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Rhamphorhynchus} is the most well-known rhamphorhynchid, which are the stereotypical long-tailed pterosaurs with large fangs, elongate jaws, long wings, and a large tail tipped by a vane. While medium-sized for Pterosauria as a whole, until the Cretaceous these were the largest flying animals, with the biggest reaching a 10 ft. wingspan. The group is known from multiple sites throughout Europe, Asia, and the Americas. They arose in the Early Jurassic (180 million years ago) and persisted until the Late Jurassic (148 million years ago), where they seem to have disappeared as part of a major faunal turnover event between the Jurassic and Cretaceous, along with several other unrelated groups.

{@i "SKI-LIE-DOH-SORE-US"} {@b (LIMB REPTILE)}

We'd been travellin' through that accursed forest for days, barely able to see the sky through the thick canopy. When we reached the forest edge, the burstin' blindin' sky over the ocean was quite a sight to behold. I daren't let us rest though, as some mighty big beasties roam these shores. That's when I saw the first of 'em. A livin' mass-o-blades. But they was nothin' like I thought they'd be. Gentle to the touch—so long as you ain't touchin' the wrong spot! One took a likin' to me and, after I gave her a bit of bread, followed me for three days! Heh, never thought I'd befriend a dinosaur so easily.

{@i Scelidosaurus} is a small basal thyreophoran, the group of armoured dinosaurs that includes stegosaurs and ankylosaurs. It is known from several Early Jurassic (195 million years ago) sites across the British Isles and is currently the only described dinosaur known from Ireland.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Scelidosaurus} was small for an armoured dinosaur, measuring about 12 ft. long and weighing around 600 lbs. Originally thought to walk on four legs (quadruped), it is now thought to have been a facultative biped (it could walk on two or four legs). It had a long and squat body, long tail, a relatively short neck, and a small skull with a pointed beak. Much of its skin was covered in thick osteoderms (bones embedded in the skin), forming either plated armour or raised pointed blades. Both types were covered in keratin, which may have given them a sharp point.

Like many thyreophorans, {@i Scelidosaurus}' narrow jaws and beak suggest that it was a selective browser, moving through ground foliage and feeding primarily on ferns and cycads. Its heavy armour would have made it relatively slow, but well defended.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Little is known about {@i Scelidosaurus}' behaviour, but research into other thyreophorans suggest that it may have lived in small groups. Its armour helped protect it from larger predators while its bladed tail could be used as a weapon, although most probably more often to hit other offending {@i Scelidosaurus}.

We recommend that {@i Scelidosaurus} live in small herds, moving through dense foliage in search of food. They should be wary but not particularly aggressive, rather like a herd of domestic sheep. While some may respond to being approached with warning swipes of their tail, others could be placid and tempted in with food. Once domesticated, they can function as livestock, mounts, or pack animals.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Scelidosaurus} is a member of Thyreophora, but its exact position within that group has been the subject of debate. Initially placed as an early ankylosaur (Ankylosauria), it was later moved to lower in the Thyreophora clade, as a separate early member belonging to neither Stegosauridae or Ankylosauria. More recent studies have rearranged Thyreophora and {@i Scelidosaurus} may have been accompanied by stegosaurs at the base of the group, with ankylosaurs being their more derived relatives.

{@i "Shar-of-ip-ter-rix"} {@b (Sharov's wing)}

The jungle was bustlin' with life. Lizards, pterosaurs, and small dinosaurs filled the canopy above. As we walked below, I spied one particularly unusual critter soarin' between branches. It was a lil' lizard-like thing that was gliding usin' only its hind legs! Never seen anythin' like that before, how bizarre. We tried to get a closer look, but it was quite skittish and leapt from the tree whenever we went to climb up.

{@i Sharovipteryx} is a bizarre basal archosauromorph from the Middle Triassic (225 million years ago) Madygen Formation of Kyrgyzstan. It had extremely elongate hindlimbs that supported a gliding membrane.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Sharovipteryx} was a small animal at approximately 8in. long and is known from a single exceptional fossil. The front half of its body was rather unremarkable, with a simple reptilian head, sharp teeth, and short forelimbs, although some soft-tissue details may have been lost due to damage. Its hind quarters, however, were very unusual, with a stiff tail accounting for half of its total length and hyper-elongated hindlimbs with a gliding membrane. Specially adapted hips allowed the legs to be held out horizontally and the membrane stretched from the innermost toe on each foot to the tail, forming gliding wings.

Since {@i Sharovipteryx}'s discovery, most research has focused on its hindlimb membrane. It is unlike any other vertebrate known and there has been extensive discussion about how well it could glide. The current consensus is that it would have required a stabilising membrane on its forelimbs to help control its movement. Unfortunately, the specimen was over-prepared (too much of the rock was removed) when it was first collected, destroying soft tissue around the upper body. This means we don't know whether or not it had a second gliding membrane connected to its arms, but aerodynamic modelling suggests that it probably did.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Sharovipteryx} almost certainly lived in wooded areas, climbing up the sides of trees and along branches. While searching for food or fleeing predators, it would have leapt into the air, extended its hindlimbs, and glided to a neighbouring tree, in a similar manner to gliding squirrels or frogs. Its size and sharp teeth suggest that it probably ate insects, snatching them up along tree trunks and branches.

We suggest that {@i Sharovipteryx} be played as an alert animal that is most active during the daytime. Adults should be territorial of their trees, defending them from competitors who might threaten their food supply. A party is unlikely to get close to one in the day but at night as light draws clouds of insects to a campsite, Sharivopteryx may descend from the trees hoping for an easy meal. Sharivopteryx should be skittish, but quickly accustomed to humanoids if they feed it. Once tamed, it can be a useful and stealthy companion.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Sharovipteryx} was originally named Podpteryx (foot wing) in its initial description, but it was quickly highlighted that this name had already been assigned to a genus of damselfly. It was subsequently renamed in honour of Aleksandr Grigorevich Sharov, the author who originally described it. Sharivopteryx's phylogenetic relationships are still poorly understood, although it can be placed in Archosauromorpha with confidence. Beyond that, there is much uncertainty. It has previously been considered a close relative of pterosaurs, but also has been placed within its own group Sharovipteryigidae as a distant relative of true archosaurs. Ultimately, {@i Sharovipteryx}'s position in the tree of life is likely to change as research continues.

{@i "Spy-no-sore-us"} {@b (Spine reptile)}

We had gotten complacent seein' so many of these giant spinos lazin' by the rivers. Despite their massive size and vicious teeth'n'claws, they seemed uninterested in us. Preferrin' to stand motionless in the water with their snouts submerged in the flow, occasionally snappin' their colossal jaws. When they did, they hurled their heads upwards and dragged huge fish out of the water to feast on. It was a sight to behold every time. All was fine passing them, so long as we didn't get too close while they was feedin'. At least that's what we thought... until we came across a territorial male.

{@i Spinosaurus} was the largest member of the Spinosauridae and is known from the Cretaceous Bahayria, Chenni, Kem Kem, and Echkar formations of North Africa. {@i Spinosaurus} is undoubtedly the most hotly debated dinosaur of the 21st century.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Spinosaurus} was a very large carnivore at about 45 ft. in length. It had an elongated snout filled with sharp peg-like teeth, a long muscular neck, and muscular forearms sporting large curving claws. The vertebrae on its back had extremely elongated spines, extending over 3 ft. above the backbone, forming a long sail along its back. Its tail was modified into a tall oar-like shape. Its hind legs were shorter than in most theropods, making it appear much squatter, with unusually long toes and less curved toe claws, similar to many waterbirds, suggesting that it had webbed toes.

{@i Spinosaurus} is one of the few dinosaurs known to be well adapted for hunting fish. Its long snout and rounded pointed teeth are perfect for spearing passing fish. Its large claws functioned well as fishhooks and its short, long toed feet made it a capable wader in shallow water. Its diet would have included a wide variety of fish including giant sawfish and sharks. Like many otherwise specialised carnivores, it would have been opportunistic and fed upon smaller land-dwelling prey or scavenged from carcasses where possible.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Spinosaurus} is now believed to have been a large, shoreline wader, hunting fish from the edge of rivers and beaches. It may have been a more capable swimmer than other theropods and able to easily move throughout estuaries in search of prey. It would have likely avoided other large carnivores where possible.

When running {@i Spinosaurus}, we recommend it be treated as a hunter that stuck to the shoreline of rivers or coasts. It should have a great deal of patience, being willing to stand still for long periods waiting for prey to approach. It may be relatively safe for a party to pass by, so long as it is given a wide enough berth. However, this seemingly peaceful animal may be waiting for a player to stray too close to the shoreline, giving it the opportunity to strike.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Spinosaurus} is the largest known spinosaurid, a group of highly successful Cretaceous predators found across the world from Brazil to China. This group included well-known animals such as the South American {@i Irritator} and the British {@i Baryonyx}. Spinosaurids are distinguished by their unusually elongated snouts filled with rounded teeth, enlarged claws on their forelimbs, and elongated spines on the vertebrae in many species.

entries.name: An Ever-Changing Picture
entries: While {@i Spinosaurus} has been known since the early 1900s, the original specimen was destroyed in World War II. This has led to a great deal of debate and speculation over its morphology, biology, and ecology. New fossil discoveries in the 2010s provided a wealth of information regarding the animal and revealed it to be highly unusual in its proportions, which resulted in many years of debate over how it looked and lived. It has been reconstructed as a four-legged ambush predator, a wader, an entirely aquatic animal, a nearly 22 ton giant, and a more manageable 8 tons. What we present here is the most up-to-date summary of its morphology, but it serves as an excellent reminder that palaeontology is an ever-evolving science where new discoveries frequently upend our understanding of an animal.

{@i "Stoh-mah-toe-soo-cus"} {@b (Mouth crocodile)}

The riverways weren't just filled with monstrous threats and titanic predators. Believe it or not, there were a few docile beasties too. One of the most surprisin' was a giant croc that gently swam the riverways. It snapped at the water and raised its mouth high, gullet swollen. We could see lil' fish tails flickin' out the sides of its mouth and water poured through the gaps in its needle-like teeth as it squeezed its throat.
{@i Stomatosuchus} is a poorly understood crocodile-like animal with an unusual appearance, known only from a single specimen discovered in the 1920s.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: Little is known about {@i Stomatosuchus}' morphology beyond it possessing an unusual U-shaped head, 30 times longer than it was deep. Its upper jaw was full of closely packed thin pointed teeth, whereas its lower jaw is thought to have been toothless. It has been suggested by some that it possessed a deep throat pouch, but this remains speculative. The skull was extremely large, suggesting an animal 32 ft. in length.

The diet of {@i Stomatosuchus} is debatable. It lacks the large conical teeth seen in most other large crocodylomorphs and some have suggested it was a planktonic feeder, using a throat pouch to push water through its thin teeth. However, an alternative suggestion is that it was a predator of small fish and used its thin teeth in unison with the broad jaw to trap them, similar to the closely-related {@i Laganosuchus} and the more distantly-related {@i Aegisuchus}, both of which have more complete fossils. As planktonic filter-feeding requires highly-specific feeding structures, we think that a small vertebrate based diet is more plausible.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Laganosuchus} and {@i Aegisuchus} are thought to have been ambush predators, snapping passing fish or small animals and {@i Stomatosuchus} probably was too. Its jaws were remarkably slender, and therefore it would not have been able to easily hold large struggling prey, preferring smaller morsels or scavenging where possible.

We suggest {@i Stomatosuchus} be played as a patient predator, willing to wait several hours for prey to come within striking distance. Many playable species should be too large to be considered prey, but smaller species could be susceptible to attack. As long as these smaller party members do not approach the water, {@i Stomatosuchus} should be relatively benign.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Stomatosuchids are thought to be part of the Neosuchia, the group of crocodylomorphs more closely related to modern crocodiles than other groups such as the notosuchians. The group remains poorly understood and it has been suggested they belong to the Eusuchia, the "true crocodiles", but without more material there remains a great deal of mystery surrounding {@i Stomatosuchus}' phylogenetic placement.

Like so many of the Bahariya fossils, {@i Stomatosuchs}' type specimen was described in the 1920s by Ernst Stromer, and was later destroyed in World War II by allied bombers. No new material has been found since, and the only information we have is from Stromer's published figures.

"Stroo-th-ee-oh-sore-us" {@b (Ostrich lizard)}

After the first night, we stumbled across another species of dinosaur–quite literally. Our unaware wizard stepped over a shrub 'n' tripped on somethin'. Turns out it was a miniature nodosaur, one of the armoured dinosaurs. Adorable lil' thin' about the size of a large dog. Short, stout, and covered in spikey osteoderms–a creature after me own heart. It shuffled away into the brush and, thankfully, our wizard escaped with all but his pride bruised.

{@i Struthiosaurus} is a small member of the nodosaurids, a somewhat contested group of heavily armoured dinosaurs that with the ankylosaurids make up the Ankylosauria. Its name comes from the bird-like morphology of its braincase.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Struthiosaurus} was small for a nodosaur, being only 10 ft. long and weighing around 600 lb. As a nodosaurid, it was less heavily armoured than the more well known ankylosaurids and lacked a tail {@item club|XPHB}, but was nonetheless still formidably defended. Its armour was made up of multiple individual sharp blade-like and domed osteoderms (bony structures in the skin) that dotted its flanks.

{@i Struthiosaurus} was a herbivorous dinosaur with coarse leaf-shaped teeth. Wear patterns on these teeth suggest that it fed mostly on tough plants. Ankylosaurs appear to have had long, flexible tongues which they would have used to strip low lying fresh plant growth. This specialisation towards ground level feeding allowed them to avoid competition with taller sauropods and hadrosaurs.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: While famous for their armour, nodosaurs are now thought to have been relatively inert animals (unless attacked). Micro-CT analysis of {@i Struthiosaurus}' skull reveal that it had less sophisticated senses than other dinosaurs, which could indicate that it was a solitary animal relying entirely on its armour for defense. This sensory loss also suggests that there were few direct predators of an adult {@i Struthiosaurus}, allowing it to reduce resource investment in its senses. It was probably oblivious to non-native threats in the same manner that dodos were reported to have been.

We suggest {@i Struthiosaurus} be played as a relaxed, almost lackadaisical animal, living a peaceful solitary life. If approached by a party it should react with mild curiosity or disinterest, but if attacked should default to a defensive stance, striking with its tail or tackling opponents.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Struthiosaurus} is usually identified as a nodosaurid, one of the main two groups of Ankylosauria. This group are identified as more lightly-built animals, with flexible, bladed tails rather than the giant, clubbed tails in animals such as {@creature Zuul|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@book The Rest of the Alphabet|PartneredDDDoD|7|Zuul}). They appeared in the Middle Jurassic and survived until the end-Cretaceous extinction. Nodosaurs were a widespread group and a major part of the herbivore population across Laurasia (North America, Europe, and Asia) and South America. However, a 2023 study suggested that Nodosauridae was not a natural group and instead put {@i Struthiosaurus} within its own clade, the Struthosauridae.
