{@i "Tan-ih-strof-e-us"} {@b (long hinged)}

We were followin' a small river upstream, searchin' for a good place to camp for the evenin'. Out of nowhere, a long neck and lil' head whipped out of the reeds and nipped one of our party members on the leg. At first, we thought it was a snake, but then it reared up several feet into the air and burst from the reeds, scurryin' into the water. As it dived, we saw the rest of its body. It was a weird lookin' beastie, with a neck twice as long as its body!
{@i Tanystropheus} is a reptile from the Middle Triassic (245 million years ago) of Europe and North America. It is well known for having one of the longest necks relative to body size of any animal.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Tanystropheus} was one of the longest basal archosauromorphs, reaching 16-20 ft. in length. Over half of that length is neck, which supported a small skull with elongate fangs. Like some pterosaurs (e.g., {@creature Rhamphorhynchus|PartneredDDDoD}), these fangs interlocked to form a "fish trap" that could grasp wriggling slippery prey. Its legs were unusual, with the hindlimbs being much larger and more robust than the forelimbs.

The lifestyle of {@i Tanystropheus} is debated, with some authors suggesting a near-water terrestrial ecology and others asserting that it was entirely aquatic. In either case, its primary food source was probably fish. The most recent study supports a semi-aquatic lifestyle, living in either marginal marine environments (near-shore) or freshwater, swimming in a frog-like manner by kicking its hind legs. In these habitats, it may have used its long neck to dip-feed whereby it hid its body onshore and plunged its head into shallow water to snatch fish and squid.

However, some small {@i Tanystropheus} had very different dentition with conical teeth changing to flatter teeth towards the back of the mouth, suggesting that it crushed harder foodstuffs, perhaps small shelly organisms.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Tanystropheus} almost certainly lived in and around water. It probably spent a significant proportion of its time swimming or wading through reedy shallows, hunting for fish, or it may also have remained stationary at the water's edge. In either case, it would have been able to flee from one medium to the other to escape predators.

We suggest that {@i Tanystropheus} be played with different behaviours depending on which environment it is in. On land it should be relatively static, dipping its head into the water to snap at fish. It will be passive until approached, when it will likely dive into the water to escape. However, it may be more aggressive if encountered in water, striking or snapping at those who disturb it while hiding its body among aquatic reeds. It will only leave the water if a large aquatic predator approaches it. A tamed {@i Tanystropheus} could be a popular companion for fishing cultures, assisting them by snatching up fish while on their boats, similar to real-world cormorant fishing.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Tanystropheus} is the largest member of the Tanystrophidae. This is a group of primarily long-necked archosauromorphs, related to animals like {@creature Sharovipteryx|PartneredDDDoD}. Exclusively Triassic, they are found on every continent and in both terrestrial and aquatic environments. The group arose around the Early Triassic (250 million years ago) and survived until the Late Triassic (201 million years ago), where they were among the many victims of the Triassic-Jurassic extinction event.

{@i "Teh-tra-pod-oh-fis"} {@b (four-footed snake)}

We were wadin' through some shallow water, searchin' for edible aquatic shoots to supplement our rations. Seemed like a good idea at the time, since we were gunna be headin' into the desert soon. Turns out stickin' ya hands where you can't see ain't always a great idea. One of our party got bit by some squiggle lil' thin'. I only caught a glimpse of it, but it seemed to be more like a long lizard than a snake. We had our hearts in our throats for a few minutes after that, waitin' to see whether it had been venomous.
{@i Tetrapodophis} (literally four-footed snake) is a snake-like Early Cretaceous squamate (the group containing lizards, snakes, and mosasaurs), but is not a true snake.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Tetrapodophis} was a small reptile measuring about 8 inches in length. It had an extremely elongated snake-like body but retained four small, although fully functional, legs. Originally, {@i Tetrapodophis} was suggested to be a burrowing animal as the short tail and squat head were thought to match burrowing lizards and snakes. It was also argued that it was unlikely to be an aquatic animal as it lacks a paddle-like tail or dense bones. However, within a year of the original description of {@i Tetrapodophis}, a second research team examined the fossils and found that the morphology of its legs were comparable to some aquatic lizards and this, among other things, identified the animal as being well-adapted for an aquatic lifestyle. This makes it much more probable that {@i Tetrapodophis} was at least semi-aquatic and would have lived or hunted along the shores of the Crato Formation waters.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Tetrapodophis} was a carnivore and fed on fish, insects, and small reptiles (and possibly unguarded eggs), as demonstrated by the small bones found in its stomach. When playing {@i Tetrapodophis}, it should be a largely skittish animal, fleeing into water if disturbed. If a party member catches one and attempts to manhandle it, it should be quick to bite to make its captor drop it, then flee.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: When it was initially described, scientists argued that {@i Tetrapodophis} was the oldest member of the snake family and that its small legs showed it to be a transitional animal in the evolution of snake leg loss. However, later researchers re-examined the fossil and argued it belonged in the group Dolichosauridae. This is the sibling group (closest relatives) to snakes, largely consisting of small aquatic lizards that may have had similar lifestyles to modern sea snakes. While this identification is currently the most widely accepted, it's important to remember that science is constantly being tested and revised. This means that further research into {@i Tetrapodophis} may reveal new unsuspected details about its phylogeny.

entries.name: The Legality of Fossil Research
entries: The original {@i Tetrapodophis} material is suspected to have been illegally exported from Brazil. Unlike {@creature Ubirajara|PartneredDDDoD|"Ubirajara"}, however, there has been no commitment to return {@i Tetrapodophis} and the original work has not been redacted. Scientists are required to conduct ethical research, but they, in turn, also expect museums to ethically source and legally house specimens in the first place. Nevertheless, all research teams that examined this specimen after the first have included Brazilian palaeontologists, which is a requirement to study Brazilian vertebrate fossils under Brazilian law.

{@i "Too-pan-dack-tal-us"} {@b (Tupan finger)}

Some of the bigger pterosaurs were nestin' just up from the water's edge. Seemed to be mostly out of harms way, but still pretty exposed. That didn't seem to phase 'em though, since they had numbers on their side. They also had these huge intimidatin' crests, nearly as big as me, and were prancin' about, swayin' their heads from side to side. They were so engrossed in their display, that they didn't even notice us pass by.
{@i Tupandactylus} was a medium-to-large sized tapejarid pterosaur with a wingspan of between 10 to 13 ft.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Tupandactylus}' most distinctive trait was its large vertical sail-like crest. This was exceptionally large on some individuals, raising the question of the function of such an elaborate structure. While it has been suggested to be some sort of steering aid, a crest that size would have likely made flight more difficult. Instead, it is much more likely that the crest developed as a means of sexual selection, with only the healthiest individuals able to grow a large cumbersome crest while maintaining the ability to fly well. It would have also been a means for both males and females to communicate through visual displays.

Like most Cretaceous pterosaurs, {@i Tupandactylus} was toothless, however it also had a relatively short jaw. This has led to a great deal of debate as to the most likely diet of this animal. It now appears that {@i Tupandactylus} was herbivorous, specifically frugivorous (fruit eating) much like modern toucans. The Crato Formation was laid down in a lagoonal/lake environment with freshwater influence and {@i Tupandactylus} would likely have been a transitional member of the fauna, primarily living and feeding in woodland areas where it foraged for food, perhaps coming to the water to drink and socialise.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Tupandactylus} was likely a primarily ground forager, moving through the undergrowth in search of food, as its huge crest would have hindered it feeding in trees. Flight would likely have been a means of moving between foraging spots or escaping predators. We recommend that {@i Tupandactylus} be played as a somewhat skittish animal foraging alone or in small flocks of a handful of individuals. They should be on the watch for potential threats and likely to take flight when threatened. They could be played more aggressive if they are nesting or defending a particularly fruitful feeding patch.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Tupandactylus} is one of the largest members of the Tapejarine. This is a group of Cretaceous pterosaurs found across the world and is most well-known for including members with large sail-like crests like Tapejara and, of course, {@i Tupandactylus}. Tapejarines were also close relatives of the giant azdarchid pterosaurs.

entries.name: Pycnofibres
entries: Since the 1950s, evidence of a fuzzy coat has been found on some pterosaurs, called pycnofibres. Several pterosaur fossils have a full-body covering of these hair-like filaments. The relationship between pycnofibres and feathers has been a topic of much debate, but a recently discovered {@i Tupandactylus} specimen preserves pycnofibre pigment that is extremely similar to those found in feathers, strongly suggesting that pycnofibres are a structure derived from feathers. This has profound implications for when feathers arose and just how many animals in our past may have been feathered.

{@i "OOH-BI-RAH-JAR-AH"} {@b (lord of the spear)}

Skirtin' around the edge of the woods to bypass the thickest undergrowth, we spotted somethin' particularly bizarre. There was this lil' fuzzy theropod dinosaur, screechin' at the top of its lungs and bouncin' around a fallen log. It had a few massive quills projectin' from its shoulders that look like you wouldn't want 'em stuck in your arm. I think it was performin' some kind of matin' dance, but whatever it was doin', we gave it a wide berth.

This compsognathid dinosaur from Brazil was described in 2020, with the name "{@creature Ubirajara|PartneredDDDoD}", however as discussed below, controversy regarding the exporting of the fossil to Germany led to the manuscript being pulled. This means that the name "{@creature Ubirajara|PartneredDDDoD}" is invalid, but following the recommendation of a study published in 2023, we will refer to the animal as "{@creature Ubirajara|PartneredDDDoD}" informally with the name in inverted commas without italics until a formal name is assigned.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: "{@creature Ubirajara|PartneredDDDoD}" was a relatively medium sized compsognathid, at about 3 ft. long. This group of small theropods are usually conservative in their morphology, that is they have three fingered arms, walk on hind legs, gracile bodies, long tails, and a 'generic theropod' appearance. This conservative morphology is indicative of a generalist predator/scavenger lifestyle (feeding on insects, small reptiles, mammals, fish, etc.), as it shows no feeding specialisations beyond predation.

"{@creature Ubirajara|PartneredDDDoD}" is exceptional in that it had a dense mane of feathers, which likely would have given the animal quite a fluffy appearance. This was accompanied by a pair of long filaments on each shoulder, jutting out like rods. The function of these structures is not known but it has been suggested they may have had some role in sexual display.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Small carnivores tend to be curious, but skittish, creatures (e.g., foxes and mongooses). We suggest playing "{@creature Ubirajara|PartneredDDDoD}" as a quick and alert animal, curious about parties but maintaining its distance. Medium and larger sized creatures/humanoids should be considered too big to hunt under normal circumstances, but weak/sickly Small sized creatures/humanoids could be seen as a potential prey. "{@creature Ubirajara|PartneredDDDoD}" did not have the tools to pin down and wrestle prey, so we suggest that it nips and claws at prey, wearing it down before moving in for the kill.

Alternatively, given "{@creature Ubirajara|PartneredDDDoD}"'s elaborate filamentous coat, it could also be played like a bird of paradise–leaping and dancing around while fluttering its display feathers. Territorial control could then be its primary concern.

entries.name: The Legality of Fossil Exportation
entries: Many countries have strict laws about fossil exportation. Brazil prohibits most fossil exportation, but fossils from Brazil are nevertheless available in numerous fossil shops and even museums. This shows an industrial-scale illegal exportation operation and a thriving black market for Brazilian fossils. "{@creature Ubirajara|PartneredDDDoD}" became the cornerstone for the discussion of this issue after the fossil was held in Karlsruhe, Germany after evidence arose that it was illegally exported. Within days of the research being published, it became the focal point of social media backlash, eventually leading to the paper being withdrawn and (2 years later) the agreement to repatriate the fossil to Brazil.

This is an {@i extremely} complex political subject and there are competing views as to the validity of national laws on the international stage, the de-colonisation of science, the impact on scientific publication and funding, the impact on local tourism, the classification of fossils as georesources, the infrastructure required to safely store type specimens, and, of course, the morality of the issue. We fully support the repatriation of "{@creature Ubirajara|PartneredDDDoD}" and other culturally significant fossils to their country of origin.

{@i "You-tah-rap-tor"} {@b (Utah plunderer)}

Unlike their smaller cousins, these ones are truly somethin' to be feared. Boundin' out of the brush in a flurry of teeth, claws, and feathers, they'll rip all but the hardiest foes to shreds in a matter of moments. No qualms about takin' on something much bigger than themselves either. We spied five workin' their way through a clearin', takin' out a large hadrosaur in one go. Thankfully, we were way up a steep cliff, otherwise we might've been puddin'.

{@i Utahraptor} is a dromaeosaurid from the Early Cretaceous (135 million years ago) Cedar Mountain Formation of Utah, North America. It was the heaviest and possibly the largest member of the dromaeosaurid family.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: By dromaeosaur standards {@i Utahraptor} was enormous, measuring at over 16 ft. long and weighing more than 600 lb. It was very robust and powerfully built, with strong jaws and limbs. Like most dromaeosaurs, it had a large retractable {@item sickle|XPHB}-shaped claw on each foot which would have been used to puncture and hold prey, rather than slash or cut. Its forelimb claws were also very large and robust. While there is no direct evidence of feathers in {@i Utahraptor}, we are confident that it was feathered, as all closely related animals are (determined through phylogenetic bracketing (see {@book Introduction|PartneredDDDoD|0|Reconstructing an Extinct Organism})). {@i Utahraptor}'s most distinctive feature, other than its size, is a slightly downturned tip of its lower jaw, splaying its lower teeth forward.

{@i Utahraptor}'s fossils are found in the Cedar Mountain Formation, a series of non-marine sediments that were deposited by rivers, lakes, and floodplains over a very long time period. During this prolonged time, the surrounding environment varied with climate, from hot arid scrubland to humid forest. {@i Utahraptor} was one of the larger predators in its environment and is clearly built for power. It would have predated upon almost every other large animal in the Cedar Mountain Formation.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: Some fossils preserve remarkable behaviour and there is one particularly spectacular specimen for {@i Utahraptor} that preserves nine individuals in a single sandstone block. These animals include adults, subadults, juveniles, and hatchlings all clustered above one iguanodont herbivore. This is hypothesised to be a "predator trap" whereby one herbivore died in quicksand and subsequently so too did many predators while trying to reach it. The age range of {@i Utahraptor} present suggests that these were large family groups and that they may have been pack hunters. However, it is also possible that this association is by chance (actually representing a flash flood deposit), or that the {@i Utahraptor} were unrelated and drawn to the same trap one after the other.

We suggest that {@i Utahraptor} be played as a highly social predator, living in groups of mated adults with subadults, juveniles, and babies in close association, generally protected by the adults. Within these groups individuals should be communicative and playful with each other. While hunting, cooperation should vary with age, with the eldest {@i Utahraptor} leading subadults on hunts, and younger {@i Utahraptor} following at a distance. Young animals may hunt small prey themselves but will also scavenge from the adult's kills in a strict pecking-order.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: Dromaeosaurs were a highly successful group of mostly small-sized predatory theropods, but {@i Utahraptor} highlights that some became very large indeed. Currently only four giant dromaeosaur species are known, but these belong to different subgroups that may have had very different lifestyles, suggesting that giantism occurred independently multiple times within Dromaeosauridae.

{@i "Veh-loss-ih-rap-tor"} {@b (swift plunderer)}

These quick lil' things really lived up to their name. Vicious as anything–two of 'em jumped me while I was takin' a wizz. Lightnin' fast attack. Thankfully, as soon as the rest of the party came runnin' to me cries for help, they scattered. Not interested in takin' on lots of prey at once it seems. The party found me all scratched up in a heap though. What an embarrassin' encounter.

{@i Velociraptor} is the most famous member of the Dromaeosauridae (popularly known as the 'raptors'). A small theropod from the Djadochta and Bayan Mandahu formations, it is one of the best-preserved dromaeosaurs with several complete specimens. Despite this, its fame has made it one of the most frequently misrepresented dinosaurs in media.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Velociraptor} was a small dromaeosaur at 2 ft. tall and 6 ft. long. It had an unusually narrow and elongate skull which gave it a distinct profile. Like most dromaeosaurs, it had long fingers ending in hooked claws and a single strongly-enlarged {@item sickle|XPHB} shaped claw on each foot. While large, this claw was not suited to slashing or cutting. Instead, it was for pinning or grappling small prey. Like other dromaeosaurs, {@i Velociraptor} was covered in feathers with well-developed 'wings' (though it couldn't fly) and a broad tail. As with many modern birds, it is plausible that males and females had sexually dimorphic plumage (possessing different feather colours and patterns).

{@i Velociraptor} was an active predator, hunting prey by leaping onto it and pinning it with its large claws while stabilising itself with its wings. It likely killed prey by biting at their necks, causing death by blood loss. One exceptional fossil even preserves the moment a {@i Velociraptor} was fighting with a Protoceratops. Both died and were preserved by a collapsing sand dune. In addition to hunting, {@i Velociraptor} would have also scavenged, like most modern carnivores.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: {@i Velociraptor} would have been an active semi-nocturnal opportunistic hunter. Alert and curious, it could have hunted alone or in pairs. Hatchlings probably stayed with their parents until they were old enough to hunt small prey themselves. {@i Velociraptor}'s wings may have been used for communication, with swift flicks similar to modern crows, and perhaps also used to mantle kills (extending them over a carcass while feeding to hide it from other predators).

We suggest {@i Velociraptor} be played as an alert predator, actively monitoring its territory. It may stalk intruding parties for a while before determining whether to attack and should not necessarily be scared off by humanoids' presence alone. Large groups may be found scavenging corpses but {@i Velociraptor} should not hunt in a pack. Instead, each individual or pair should function as their own unit, similar to modern birds of prey.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Velociraptor} was a dromaeosaurid, a very well-known family of generally small to medium sized theropods that occurred on every continent and are commonly referred to as "raptors". Within Dromaeosauridae, {@i Velociraptor} is part of the Velociraptorinae sub-family, which are mostly small dromaeosaurs with elongate skulls.

entries.name: The Price of Fame
entries: {@i Velociraptor} rose to fame in the late 80s and early 90s through its prominent role in the {@i Jurassic Park} franchise, based on Michael Crichton's books. While dramatic and popular, it was inaccurately portrayed in the franchise. This was, in part, due to science at the time considering {@i Velociraptor} a potential synonym of the larger Deinonychus, which Crichton incorporated into his writing. This resulted in {@i Velociraptor} being misrepresented in media as a large hyper-intelligent pack hunting animal for decades. While recent studies have suggested some large predatory dinosaurs may well have been much more intelligent than previously assumed, {@i Velociraptor} is not believed to have been particularly smart or {@condition Prone|XPHB} to pack hunting. Today, incorrect depictions of animals like {@i Velociraptor} in the media have led to an increasingly vocal movement to find a balance between scientific accuracy and engaging science fiction–exactly what we are attempting in this book!

Chosen by Lucian T. Moreman

I've done me fair share of minin' while studyin' subterranean geology. When our rogue suggested some spelunkin' to explore further into the cave systems that the locals lived in, I thought it'd be a nice break from the dangers of the forest we'd been trekkin' through for the last month–a bit of peace 'n' quiet and no giant dinos tryin' to eat us. How wrong I was...

As we moved deeper into the caves from their entrance settlements, the limestone walls grew damper with ground water. We dove for a few hours and the deeper we went, the bigger the stalactites were, undisturbed for thousands of years. Puddles of milky water would slap as we stepped into 'em, and in deeper pools tiny eyeless fish flittered away from the splashes. Occasionally, a big drip would fall onto me neck–sending a shiver down me spine. About six hours in, one of the bigger drips caused me to leap forward, slippin' on the slick stone. I dropped my torch and it sizzled 'n' died on the wet floor. After a moment of blurred vision in the dark, the walls slowly lit up with a dull bioluminescent glow. Seems torches were unnecessary from then on.

An hour or so later, the last cavern we entered opened up into a huge partly-flooded chamber. The far end of it had deep blue water, suggestin' that it was connected to the outside world. I moved up and took a knee to have a cursory taste–salty, definitely connected to the ocean. As I knelt over the water, a bright glow caught me attention. About 30 ft. in front of me and maybe 50 ft. deep there was a white glowin' orb. I beckoned the party over and the rogue commented that it could be a magical item washed in from the ocean. We stared at it for a moment as it seemed to gently pulse. That peaceful moment of curiosity was broken when two lines of smaller orbs started to light up dull blue one by one in a parrel line behind it. As they did, an enormous oily black bioluminescent monster was revealed in the murky depths. The big orb was a massive lure danglin' from its head like some mega-anglerfish, 'cept this was no fish.

Its huge bulk rose steadily through the water and I fell backwards from the shock, scurryin' away from the colossal jaws approachin'. As it breached the water, it hissed with a maw full of contorted needle-like teeth. Its inky eyes met with mine and I could see a cold intelligence. It reared then burst forward at me, lettin' loose a colossal and dazzlin' flash of light. Instinctively, a quick tuck'n'roll saved me despite bein' {@condition blinded} by the flash. Some other members of the party weren't so lucky–bein' hit by those fearsome jaws.

The fight was now on and although we were dazzled, we were ready. It swung its massive tail through the water, pushin' a wave over the party, knockin' a couple of 'em {@condition prone}. The paladin stood her ground and slashed at the beast with her {@item longsword|XPHB}. It didn't seem to like that and turned its gaze to her, tiltin' its head slightly as it planned its next move. As she took another swing, it started to strobe its bioluminescence, causin' her to stumble 'n' miss entirely. Thankfully, our rogue took that opportunity to plunge their daggers into its thigh. Enraged, it swung its whole body around, knockin' 'em over.

We fought for what seemed like hours, but eventually drove the beast back to the murky depths. Battered 'n' bruised from the battle, we moved back into the narrower caves so it couldn't follow. No doubt it'd be lookin' for another go once it'd licked its wounds. We definitely made an enemy that day, one that I reckon will remember our faces. We decided to name the beast appropriately. Wretchglow, after its wretched glow–the last light some people see.

{@creature Wretchglow, the Last Light|PartneredDDDoD} is a monstrous dinosaur that was once a {@creature Spinosaurus|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@b {@book The Bahariya Formation|PartneredDDDoD|4|Spinosaurus}}). Twisted by magical energies, it has been combined with a variety of deep-marine organisms to create a grotesque hybrid that inhabits the deep sea and damp subterranean caves.

It is an ambush predator that attracts prey with its bioluminescence, gently pulsing light and snatching unwary animals that venture to investigate with its needle-sharp, protruding teeth. Despite this static approach to hunting, it is extremely intelligent. Perhaps the mind of whatever mad scientist created this beast is locked away within it. It harbours a malicious intent but is still subject to its animalistic hunting instincts.
Chosen by Mitchel Rios

It was well-known that throughout the highlands were a series of massive tarns, huge lake-like pools of water formed in the rugged glacially excavated expanse of the region's upper ranges. Flanked on all sides by sheer mountain cliffs, these formed lil' pockets of life among the otherwise sparsely vegetated rocky faces. In the western-most expanse, we came across a particularly large tarn that was surrounded by huge iridescent crystals. The mineralogy of these thin's baffled me–they were unlike any natural mineral known. We figured they must've been magical in nature and were {@status surprised|XPHB} that no one had started minin' 'em for their obvious rich power.

There were signs that others had been here before, albeit a long time ago. Burnt out campfires 'n' ripped tents–destroyed by the howlin' mountain gales. We investigated them a fair bit, all while the deep hummin' of those crystals reverberated in the background. Our ranger was the first to notice somethin' amiss. He pulled a femur from one of the campsites, crushed to splinters. It suddenly dawned on us; these camps weren't abandoned, they were attacked. We gathered our thin's 'n' prepped to move along swiftly, but were rudely interrupted by the crack 'o' thunder and a bellowin' roar. The sound wasn't commin' from the sky, where thunder aught to be. No, it was emanatin' from a nearby cave–the flicker of red light suggestin' that it led to a volcanic lava chamber. We tried scramblin' to leave, but we was too slow. Out stepped a huge predatory dinosaur. Mean as anythin' and eyein' us up for supper.

It was some sort of {@creature Spinosaurus|PartneredDDDoD}, evidently fed in the tarns, but it was warped by the magical energies of these odd minerals. Fat angular crystal shards were embedded in its hide, and more encrusted along its mouth–I thought perhaps it'd been driven to madness and been eatin' the crystals themselves. Whatever it had been doin', it wasn't too happy about it. Twitchin', it seemed to swell with power. Painfully so, as though it could hardly contain the raging energies that permeated its body.

Arcs of magical energy sparked between the crystals on its back as it lunged towards us. With every step, it seemed to surge with more power and rapidly picked up pace. There was no way we could outrun this thin', we had to fight. It shimmered with a rainbow of colour as it bit and swiped at us, deflectin' spells as though they were nothin'. Our paladin tanked three blows, which just seemed to piss it off. Its breath was heavy and, as it exhaled, shards of crystal scraped across me skin like sandpaper. In its frustration, it seemed to lose control of the power within it, tilting its head back and bellowin' to the sky. Massive bolts of energy crackled in all directions, rippin' the ground up as they discharged from the beast. It took all of us a moment to steady ourselves afterwards. Now we knew the fight was really on.

{@creature Xu'thul, the Prismatic Terror|PartneredDDDoD} is a {@creature Spinosaurus|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@b {@book The Bahariya Formation|PartneredDDDoD|4|Spinosaurus}}) that has been augmented by the magical energies of the strange minerals that surround some highland tarns and deep mountain caves. Originally migrating to these waterbodies in search of alternative feeding grounds, Xu'thul became increasingly hungry as it slowly starved due to the lack of large fish in these waterbodies. Through happenstance, it ingested some of the crystals around the lake, whose magical energies began to sustain its massive bulk. Over several decades, Xu'thul's body became increasingly composed of these ingested crystals, forming crystalline structures protruding from its flesh. This was (and continues to be) a painful process, making Xu'thul particularly ill-tempered and untameable.

{@creature Xu'thul, the Prismatic Terror|PartneredDDDoD} was given its name by a Jeholrak survivor who skulked away after an attack on a prospecting expedition. In the native tongue of Archosauric, Xu'thul translates to "horror of many colours" or "prismatic terror".
{@i "Tie-ran-o-sore-us"} {@b (Tyrant Lizard King)}

We pushed through thick undergrowth that reeked of rotting meat, the sickly smell fillin' me nostrils. The half-devoured carcasses of various herbivores lit'ered the area, decayin' slowly. "This is rex territory" I whispered to the rest of the party. "But tis OK, we'll hear 'em comin' long befo-". My words were split by the sudden crash of bushes and trees bein' crushed beneath the thunderin' charge of a dinosaur. Far smaller than expected, but also far faster, a {@creature young Tyrannosaurus|PartneredDDDoD} rex was barin' down on us somethin' fierce.

{@i Tyrannosaurus} is inarguably the most famous fossil animal and was the heaviest land carnivore known. Much of {@i Tyrannosaurus}' ecology and morphology has been studied extensively, and one area of particular interest is the stages of growth that {@i Tyrannosaurus} underwent. Several immature fossils of {@i Tyrannosaurus} demonstrate that it underwent dramatic changes throughout its life that not only altered its size and general appearance, but also its niche within an ecosystem.

entries.name: Ontogeny
entries: Ontogeny is the study of how an animal changes through life, from the fertilisation of its egg to it maturing into an adult and beyond. In addition to increasing in size, the young of many animals undergo dramatic changes as they mature. The classic extreme example of this is the metamorphosis that a tadpole undergoes when becoming a frog. In dinosaurs, ontogenetic changes include bones fusing together, jaws size ratios changing, developing horns or frills, growing elaborate feathers, changes in their teeth, and much more.

{@i Tyrannosaurus} has very interesting ontogeny, as juveniles were strikingly different from their parents. So different in fact that some juvenile skeletons have been described as new genera. The most famous example of this is a specimen that was initially assigned to the new genus '{@i Nanotyrannus}'. Young {@i Tyrannosaurus} was lightly built with long thin legs, making it a faster animal. Its skull was also much lighter and elongate, although still distinctly tyrannosaurian, reducing its bite strength to size ratio significantly. It retained this gracile morphology until it was at least 13 years old, at which point it underwent a rapid period of growth and bulking until the age of about 15-18 years, but continued to grow afterwards (see {@book Ancient Tyrannosaurus Rex|PartneredDDDoD|8|Ancient Tyrannosaurus}).

entries.name: Niche Partitioning
entries: We know that young {@i Tyrannosaurus} was at least semi-precocial (able to fend for itself somewhat) and probably hunted its own food. The smaller size and gracile build of juvenile {@i Tyrannosaurus} made it a fast predator, but one that" could not tackle large prey. It likely would have snuck within charging range, then run down prey smaller than itself. This means that the two life-stages occupied different niches, relying on different resources to avoid direct competition with one another.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: We recommend that young {@i Tyrannosaurus} be played as an ambush predator, quietly stalking prey until it is close enough to charge. It can be significantly more active than its adult counterparts, since it will require lots of food to fuel its growth. Young {@i Tyrannosaurus} may have been less territorial than other similarly sized predators, as it was likely operating within one of its parent's territories. When challenged, it could flee to a parent, prompting them to seek out whoever upset its offspring.

entries.name: References
entries: Horner J.R., Goodwin M.B., and Myhrvold N. 2011. Dinosaur census reveals abundant {@i Tyrannosaurus} and rare ontogenetic stages in the Upper Cretaceous Hell Creek Formation (Maastrichtian), Montana, USA. {@i PLoS One}, {@b 6(2)}, e16574.
Peterson, J.E., and Daus, K.N. 2019. Feeding traces attributable to juvenile {@i Tyrannosaurus rex} offer insight into ontogenetic dietary trends. {@i PeerJ}, {@b 7}, e6573.
Peterson, J.E., Henderson, M.D., Scherer, R.P., and Vittore, C.P. 2009. Face biting on a juvenile tyrannosaurid and behavioral implications. {@i Palaios}, {@b 24(11)}, 780-784.
Peterson, J.E., Tseng, Z.J., and Brink, S. 2021. Bite force estimates in juvenile {@i Tyrannosaurus rex} based on simulated puncture marks. {@i PeerJ}, {@b 9}, e11450.
{@i "You-tie-ran-us"} {@b (Feathered tyrant)}

The silence of the frigid night-time forest was broken by the sound of deep, growlin' breathin'. In the darkness, those topaz eyes pierced the black veil, locked directly with mine. An eerie shiver ran up me back as a second, then third pair appeared.

{@i Yutyrannus} is an early tyrannosauroid. While much smaller than the true giants like {@creature Tyrannosaurus Rex|XMM} (see {@book The Rest of the Alphabet|PartneredDDDoD|7|Young Tyrannosaurus} and {@book Pledger's Custom Dinosaurs|PartneredDDDoD|8|Ancient Tyrannosaurus}), it was still a very large predator and is the biggest animal known with direct fossil evidence of feathers.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Yutyrannus} was a sizeable animal, estimated to be about 30 ft. long and weighing 1.5 tonnes. It was more lightly built than its larger cousins, although was still a powerful animal, and retained relatively long arms with three clawed fingers. It also possessed a small but distinctive head crest, accompanied by small, pointy brow horns.

{@i Yutyrannus} was covered in a thick layer of feathers, and these are preserved in some of its fossils. These feathers were undoubtedly used for insulation in the chilly Yixian Formation environment, but also perhaps for camouflage. As the largest predator currently known from Yixian, {@i Yutyrannus} is thought to have preyed on a variety of potential food items including ceratopsians, sauropods, therizinosaurs, hadrosaurs, ankylosaurs, and other theropods. It is presumed to be the arch-predator of the Yixian food chain.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: The first {@i Yutyrannus} fossils found were a near complete adult specimen associated with two smaller {@i Yutyrannus}, with one at least eight years younger than the adult. This association is unlikely to be chance and the assemblage probably represents an adult with its large (but still immature) offspring. The association of these three together suggests that {@i Yutyrannus} reared its young well past the hatchling stage and could indicate that they were group hunters. While still speculation, this hypothesis is supported by research into other large social predators and additional evidence also suggests that some tyrannosaurids probably lived in social or family groups.

We suggest that {@i Yutyrannus} be played as a dominant active predator living in small groups. During colder periods, they should be hunting considerably more to help maintain their energy reserves. Hunting {@i Yutyrannus} should be a deadly threat, able to pursue prey for a long time and potentially coordinate their attacks. When not hunting, they can be resting or be socialising, bickering and playing with each other. Nevertheless, they should opportunistically attack a party if they see them as easy prey.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Yutyrannus} was a tyrannosauroid, a highly diverse group of theropods ranging from 10 ft. long average-sized animals to 40 ft. long giants. They arose in the Middle Jurassic of Asia, and became one of the dominant theropod groups, spreading to modern day North America, across the northern palaeo-continent of Lauraisa. There is currently no record of them from the southern palaeo-continent of Gondwana, excluding perhaps one putative bone from Australia.

{@i Yutyrannus} is the largest dinosaur with preserved feathers, but other larger tyrannosauroids appear to have secondarily lost their full feather coat and replaced them with scales, or perhaps reducing them to a thin covering of small, sparse feathers.

entries.name: References
entries: Bell, P.R., Campione, N.E., Persons IV, W.S., Currie, P.J., Larson, P.L., Tanke, D.H., and Bakker, R.T. 2017. Tyrannosauroid integument reveals conflicting patterns of gigantism and feather evolution. {@i Biology letters}, {@b 13(6)}, 20170092.
McCrea, R.T. 2014. A 'Terror of Tyrannosaurs': The First Trackways of Tyrannosaurids and Evidence of Gregariousness and Pathology in Tyrannosauridae. {@i PLOS ONE}, {@b 9(7)}, e103613.

Snively, E., and Samman, T. 2015. Unexpected behavior in the Cretaceous: tooth-marked bones attributable to tyrannosaur play. A comment by E. Snively & T. Samman. {@i Ethology Ecology & Evolution}, {@b 27(4)}, 422-427.
Xu, X., Wang, K., Zhang, K., Ma, Q., Xing, L., Sullivan, C., Hu, D., Cheng, S., Wang, S., et al. 2012. A gigantic feathered dinosaur from the Lower Cretaceous of China. {@i Nature}, {@b 484}, 92-95.
{@i "Zal-mocks-ees"} {@b (Zalmoxis, a Dacian god)}

By far the most common dinosaurs we encountered on that bizarre island were the miniature ornithopods. They were awfully calm considerin' we was so much bigger than 'em. I only saw 'em spook when they were out of cover–obviously knowin' what circled above, or when someone made lots 'o noise and commotion. Otherwise, they seemed to just eat and make lil' chirpin' sounds at each other.
{@i Zalmoxes} is a small bipedal ornithopod and has been used as the textbook example of insular dwarfism in the fossil record.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Zalmoxes} is thought to have reached about 8-10 ft. in length and weighed 100-110 lb. It was a stout animal with relatively long forelimbs and a robust skull. Its teeth were simple and leaf shaped, set in a mouth tipped with a sharp beak.

{@i Zalmoxes} is quite small for its group, the Rhabdodontidae. This group of herbivorous ornithopod dinosaurs includes many large animals such as {@i Rhabdodon} and {@creature Iguanodon|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@book The Rest of the Alphabet|PartneredDDDoD|7|Iguanodon}), which could reach up to 20 ft. in length. This size difference, and the occurrence of {@i Zalmoxes} on Hațeg island, has led to it being the textbook example of insular dwarfism. However, a study in 2012 challenged this, arguing that the primitive {@i Zalmoxes} represents the ancestral size range for this group and that the other members instead evolved to be larger.

As a herbivore, {@i Zalmoxes}' strong jaws and powerful muscles allowed it to slice plants in a cutting action. Like many ornithopods, it was a capable chewer, allowing it to process a variety of tough plants effectively. However, its narrow head suggests that it may have instead been a selective feeder, picking out softer nutritious plant material. Either way, this allowed it to occupy a separate ecological niche on Hațeg Island from the larger herbivores, avoiding competition.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: While {@i Zalmoxes} had a strong bite, it was ultimately a small animal that would likely have run from threats, rather than fight. There is some evidence that rhabdodontids lived in herds and {@i Zalmoxes} may have moved in groups as a means of protection. We recommend that {@i Zalmoxes} be played as a very skittish animal. Herds should include sentries who frequently scan for threats and will sound an alarm if any are spotted. The sight of a party may cause them to flee, and they should only attack if cornered or trapped. Their stout body and timid nature would make them excellent options for taming as livestock.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: The Rhabdodontidae were a group of very successful relatively primitive ornithopods that included animals like {@creature Iguanodon|PartneredDDDoD} and Hypsilophodon. Rhabdodonts are currently exclusively European, as species previously considered rhabdodonts from Australia (Muttaburasaurus) and America (Tenontosaurus) have recently been reclassified as a sibling taxon (closely related but not part of the true group).

entries.name: References
entries: Benton, M.J., Csiki, Z., Grigorescu, D., Redelstorff, R., Sander, P.M., Stein, K., and Weishampel, D.B. 2010. Dinosaurs and the island rule: The dwarfed dinosaurs from Haţeg Island. {@i Palaeogeography, Palaeoclimatology, Palaeoecology}, {@b 293(3-4)}, 438-454.

Dieudonne, P.E., Tortosa, T., Torcida Fernandez-Baldor, F., Canudo, J.I., and Diaz-Martinez, I. 2016. An unexpected early rhabdodontid from Europe (Lower Cretaceous of Salas de los Infantes, Burgos Province, Spain) and a re-examination of basal iguanodontian relationships. {@i PloS one}, {@b 11(6)}, e0156251.

Weishampel, D., Csiki-Sava, Z., and Norman, D. 2003. Osteology and phylogeny of {@i Zalmoxes} (n. g.), an unusual Euornithopod dinosaur from the latest Cretaceous of Romania. {@i Journal of Systematic Palaeontology}, {@b 1(2)}, 65-123.
{@i "Zool"} {@b (after Zuul from Ghostbusters)}

As we moved over the rollin' scrub, we came across somethin' remarkable. A lone dinosaur feeding on scrub, entirely oblivious to us. Few times in my life had I ever come across such an unyieldin' amount of muscle and armour. When I first saw this thing, I knew it was built for one thing and one thing only–defence. We studied it in detail. Armoured back, armoured limbs, even armoured eyelids. Unbelievable. It didn't even seem to mind us flittin' around it.

{@i Zuul} is an ankylosaur from the Late Cretaceous (75 million years ago) Judith River Formation of North America. A close relative of {@i Ankylosaurus} that takes its name from the Ghostbusters franchise, it has recently revealed behavioural interactions of ankylosaurs.

entries.name: Ecology
entries: {@i Zuul} was a medium sized ankylosaur that measured approximately 20 ft. long and may have weighed 2 tonnes. Its morphology is typical for the ankylosaurs, with short stout legs, a wide body, rows of spikey osteoderms (bones embedded in the skin) that form a layer of armour, a broad head, and a heavy {@item club|XPHB} on the end of its tail. It had an enormous gut for its size, making it an extremely rotund animal.

{@i Zuul} was a low-grazing herbivore with broad, leaf-shaped teeth, and fed on a variety of ferns, shrubs, leaves, succulents, and fruits. It probably could not process hard woody plants like some other dinosaurs, although may have swallowed small stones (gastroliths) to help grind material in its stomach. It lived in coniferous forests among shade-dwelling plants, rather than in open fernland.

entries.name: Behaviour
entries: For many years it was assumed that ankylosaurs used their clubs exclusively to fight off predators. However, recent studies of {@i Zuul}'s holotype have revealed that several healed injuries were likely the result of tail-{@item club|XPHB} attacks from other {@i Zuul}. This indicates that it engaged in intraspecific combat, although its {@item club|XPHB} was undoubtedly also used as a defensive weapon. Additionally, an exceptionally preserved larynx found in Pinacosaurus, a small Asian ankylosaur, showed much stronger similarities to modern birds than crocodiles or reptiles. This suggests that the group produced complex high-pitched sounds and were quite vocal, perhaps even melodic, animals.

We suggest that {@i Zuul} be a relatively sedate animal, lumbering through the undergrowth, perhaps in small herds of ٤-٥ animals. A party might hear the clash of clubs against armour or a chorus of calls long before they see {@i Zuul}. As long as the herd isn't disturbed, {@i Zuul} should be non-aggressive, instead focusing on feeding and socialising. When threatened, any {@i Zuul} should stand its ground, making intimidating motions by swinging its heavy tail.

entries.name: Phylogeny
entries: {@i Zuul} is a member of the Ankylosauria. This group of armoured dinosaurs is divided into several subgroups, and included the relatively small animal {@creature Struthiosaurus|PartneredDDDoD} (see {@book Hațeg Island|PartneredDDDoD|5|Struthiosaurus}) and the larger well-known {@i Ankylosaurus}. Like {@i Ankylosaurus}, {@i Zuul} was an ankylosaurid and the two were closely related. Ankylosaurids seem to be restricted to Laurasia (North America, Europe, and Asia), but were very successful within that geographic range, appearing in the Early Cretaceous and surviving until the end-Cretaceous extinction.

entries.name: References
entries: Arbour, V.M., and Evans, D.C. 2017. A new ankylosaurine dinosaur from the Judith River Formation of Montana, USA, based on an exceptional skeleton with soft tissue preservation. {@i Royal Society Open Science}, {@b 4(5)}, 161086.
Arbour, V.M., Zanno, L.E., and Evans, D.C. 2022. Palaeopathological evidence for intraspecific combat in ankylosaurid dinosaurs. {@i Biology Letters}, {@b 18(12)}, 20220404.

Botfalvai, G., Prondvai, E., and Ősi, A. 2021. Living alone or moving in herds? A holistic approach highlights complexity in the social lifestyle of Cretaceous ankylosaurs. {@i Cretaceous Research}, {@b 118}, 104633.
Yoshida, J., Kobayashi, Y., and Norell, M.A. 2023. An ankylosaur larynx provides insights for bird-like vocalization in non-avian dinosaurs. {@i Communications Biology}, {@b 6(1)}, 152.

data.name: Introduction

entries.altText: Hunting ichthyosaurs leap out of the ocean to grab pterosaurs flying too close to the surface.

entries: Welcome adventurer and thank you sincerely for supporting our book. We are delighted that you've chosen to include palaeontological elements into your games and we hope that you enjoy using these rules and artwork as much as we did creating them.

We are PalaeoGames, a team of palaeontology research scientists and artists who have a passion for tabletop roleplaying games. {@i Dr Dhrolin's Dictionary of Dinosaurs} is our first major palaeontological outreach project, and we are immensely thankful to the wonderful pledgers who have helped make this dream a reality.

entries.name: What's in the Book?
entries: This book contains homebrew rules for including a variety of scientifically credible prehistoric elements in your 5e tabletop roleplaying games. These include reconstructions of Mesozoic reptiles, environmental reconstructions, and behaviour tables all based on real science. We've also included a variety of fantasy rules, such as playable species, subclasses, items, backgrounds, mutations tables, etc. With these prehistoric elements, you can build a prehistoric campaign, or add deep history to your existing world.
In addition to these gaming elements are sections addressing some of the science of palaeontology. We hope that you find them accessible and informative to read.

entries.name: Design Philosophy
entries: Life is diverse. We find that the current 5.5e system of normal, proficiency, and expertise for saves/skills/attacks/etc. calculations based on one chosen stat is insufficient to express that diversity. To give us more granularity in our designs and to better represent what we think these animals were like in real life, we have largely disregarded this system. This allows us to increase/decrease the offensive/defensive capabilities of our Mesozoic reptile designs without over-inflating/deflating their base stats.

We've also added names to the armour class of each of our creatures, describing their defensive integument (skin/fur/feathers). This is purely to give DMs and players the opportunity to better visualise and describe combat. While reading this book, you will notice that a creature's modifiers do not necessarily match its stat bonus and {@variantrule Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus}.

If you wish, you may recalculate any of these creatures' Saving Throws, skill bonuses, attacks or abilities, using their ability score bonuses and {@variantrule Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus}, applying proficiency and expertise where you see fit. You may also rename their armour to "Natural Armour".

entries.name: Why Include Palaeontology in Your Games?

entries.title: Cosmolepis
entries.altText: A classical illustration of a slab of rock with an exceptionally preserved fossil fish on it called Cosmolepis. It has a deep wide body and a rounded head.

entries: We believe that there are several compelling reasons to include realistic ancient creatures and palaeontology in your campaigns. They are:

items: Including unusual ancient creatures can be a fun way to mix up the typical fantasy tropes of dragons and goblins, and give your players a chance to encounter creatures they may not have encountered before in other campaigns. Entire story arcs can be created around these creatures, providing a wealth of inspiration for your campaign.

They can be used to add further depth to an already established dinosaur-themed setting. For example, an ancient Lizardfolk temple might be defended by Lizardfolk riding dinosaurs and this book provides dozens of creatures that could be used as alternative mounts.

Palaeontology can be used to add realism and authenticity to your game world. For example, the presence of fossilised remains can give your players a sense of the history and age for the world they are in.

Creatures that look and behave in realistic ways can add a sense of immersion and believability to your game world. Your players may end up being more invested in the story if they feel like they are interacting with creatures that could have actually existed. When combined with scientifically accurate environmental reconstructions, you can provide a truly immersive experience.

entries.name: Why do We Feel This is Important?
entries: Palaeontology is a gateway science. That is, it is one of the first sciences that children and young adults are introduced to and acts as a point of entry for general scientific interest. It inspires awe in the natural world via the reconstruction of animals so dynamic that they seem like mythical monsters, as well as introducing topics like evolution that are fundamental for understanding the world around us. We have no doubt that, without it, many of the world's top scientists would be in other careers.

However, with this excitement and adoration comes an unusual negative side effect. Unlike most other sciences, palaeontology seems to hold a special place in people's hearts, leading to a deep nostalgia for the toys and media that they experienced as a child. Notably, this includes monstrous depictions that echo inaccuracies of the earliest outdated reconstructions. Correcting those inaccuracies has generally been met with vicious opposition, ridicule, and claims that "science is ruining dinosaurs", although it is worth noting that this has changed drastically in the last 10 years or so. While seemingly innocuous, this scientific dissidence has given space for a small, but vocal, group of science deniers to air their views. Those views are typically grounded in religious extremism, but have far-reaching consequences, particularly when they enter the school curriculum.

In addition to the more serious concern outlined above, there are other issues caused by palaeontology's unusual popularity and nostalgia. In public discourse, palaeontology functions more like pop culture, with large fan-based communities that idolise or despise particular scientists and their research. There is more to discuss there than we can adequately address in this book, but it is important to highlight some of the challenges faced by scientists while disseminating research. This is why we invest so much time and effort into projects like this.

entries.name: Who are we?
entries: The gaming world is full of wonderful people who have a deep passion for palaeontology and want to share that passion with others through their artwork and designs. PalaeoGames falls into that category, but also brings something more. PalaeoGames is composed of scientists publishing in the field of palaeontology, rather than enthusiastic amateurs. We are active researchers who form our designs and reconstructions based on published data. That means that the way these animals are portrayed is done so to the best of our scientific understanding of them, albeit with a little flexibility for things like movement speed and perception to allow them to function properly in-game. entries.name: Understanding Palaeontology

entries.altText: Four small tyrannosaur chicks examine a surrounding tall conifer forest, sniffing at the air.

entries: In this section, we outline educational information about palaeontology and its associated subjects, as well as how to be a palaeontologist.

entries.name: What do Palaeontologists do?
entries: Palaeontology (UK spelling) or paleontology (US spelling) is the study of ancient life and the natural world. Palaeontologists use fossils and associated evidence in the rock record to interpret the past. It is an extremely complex interdisciplinary science, requiring a strong foundation in geology (including sedimentology, geochemistry, radiometric dating, palaeotopography, and palaeoclimatology), biology (evolution, biochemistry, anatomy, ecology, behaviour, and phylogeny), and mathematics (data analysis [usually statistical] and modelling). Specialist aspects of palaeontology may require further expertise in physics, programming, cosmology, science communication, and many other disciplines. In this section, we will cover the fundamentals of palaeontology.

entries.name: Types of Palaeontologist and Associated Careers
entries: There are many different types of palaeontologist and anyone can contribute to the field. The good news is that you don't need any formal education to make ground-breaking (literally) discoveries in this field. We like to summarise different contributions to palaeontology as, academic, semi-academic, and associated roles.

{@b Academic} palaeontologists include scientific researchers, lecturers, and some research museum {@item staff|XPHB}. A long career may encompass several or all of these aspects, as well as consultancy work for several industries. Academic palaeontologists require the most time and investment to achieve the level of education needed to fulfil their roles and there are few positions world-wide. This effort is rewarded by the opportunity to investigate and examine the best fossils in the world, as well as to be on the cutting edge of research.

There is an unbelievable variety of research areas and working styles within academic palaeontology. Some spend almost their entire careers behind a computer screen, reading and re-evaluating decades-old datasets, others program complex analyses to determine evolutionary relationships, some examine and describe the characteristics of new species, some test the mechanics of fossil anatomy, and others undertake field excursions to examine rock outcrops. Many palaeontologists specialise in several areas and their jobs could include several such aspects, while others hyper-specialise in one specific attribute of one group of organisms.

{@b Semi-academic} palaeontologists generally include field guides, museum {@item staff|XPHB}, palaeoartists, and science communicators. Their work is vital for helping disseminate knowledge to the general public and the level of education among these individuals varies greatly. Some may have considerable education in palaeontology, including post-graduate studies, while others may be entirely self-educated.

Caution must be used when listening to a self-proclaimed palaeontologist, as the field is prone to "armchair experts" who spread misinformation. For every real expert, there are a hundred misguided amateurs who repeat misinformation they read online, or even embellish it with further misinformation to garner greater traffic to their social media profiles. This is a serious issue within palaeontology that has real-world impacts.

{@b Palaeo-associated} roles include fossil preparators, fossil collectors, and fossil dealers. There is an entire industry around the extraction, cleaning, and sale of fossils, and these individuals facilitate it. They are typically not formally trained in palaeontology, but some can still be exceptionally knowledgeable. Their roles enable the safe recovery of millions of fossils that would otherwise be destroyed by weathering. The discovery of thousands of species can be attributed to non-academics such as these and their activities are an extremely important component of palaeontology as a whole. There is also a colossal community of people who fossil hunt as a hobby (including many of the academics and semi-academics). No formal education is required to be a fossil hunter, but it helps to have a good understanding of what you're looking for.

entries.title: Classic 1880s dinosaur skeletals. {@i Stegosaurus}, {@i Diplodocus}, {@i Triceratops}.
entries.altText: Classical reconstructions from the 1880s of the skeletons of Stegosaurus, Diplodocus, and Triceratops.

entries.name: Types of Fossils
entries: To study ancient life, we examine evidence left in the fossil record. There are many different types of fossils and they can range in age from a few thousand years to billions of years old. They all preserve information about an organism or its behaviour. Below are the key different types of fossils:

entries.name: Body Fossils
entries: {@b Preserved organic remains and unaltered mineralised remains.}

items: Some carcasses preserve the actual body parts of an animal for thousands of years–that is, the original tissues are stabilised in a way that some of the in-life components remain. Technically, these aren't fossils, but palaeontologists often still study them. This type of preservation is very young (just a few thousand years) and usually occurs as mummified or frozen remains, or hard parts (shells and bone) that remain chemically the same as in life.

entries: {@b Carbonisation.}

items: Organic remains can be carbonised by the temperatures and pressures of geological processes. The crushing weight and baking heat cook the fossil, resulting in a carbon residue. Many feathers on dinosaurs are preserved in this manner.

entries: {@b Mineral replacement (permineralisation).}

items: This is what most people think of when hearing the word "fossil". These are components of an organism that have been replaced by minerals such as calcite or silica. Iconic dinosaur bones and mineralised arthropods/plants all fall under this category. Dissolved minerals are usually carried in water flowing through the sediment. The organic tissues, or cavities within them, act as a point for those dissolved minerals to precipitate, and they replicate the original shape of whatever they are replacing. There are a huge variety of minerals that can replace tissues, and some of them only require a few hours to do so. Some minerals can also form spontaneously within a carcass from elements freed by the processes of decay.

entries: {@b Moulds and casts.}

items: When sediment deposits around an organism and hardens, but then the body parts dissolve or rot away, it leaves behind a cavity with the same overall shape as the remains. This often occurs when shelly fossils are preserved in sediment, but then subsequently dissolve. In some cases, the cavity (mould) is then infilled by another mineral or sediment, creating a rough replication (cast) of the fossil.

Trace fossils are evidence of an animal interacting with its environment; usually deforming soft sediments that then cement into hard stone. These can be footprints, swim marks, burrows, nests, or marks from an organism tunnelling within sediment.

Some fossil information can be inferred from other fossils. For example, chew marks on a fossil leaf can provide evidence of certain insects that are otherwise not preserved. Although this is a type of trace fossil, we distinguish it here as it requires other organisms to be preserved.
Some organisms have no physical parts of their bodies preserved, but the presence of their remains changed the chemistry of the host sediment.

Overarching geological changes in our world can be evidence of past life. The most obvious of these is the addition of abundant gaseous oxygen into Earth's atmosphere from photosynthesis. This caused a dramatic change in the chemistry of our planet's rocks.

entries.title: {@i Aspidorhynchus}
entries.altText: A classical illustration of a slab of rock with an exceptionally preserved fossil fish on it called Aspidorhynchus. It has a long, thin body and a pointed snout.

entries.name: How is a Fossil made?
entries: This is a surprisingly complex question to answer, depending on the type of fossil. The truth is that there are many ways in which an organism may be preserved in the fossil record (as outlined above by the types of fossils). It may seem obvious that slowing the processes of decay is the key factor, either through harsh environmental conditions (like extreme salt levels or total lack of oxygen) or rapid burial under metres of mud. In actuality, to preserve soft tissues, a fine balance is required between these preservational processes and decay itself. Decay is necessary to create chemical bonding sites for mineral deposition and to liberate elements from a carcass. These, in turn, create chemical gradients that stimulate mineral precipitation. We now also know that, in some situations, this process can occur within hours, rather than millions of years.
Nevertheless, the most common steps that yield large three-dimensional fossils are:

items: An organism dies (usually near water).
The carcass is rapidly buried by mud/sand or sinks into soupy sediments.

In some cases, oxygen is depleted from the sediment, preventing excessive decay and allowing the preservation of soft tissues. This is not necessarily required for the preservation of shells and bone.
Dissolved minerals in the sediment pore waters deposit in/on the carcass, mineralising it.
The surrounding sediments cement into solid rock.
The rock is in a relatively geologically stable area, and so the fossil is not exposed to excessive heat or pressure.
The rock is uplifted (or sea levels drop) and weathered by wind and rain to expose the fossilised remains.

entries.name: Studying Fossils, Creating a Hypothesis, Collecting Evidence
entries: Once a palaeontologist has gained access to a fossil or fossil collection (either acquired themselves or accessed through a pre-existing collection), they utilise the scientific method to learn more about it and disseminate their findings through scientific publications. This can be broken down into the following steps:
{@b Project:} Determining what is being studied and setting general goals is the first step. These could include:

items: Describing the characteristics of a new fossil and finding its position in the tree of life.
Determining what factors have allowed for the preservation of a fossil, or have altered it over time.
Improving understanding of a particular fossil species (with regards to its evolutionary relationships, how it looked, how it behaved, where it lived, what it ate, etc.).
Undertake new largescale analyses that provide information about a collection of fossils (i.e. reassessing the evolutionary relationships between multiple organisms).

entries: {@b Hypothesis:} In some cases, a hypothesis based on current observations must then be formed. A well-designed scientific hypothesis should be clear, concise, and based on existing knowledge and evidence. It must also be falsifiable, meaning that it can be tested and potentially proven incorrect. It usually makes a statement about the relationship between two or more variables. i.e. "{@i Tyrannosaurus rex} specalised in feeding on large herbivorous dinosaurs."

entries.title: {@i Asteracanthus} fin spine
entries.altText: The well-preserved fossil fin spine of the extinct cartilaginous fish Asteracanthus.

items: {@b Exceptions:} Classic hypothesis-driven science isn't always applicable in palaeontology. When describing a new species, the goal is to determine whether a specimen possesses enough new characteristics to warrant the erection of a new species/genus. This is a somewhat subjective decision, although there are precedents established within the palaeontological community.

{@b Null Hypothesis:} Some researchers include a null hypothesis, which is the inverse of the hypothesis. The null hypothesis provides a baseline against which the results of the experiment can be compared to ensure that the observed results did not arise by chance. i.e. "{@i Tyrannosaurus rex} did not specalise in feeding on large herbivorous dinosaurs."

entries: {@b Data collection:} As much data as possible must now be gathered to prove/disprove the hypothesis.

items: In our example, we might seek for evidence of tyrannosaur bite marks on large herbivorous dinosaurs, examine suspected tyrannosaur coprolites (fossilised dung) for bone fragments, and examine the mechanics of tyrannosaur jaws.

Data collection should be as comprehensive as possible, but must also be realistic within the timeframe and budget of the research project. Some evidence may be contradictory and its important to gather diverse data, rather than focus on one supporting point.

There are myriad techniques to collect fossil data. These may be simple measurements taken with a ruler and microscope, or they can be complex geochemical analyses that use sophisticated analytical tools like x-ray diffraction, hyperspectral phasor analysis, or energy dispersive x-ray fluorescence. Some data collection involves recording fossil characteristics in a data matrix, then processing them through complex algorithms that assess how similar fossils with different characteristics are to each other.

entries: {@b Testing:} One of the key things that must be tested is statistical significance. This isn't a measurement of how important results are, but rather a mathematical calculation to determine whether the results could have arisen by chance. It helps give a degree of confidence.

items: Algorithmic results may be run thousands of times to search for the most parsimonious (least complex) answer.

However, it is not always possible to perform 'neat' statistical analysis when studying fossils, as data sets are often incomplete. We frequently have to work around gaps in the fossil record and the inherent variability of biology in general.

entries: {@b Discuss and draw conclusions:} Once a data set has been collected and its robustness assessed, discussion of key points can begin and ultimately conclusions can be drawn. These should determine which hypothesis is supported.

{@b Peer review:} One of the most important steps in the scientific process is peer review. Before results can be published, they must be reviewed by other experts in the same field. These are often anonymous and provide comments and recommendations about how research can be improved, or whether further testing is required.

items: {@b Self-correcting:} Science is not flawless, and errors often bypass peer review. However, review and reassessment tend to tease out errors over time. Steadily, our understanding is refined as new generations of scientists reanalyse and verify/adjust older results.

entries.altText: A side view of a skull belonging to the horned dinosaur Chasmosaurus.

entries.name: Reconstructing an Extinct Organism
entries: Once palaeontologists have gathered enough information about an organism, they will often provide a reconstruction of the animal's morphology and/or behaviour to provide a clearer picture of how the animal lived. This may be accompanied by a reconstruction of the environment in which it lived. Palaeontologists use a variety of techniques to reconstruct extinct animals, including functional morphology, comparative anatomy, phylogenetic bracketing, and an understanding of the animal's environment.

Functional morphology involves the study of the structure and movements of an organism's tissues, and how they interact to allow for a particular function. This process is essentially reverse engineering–working out the task using only the tools. Functional morphology is combined with comparative anatomy to determine the most likely use and appearance of fossil tissues. Comparative anatomy is the comparison of the anatomy of extinct animals with the anatomy of living species. This allows palaeontologists to provide evidence of the possible uses of a particular tissue/organ/structure by watching similar structures being used in the modern world.

These techniques are further combined with phylogenetic bracketing to extrapolate missing components of the fossil. Phylogenetic bracketing uses evolutionary relationships to infer the unknown characteristics of extinct organisms by looking at the known characteristics of closely related organisms. For example, if a new fossil wolf species is found only from bones, we can safely say that it was likely covered in fur, as all other known wolves (both alive and extinct) are covered in fur.

Finally, the environmental context in which an extinct animal lived can also provide valuable information for its reconstruction. Paleontologists study the geological and paleontological context of fossil finds, including the types of rock formations, the climate and vegetation at the time, and the presence of other fossils. This information is used to understand the habitat and lifestyle of extinct animals and inform their reconstruction.

entries.name: Palaeontology Associated Information

entries.altText: Two broad-winged pterosaurs called Anhangeura fly high above coastal waters, disturbing a flock of birds as they pass. Moody clouds rest in the sky above the mountainous coast.

entries: Palaeontology is a broad subject that intermingles with many other sciences. In this section we provide introductory information about the geological timescale, the processes of evolution, and the formation of life on Earth. If you are interested in fossils, these are extremely useful subjects to be familiar with. There are many other useful associated topics and we recommend you seek out further introductory information on geochemistry, biochemistry, and sedimentology. We have not covered those subjects here as they require much more information than is feasible for us to include in this chapter.

entries.name: Deep Time and the Geological Timescale
entries: The Earth is about 4 billion years old. We know this because of a method called radiometric dating. Radiometric dating works by looking at the different types of atoms, called isotopes, that make up any given material, and how those atoms have changed over time. Certain isotopes are unstable and change into other types of atoms over time by giving off radiation. By measuring the amount of these isotopes in a rock or other material and comparing it to that isotope's half-life, we can figure out how long it has been since that material formed.

An isotope's half-life is the amount of time it takes for half of the isotopes in a sample to change into a different isotope. For example, the isotope carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years, which means that if you start with a sample of carbon-14, after 5,730 years, half of the carbon-14 atoms in the sample will have changed into nitrogen-14 atoms. After another 5,730 years, half of the remaining carbon-14 atoms will have changed (so you would have only a quarter of what you started with), and so on.

This works on much larger timescales too. For example, rock containing a lot of uranium-238 and very little lead-206, tells us that the rock is relatively young, because it hasn't been around long enough for all of the uranium-238 to change into lead-206. Isotopes like this are not present in all rocks. They're usually restricted to igneous and volcanic deposits, and so we have to estimate the age of different rocks by their nearest volcanic deposits. We can improve this estimate using biostratigraphy.

Biostratigraphy is the process of establishing occurrence ranges of different fossil groups (usually in a place where radiometric dating can corroborate their age), then using those fossils to determine the age of rock elsewhere where radiometric dating cannot be used. The best fossils to use are those that had wide distributions and floated in water, like ammonites and graptolites. By determining the occurrence and absence of multiple groups, we can pinpoint a rather accurate age range of rocks that include these fossils.

With all of this information, geologists have created the geological timescale, which is a way of dividing up Earth's history into different divisions and subdivisions of time. These divisions are determined by the types of rocks that formed and the major changes in fossil groups through Earth's history. In this book, we focus on the Mesozoic era (252-66 million years ago), which is subdivided into the Triassic period (252-201 million years ago), Jurassic period (201-145 million years ago), and Cretaceous period (145-66 million years ago).
