entries.name: Understanding Evolution
entries: Evolutionary theory is the foundation of our modern understanding of biology, ecology, and medicine, and misinformation about evolution is a genuine threat to everyone's wellbeing. You've no doubt had people claim that evolution isn't real or is "just a theory" (a misunderstanding of the term "theory"; in terms of science, a theory is the highest category of knowledge and understanding, and therefore also confidence, in an idea). These people are mistaken and, in our experience, usually have a political or religious agenda behind their statements. Regardless, evolution is observable and below is a brief summary of how it occurs in living organisms.

Evolution is the process by which lineages of organisms change over time. When organisms reproduce, their offspring inherit a mix of traits from the parents (i.e. eye colour, hair colour, height, etc.) by the passing on of particular genes. Genes have heritability, which is the measurement of how variable their associated traits are. This allows a population of individuals to differ subtly, and if a particular variation increases an organism's chances of survival, it will accumulate and spread within the population over time. The iconic example of this is a giraffe's long neck. The gene that codes for neck length allows for some variation in length. Giraffes underwent a period where food was scarce, and so those with slightly longer necks were able to access more leaves on higher trees than others, increasing their survivability. Over time, fewer giraffes with short necks survived and reproduced, and the variance of neck length shifted to include longer necks and exclude shorter necks. This scarcity of food was a selection pressure, and the increased survivability of long-necked giraffes was natural selection at work.

In addition to heritability, mutation contributes to the variability of offspring. None of us are identical to our parents, even when accounting for heritability. This is because errors can occur during gene replication and these result in further subtle variations. Most have little impact on the overall function of an organism. However, when they do and if they are advantageous, just like favourable heritability variations, they may then propagate within a community.

While the survival of individuals is important, there are also factors that influence the survival of groups of closely related organisms. A trait that appears detrimental to one individual's reproductive success can be advantageous for other closely related individuals, and so despite the first individual not producing offspring, the gene coding for it is propagated in the offspring of their relatives. There are many examples of this, with the most heavily investigated example being homosexuality. Competing hypotheses have been presented to precisely explain the origin of this trait (see "Evolution of Homosexuality" by Savolainen and Hodgson), but its occurrence across the animal kingdom (including in mammals, birds, reptiles, and insects) is indicative of its role in group survival.

There is another key process in evolution. A group of individuals that become isolated from other members of their species may be affected by different selection pressures. After many generations, these different pressures cause them to become so different genetically that they can no longer successfully interbreed with their former species if they were to return. In essence, this causes them to become a new species and is a process we called speciation. When enough changes accrue over thousands of generations, the new species can look drastically different and eventually they may differ enough that we categorise them as an entirely new group of organisms.

entries.name: The Origin of Life on Earth
entries: We have a hypothetical understanding of how life arose on Earth from non-living material. We call this process abiogenesis. We also know that this occurred relatively early in Earth's history and so is likely to have occurred in many places within our galaxy. Below is an extremely simplified summary of this process:

items: In Earth's early history, abiotic (non-living) chemical processes created simple molecules similar to the individual bases of ribonucleic acid (RNA) and deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) in a water medium. This is sometimes referred to as "primordial soup". These molecules are not alive, but their structure stimulates the formation of another paired molecule adjacent to them, which in turn allows self-replication of the original molecule.

When the first molecules like these were encased in oily bubbles, they formed the basis from which all life evolved. The individual bases were small enough to move freely in/out of each oily bubble, but when they first form chains within an oily bubble, they became too large to leave and the first "protocells" were formed. Chains of bases replicated themselves, and the replicated base chains were also constrained within the protocell.

Osmotic pressure created by these chained bases made the protocell more physically resistant than bubbles without internal molecules. This allowed protocells to absorb smaller, less resistant bubbles, causing them to grow in size.

As they increased in size, with more molecule chains forming inside them, they eventually reached a size where the physical flow of water broke them apart, with each subsequent protocell containing some of the internal molecules. This is the origin of reproduction.

Some chains of molecules were able to interact with other types of molecules (namely amino acids, which also can occur naturally), causing those molecules to form chains where they wouldn't normally. These chains of amino acids formed proteins.

In certain proteins, the chains of amino acids form at angles, causing the protein to fold or curve. This, in turn, can cause a complex interplay of atoms positioned around a particular point that creates an area on the protein that functions chemically. We call this an active site.

Any protein that increased the resistance of the protocell, or increased the speed/efficiency that it replicated, passively propagated more than others. This was the first occurrence of evolution and essentially the start of life. Every single iteration and development of life as we know it was a derivation of this process.

entries.name: So, You want to be a Palaeontologist?

entries.title: Top: {@i Kritosaurus} (left), {@i Diplodocus} (right) Bottom: {@i Triceratops} (left), {@i Tyrannosaurus} (right)
entries.altText: The skulls of multiple dinosaurs including the hadrosaur Kritosaurus, the sauropod Diplodocus, the ceratopsian Triceratops, and the theropod Tyrannosaurus.

entries: If you want to be a palaeontologist, academic or otherwise, the first step is getting a basic education in geology and biology. This doesn't necessarily require schooling, as beginner information can be found online and in many widely available books. This core understanding will allow you to avoid the pitfalls that many enthusiastic novices fall into, such as mistaking common geological structures for fossil material.

Once you have this basic understanding, you can either pursue further education within academia, or just get fossil hunting! However, if you're diving straight into hunting, {@b you must familiarise yourself with local and national laws on the extraction of fossils.} In some countries, fossil collecting is illegal without a permit. In others, you can collect loose fossils, but digging into rock is prohibited. You can seek out local fossil hunting groups for guidance on these matters.

To pursue an academic career, you will likely need a degree in palaeontology, geology, or biology. Many universities around the world now offer dedicated degree pathways for the study of palaeontology (sometimes called palaeobiology), and the entry requirements vary depending on the university. Almost every university with a geology department will teach modules on palaeontology.
The typical education requirement (in the UK) is as follows:

items: School education (typically until the age of 18).
Undergraduate education (3-4 years).
Master's education (1-2 years).
Doctoral education (3-5 years).
2-4 Postdoctoral research positions (2-4 years each).

entries: This is an intimidating timeframe, but don't worry–some full-time working positions only require an undergraduate degree. For more information about becoming a palaeontologist, we recommend the book "So you want to be a palaeontologist" by Dr David Penney ({@link https://siriscientificpress.co.uk/products/so-you-want-to-be-a-palaeontologist|https://siriscientificpress.co.uk/products/so-you-want-to-be-a-palaeontologist}).

Another great resource is the "Archosaur Musings" by Dr David Hone covering how to become a palaeontologist ({@link https://archosaurmusings.wordpress.com/2018/07/04/how-do-i-become-a-palaeontologist/|https://archosaurmusings.wordpress.com/2018/07/04/how-do-i-become-a-palaeontologist/}).

entries.name: Finding, Understanding, and Interpretting Fossils
entries: Anyone can find a fossil, and anyone can learn to identify it. However, there are important steps to take in this process:

items: {@b Where should you look?} Keep in mind that fossils are preserved in sedimentary rocks and distorted versions of them may be infrequently preserved in metamorphic rocks. Igneous rocks do not directly preserve fossils. So, understanding the basic geology of where you're looking is the first step to knowing whether fossils will be present.
{@b How old it is?} It is important to understand the age of the rocks you're looking at so that you know what could be found.

{@b Temper your expectations.} Fossils are not found in all sedimentary rocks. In fact, the process of fossilisation is phenomenally rare, and it is only the overwhelming abundance of life on Earth that has given us the misrepresentation that fossils can be common. That said, when the right conditions are present, you can find a remarkable number of exceptionally preserved fossils together. We call these locations Lagerstätten (German for "deposit").

{@b Instant museum quality.} You very rarely find perfectly preserved fossils visible lying around. More often than not, they will be partially worn and mixed into beach sand/shingle, or will be encased in rock with only small marks indicating their presence. The latter of these may be exposed through a few preparatory techniques. Expert preparers will take hours, days, or even weeks of painstaking work to expose a fossil perfectly.

{@b Learn cross-sections.} Rocks split along their points of weakness. This can be around a fossil, but may equally be through it, splitting the fossil as well. It is important to be able to interpret a fossil as a cut cross-section through any angle. Cross-sections often look drastically different from complete fossils, and it takes time to learn to interpret them.

{@b Pseudofossils.} Some geological structures can look like body fossils at first glance. Flint is the biggest culprit of tricking novice fossil hunters into thinking they've found a piece of bone (although flint can form trace fossils when infilling a burrow). It is always worth familiarising yourself with the local geology to ensure you don't misinterpret something.

entries.name: Wrap up
entries: We hope that you found the information in this chapter both interesting and digestible. With it, you could take the first steps to becoming a palaeontologist as a full-time career or explore collecting your own fossils. There is so much more that we would love to discuss and explain, but it's time to get to the meat of this book–the roleplaying content. Let's get some dinosaurs into your games!

data.name: Including Palaeontological Elements in Your Games

entries.altText: A fish-bowl view of an ancient environment with the perspective being partially submerged in water, showing an array of grey rocks and tree stumps in shallow water, while a forested coastline sits off to the right and a large flock of pterosaurs fly past above.

entries.name: Campaign Settings
entries: There are many ways that you could include palaeontological elements in your campaigns. You can build an entire campaign setting based on these rules, add in a specific story arc to an existing campaign, or simply scatter these elements throughout your established worlds. Below are four story prompts, pulling from popular fiction, to help inspire you.

entries.name: Necromancer Island

entries.altText: A boat pulls into a small dock at the base of a large, mountainous and an ominously lit island. The island is heavily forested with large walls and fire-lit watch towers spanning it, separating the forest into paddocks.

entries: From the ship's brow Dr Dhrolin could see a dark outline through the thick mist. As the ship approached, the fog cleared sluggishly, revealing a small mountainous island. Dotted along its imposing silhouette were the outlines of stone buildings nestled among dense jungle. The ship slowed to a stop as it pulled into a shallow harbour. Standing on the dock was a well-dressed figure in white, clutching a {@item staff|XPHB}. His trimmed white beard parted into a broad grin. "Welcome to Necromancer Island, travellers. I trust your stay will be eventful", he bellowed, beckoning Dr Dhrolin off of the ship. Little did he know what horrors awaited him there.

Taking cues from popular culture is an ideal way to incorporate unusual elements into your games. The suggestion above may be the most obvious reference, but fleshing out your world with additional elements can make for a unique and compelling story. Necromancer Island is fundamentally based on the re-animation of ancient creatures, either by one powerful necromancer, or by a dedicated cult. However, the main question is why? Why would these individuals want to re-animate such creatures? Are they academic curiosities, weapons of war, or flights of fancy for a rich benefactor? Could they be all three? We like to envision Necromancer Island as the pursuit of several powerful wizards, driven by academic curiosity, but funded by a mysterious noble. The motives of that noble remain a unknown, but the avarice of the wizards keeps them from asking further questions. You can flesh out the background of that mysterious noble in any manner of ways. Perhaps they are a dragon in disguise researching an alternative origin for their species, or an ambitious politician preparing to launch a coup with an army of dinosaurs.

entries.altText: A bald elderly orc with bushy white beard, wearing white furs, and carrying a cane topped in an amber crystal, throws his arms up in excitement. A large metal skull amulet hangs around his neck.

entries: In your world, how is Necromancer Island constructed? Is it a single fortress surrounded by dense jungle filled with dinosaurs, or is it a series of enclosures housing different species? Are those enclosures bound by magical means, or simply high walls? Is it far out in the ocean, or just off the coast of a populated region? We like the idea that the island is dotted with wizard towers, each housing a single necromancer who specialises in one species of dinosaur, pterosaur, or other ancient creature.

It's worth putting time into planning how these creatures will behave. Are they under the complete control of the necromancer(s), or are they essentially wild? You can run these creatures as wild animals based on the behavioural details we have provided, or you can have them enact the will of another. What would happen if these creatures escaped from Necromancer Island, either by their own means or by sabotage?! The various planes of existence offer even more variety to the consequence of this. What would happen if an entire ecosystem of dinosaurs spilled into the Plane of Air or the Nine Hells? Better yet, what would happen if they then persisted there for hundreds or thousands of years? How would they be transformed by the natural energies or alignment of that plane?

entries.name: The Ancient Plateau

entries.altText: A pair of pterosaurs fly past a high, flat plateau that rises above the clouds. Its sheer cliffs drop off below the cloud line.

entries: Before him stood an impossibly high cliff, extending well beyond the clouds above. Droplets of water dribbled down the cliff wall, giving it a dull and soft edge, glistening with a moist shine. The slippery sheer face seemed nigh impossible to climb and the howling winds above prevented those that had preceded him from ascending. But, in all those decades of searching, none had the skill, determination, and luck of Dr Dhrolin and his team. He held the scrying key to the cliff face, revealing four arcane glowing runes. Gibberish to anyone but the most ancient of gods, they spelt out a command to open a path. A path that no being had trodden for eons. All he needed to do now was decipher the command. Easy-peasy.

What happens if these environments are already present in your world, just entirely concealed from prying eyes? Some classic sci-fi works have envisioned ancient plateaus hidden from the rest of the world, where prehistoric ecosystems persist. Alternatively, an isolated island could achieve the same effect. This is a phenomenon we see in the real-world, with island habitats allowing relic species to persist long past their extinction in other areas.

When implementing an ancient plateau-style environment, think about how this could be possible in a world full of magic and mystery. Are there natural or artificial barriers protecting the region from discovery? These could be howling, perhaps magical, winds that prevent air travel, powerful magnetic fields that prevent navigation and teleportation, or simply vicious predators that pick off would-be adventurers.

Maybe the plateau is a well-known phenomenon, but is simply inaccessible. If this is the case, what might tempt adventurers to explore it? Does the fame and glory of simply discovering the world above provide all the motivation needed, or are there rumoured ancient ruined cities of gold, relics of long-dead civilisations lost to time, to tempt adventurers up? Perhaps the adventurers are accompanying (or running) a scientific expedition, harking back to the days of Charles Darwin and his voyages on the Beagle.

entries.name: The Mad Chronoficer

entries: Banging rhythmically on the heavy wooden door, the city guards were eventually able to burst through, splintering wood across the stone floor. They piled in and scattered throughout the exposed hall, clearing a path for Dr Dhrolin and his party. Inside, the air hung coldly. Tiny ice crystals drifted suspended in the air, stinging at Dr Dhrolin's skin as he moved through the building. Eventually, the group reached a grand hall. The floor and walls were embossed with beautifully sculpted gold filigree in broad spiral patterns. Atop the end of the hall was a balcony with a smartly dressed dragonborn glaring down at the party and guards. Wafts of cloudy breath emitted from her as she muttered under her breath "No, no. It's not time yet.". Reaching to her side, she pulled a large lever, springing the room into unnatural life. The filigree illuminated with an icy blue glow and the party found themselves floating helplessly for a moment. The last thing they recall was a bright blue flash and a piercing headache. From that point on, all they could sense was the press of a dense humid jungle around them and the cawing of strange creatures in the distance.

entries.title: Plataleorhynchus
entries.altText: Several Platelorhynchus pterosaurs fly high in the sky.

entries: Our preferred means of introducing palaeontological elements into your games is to have the player characters hurtled through time. This places them wholly within the environments and ecosystems described in this book, allowing you to make the most of everything in a cohesive manner. We recommend that this be caused by an NPC who has limited and poorly controlled power over time (the Chronoficer). That way, you can explain why they opened a portal to such an unknown wilderness, accidentally sending themselves and others hurtling through time. Alternatively, they could be a master of this power and you could construct a dungeon or fortress deep in an ancient environment for them to hide in.

Regardless, the first question to address is how the players get there. There are at least three possible answers. The players could be chasing the Chronoficer, who takes refuge by activating their time machine. This might force the players to follow through a portal or seek another means to pursue their foe. Perhaps they could arrive before the Chronoficer, giving them time to prepare an ambush, or perhaps long after the Chronoficer has fortified their hideout. The second possible option is that the Chronoficer simply sends the players through time in an attempt to dispose of them. This could result in a tense and gritty survival situation, where the players need to stay alive until the magic wears off or they find another means to travel back. Finally, the players may work with the Chronoficer to travel through time intentionally, perhaps to retrieve a long-destroyed artifact or prevent some past catastrophe.

You can put a lot of creativity into imagining the device that allows your players to travel through time. It could be a simple circular portal embedded in an ancient temple. Stepping through it brings you back out in the exact same spot, but in a vastly different time. Perhaps the device is a rideable steam-punk-esque machine that the party can sit in. Whirling cogs and hissing pistons encompass the party as the world spins around them. Or, on a much grander scale, the device could be an entire castle capable of magical transportation. Blinking in and out of existence as it shifts through time, acting as a base of operations for your players. When constructing a story like this, it's important to provide multiple means of returning the players back to their normal timeline. The last thing you want is to have a singular fragile device that is immediately destroyed upon the party's arrival (unless of course that is your intention!). We recommend using some of the examples above as contingency in case the party becomes stranded.

entries.name: Hollow World

entries: It had been three months in this darkness. "Treasures beyond imaginin' in the depths below they said.", scoffed Dr Dhrolin, remembering the words of the Spelunking Guild's representative. He and his party had expected to find precious georesources–gemstones, gold, and fossils. Instead, after two weeks of delving, they were greeted by the enraged denizens of vast underground cities. Clearly the party's presence must have greatly offended them, as they had been hunted for a further 10 weeks now. A long game of cat-and-mouse in the endless caverns, stumbling past ancient eyeless horrors in the dark. They were sick of it but had little choice other than to press on. "Oh well", thought Dr Dhrolin. "Move forward, or face death." He swung his pickaxe down on the cave wall, the twang echoing back up the tunnel. Hope had left them long ago, but they carried on. Twang! A second strike cracked the rock. When the third strike hit, the familiar twang was smothered by the sound of crumbling rock and shrill gasps. Everyone instinctively covered their eyes as a beam of pure yellow light pierced the darkness through the newly opened hole, illuminating Dr Dhrolin's feet. "What in the hells have we found?", he whispered.

Similar to the Ancient Plateau, the Hollow World proposes that your ancient environment persists in the modern day, but is sealed away from civilisation. Imagine a vast underground chamber, encompassing the centre of the planet and lined with its own inner surface, just like the outer surface. Instead of a roiling core of molten rock held solid under great pressure, the planet is held structurally sound by a giant prismatic crystal.

This enormous crystal is the source of all light and warmth in the Hollow World. Imagine that it glows with a dim yellow or white hue and illuminates the entire cavern, radiating a brilliant heat like the sun. Perhaps it pulses in a cycle that mimics night and day, albeit on a different timescale or with different intensities. This could lead to interesting variations on normal environments. For example, mountain peaks that stretch towards the crystal could be scorching deserts towards the top, and caverns and canyons might be icy frozen pits away from the crystal's warmth. Where it anchors to the crust could be extremely hot volcanic areas.
There is also an official 5e setting that explores this narrative in more detail.

entries.title: {@i Yutyrannus}
entries.altText: A lone Yutyrannus wanders through a snowy environment, its nose pointed skyward.

entries.name: Final Comment
entries: These settings are only some of the potential story hooks you could use and we encourage the inclusion of palaeontological components in any world you can imagine. These palaeontological components could be within specific regions just outside the borders of a grand city or on the edge of a frontier. Imagine how these creatures might interact with the denizens of your world. Do they use them as hunting animals, companions, or are they merely dangerous beasts of the wilds to be feared? Perhaps, all three.

entries.name: Story Hook NPCs
entries: We have created two NPC stat blocks to facilitate introducing these elements into your games. These are the {@creature Chronoficer|PartneredDDDoD}, and {@creature Dr Dhrolin, Palaeontologist|PartneredDDDoD|Dr Dhrolin} himself. For the Chronoficer, we have provided a named character in Miss Nemona Hemsworth-Pennyfarthing, but feel free to design your own however you wish.

entries.name: Chronoficer
entries: A Chronoficer is first and foremost an inventor. They explore the manipulation of time and invent grand devices to control it, either distorting it, creating temporal portals, perceiving the past, or pausing it temporarily for others. As such, they are invariably forces of chaos within their worlds, disturbing the natural order of events. Their experiments attract interest from those seeking power and draw ire from those wishing to maintain the status quo. This usually pushes their research into the shadows, and their laboratories are often hidden in basements or secret chambers.

entries.altText: Miss Nemona Hemsworth-Pennyfarthing, a grey scaly dragonborn chronoficer, manipulates a mysterious glowing cube. She has a white shirt, neat grey waistcoat, leather wrist straps, and a monocle. Two horns protrude from the top of her head backwards and curve up at the tips.

entries: Each Chronoficer may have a different ultimate goal, ranging from the impartial pursuit of knowledge following a noble non-interaction principal, to the desperate resurrection of a deceased loved one, to the selfish redirection of events allowing them to hoard wealth. They may even have overarching grand ambitions for the restoration of what they perceive as the 'correct timeline', but in all cases there are unintended consequences.

The evidence of a Chronoficer's experiments can range dramatically, sometimes affecting only a single building or room, other times wreaking havoc across entire regions. Strange creatures may be pulled from the past or future into the current time as they stumble through unstable temporal rifts, time may speed up or slowdown in isolated spots, or temperatures may plummet in specific locations as a temporal flux momentarily creates a point of absolute zero. In any case, a Chronoficer's experiments are rarely subtle.

Tracking and capturing a rogue Chronoficer is extremely difficult. Even if their actions become predictable, their equipment allows them to escape through a variety of manipulations of time. They can routinely slow or stop time in small areas, escape to other time periods, or (in some cases) rewind time to reattempt their escape. However, their control is far from flawless and paradoxes or butterfly effects can completely disrupt any situation.

One such Chronoficer is the dragonborn Miss Nemona Hemsworth-Pennyfarthing. Born and raised in Urgleshire noble district, she was the child of a union between the Hemsworth and Pennyfarthing households, who both sought to consolidate their dwindling political power through the marriage of Miss Myarya Hemsworth and Sir Garroguk Pennyfarthing. Nemona grew up as an isolated child, busying herself with the study of engineering and the invention of her own mechanical toys. As she aged, this hobby grew into a passion, then an obsession. By the chance finding of a tome of temporal studies in her father's library, she dove into chronological research, enamoured by this new science. She is the sole heir to both the Hemsworth and Pennyfarthing estates and this wealth allowed her to construct a bespoke laboratory within the confines of her properties.

Despite her family's efforts, her interest in politics, marriage, and the continuation of the joined family name was limited. Instead, she poured her time into her research. When anomalies began to form in her laboratory, she shielded her family from the truth, burying as much evidence as she could.

Inevitably, a catastrophic disaster struck and pulled two large predatory dinosaurs into her time. Unleashed upon the Pennyfarthing estate, they subsequently slew both Myarya and Garroguk before she was able to return them to their time. It was at this point that the authorities began to investigate. However, with her parents dead and the invading dinosaurs returned, Nemona had unlimited access to her family's wealth. In her grief, she sought to undo her mistakes–leading to several grievous errors and major prehistoric incursions. In their wake, Urgleshire authorities opted to dispatch an adventuring party headed by Dr Dhrolin to the Pennyfarthing manor to investigate these strange occurrences.

entries.name: Dr Dhrolin, Palaeontologist
entries: Dr Reginald Dhrolin is a dwarven scientist, and associate professor in palaeontology at the University of Urgleshire. His research areas include pre-draconic Urgleshire fauna and macroevolutionary/magical-evolutionary trends among animals.

During our story, Dr Dhrolin is on sabbatical research leave, meaning that his teaching responsibilities are covered by other members of {@item staff|XPHB} while he undertakes prolonged field research. This usually lasts a year and is provided to research {@item staff|XPHB} to allow them to collect new data for future projects. The creature and environment pages in this book represent Dr Dhrolin's research notes during a particularly eventful sabbatical.

entries.altText: Dr Dhrolin, an olive-skinned dwarf wearing a wide brimmed hat and explorer

entries: "Ya see, the changes that an organism undergos between successive generations are influenced by the world around 'em, be it magical or mundane. If we understand what happens in this process, we can bet'er understand what happened to us in our own past."

During this sabbatical, Dr Dhrolin was contacted by Urgleshire law enforcement to assist with the investigation of strange prehistoric occurrences in the city's noble district. Accompanied by an adventuring party, this is where his fate was intertwined with Miss Nemona Hemsworth-Pennyfarthing, whose reckless creations had thrown all of them hurtling through time. Awakening to strange sounds of unfamiliar wildlife, Dr Dhrolin and his party found themselves stranded in a strange land with only fleeting signs of Miss Hemsworth-Pennyfarthing's presence. It took several months of tracking and travelling through remnant temporal rifts, hopping between time periods, before they were able to capture Miss Hemsworth-Pennyfarthing and return to their own time. The consequences of their actions during this time are yet to be seen.

"Our travels pursuin' Miss Hemsworth-Pennyfarthin' allowed us to collect an astonishin' amount of information on our past. We'll be studyin' these notes for decades to come, but I do wonder whether the cost was too high. Who knows what but'erfly effects we may have caused while through the past."

We envision Dr Dhrolin as a dwarf that speaks with a thick British rural Westcountry accent and has an enthusiastic demeanour, as well as an eagerness to explain the science behind his observations. Our dictations for Dr Dhrolin are based on the accent of a real person who lived in both the Midlands and Southwest, so include components of both dialects. We also imagine that he is easily distracted and sometimes ignores danger. Ultimately, you may give him any accent and personality you wish, play him however you want, or use his stat block as a basis to create your own palaeontologist character.

entries.title: {@i Oxygnathus ornatus}
entries.altText: A classical illustration of a slab of rock with an exceptionally preserved fossil fish on it called Oxygnathus. It has a long body with a pointed snout.

data.name: Holistic Environments

entries.altText: A herd of the enormous sauropod Giraffititan walks along a beach as pterosaurs circle their heads and small dinosaurs forage in the shallows.

entries: Four of the most recognisable environments that Dr Dhrolin and his party visited on their chronological travels are presented in this section. Each provides a reconstruction of a place that existed in the real world, with roleplaying rules for in-game environmental effects, based on their actual palaeoenvironment. We have populated each of these environments with five animal and five plant species, although they contained many more. Each of these are accompanied by rules that let you interact with them in your roleplaying world. Some of these environmental reconstructions and species have never been illustrated in such a comprehensive manner before. As such, we've undertaken considerable research to make them as accurate as possible.

entries.name: Environmental Icons
entries: Each of our Mesozoic reptiles (and mutations later in the book) are accompanied by environmental icons that represent the habitats that these animals lived in. This system allows you to rapidly populate your own environments with appropriately adapted animals.

entries.name: Creature Encounter Table
entries: The list below outlines all of the Mesozoic reptiles presented in this book. We have included their {@variantrule Challenge Rating|XPHB} (CR) and Magical {@variantrule Challenge Rating|XPHB} (MCR), the latter of which is applied if you are including their optional magical rules.

entries.altText: The landscape of the Yixian Formation, a rocky and forested volcano smoulders while covered in thick snow. A large chilly lake is filled with pale blue water. A giant pterosaur flies over the landscape.

entries: Four weeks of trudgin' took us right into the heart of the continent. The further north and higher we pushed, the colder it got. Our path eventually required that we crossed a dangerous high-peaked volcano durin' mid-winter. As we ascended the towerin' volcano, the once lush conifer forest slowly began to give way to sparce snow-covered trees, then eventually to bare frosty stone. The only break from the bitter cold n' bitin' wind were patches of dense forest surroundin' warm volcanic lakes that steamed away on the slopes. Some of 'em were a welcome rest stop, but others were flanked by icy skeletal remains, revealin' their deadly nature.

entries.name: Background
entries: The Yixian Formation is a body of rock in North-eastern China that was deposited approximately 123 million years ago. This makes it Early Cretaceous in age, a time when the world was quite warm and flowering plants were becoming widespread. The Earth was dominated by dinosaurs, pterosaurs, and marine reptiles, but early mammals scurried around in the undergrowth and true birds flew among the trees. The Yixian Formation was first formally described in 1933, however it's most famous fossils were not discovered until the mid 1990s.

entries.name: Description

entries.title: Gryphaea
entries.altText: A Gryphaea oyster resting on the seabed.

entries: We often characterize any Early Cretaceous environments as humid, tropical, and sunny. However, the Yixian Formation does not fit this archetype. It is unusual as it was deposited at a relatively high altitude with cyclic wet and dry seasons. The dry season had an average temperature of only 10°C (50°F), and so would have had frigid and potentially snowy periods. The dominant trees in this environment were conifers and we can imagine an environment closer to the mountainous parts of North America or Russia. Although perhaps sounding idyllic, the Yixian palaeoenvironment was far from peaceful. Dotted amongst the hills and mountains were volcanoes. These periodically erupted, clouding the skies with ash, sparking wildfires, and flooding hillsides with lava. Tranquil volcanic lakes would have boiled and bubbled with noxious gasses, creating deadly clouds of mist. The forests around these volcanoes would have been annihilated and rapidly regrown from the fertile volcanic soils.

entries.name: Geology

entries.title: {@i Substeueroceras koeneni}
entries.altText: A classical illustration of a partially preserved ammonite shell, belonging to Substeueroceras. It is cracked in half, with the bottom half missing.

entries: The Yixian Formation is a complex set of sediments formed of fluvial (river), alluvial (floodplain), lacustrine (lake), and volcanic material. This means that the rock was formed by loose silt and sand being deposited by rivers, streams, and water flowing across the ground's surface, deposition within volcanic lakes, and the volcanic ashes and lavas themselves. It contains some layers of basaltic flow and breccia, which are rocks formed by flowing lava that sometimes contain angular shards of other rock types. However, the parts of the Yixian Formation that preserved fossils are the sediments deposited in an ancient lake. The bottom of this lake cycled between being well-oxygenated and lacking oxygen. When there was little oxygen, combined with volcanic ash, animals couldn't scavenge carcasses from the lakebed, nor could bacteria rot the carcasses. This allowed them to be covered by very fine volcanic sediment and ultimately preserved as beautiful fossils.

entries.title: {@i Liaoningocladus boii} historic reconstruction
entries.altText: A sketch of Liaoningocladus

entries.name: Fossils
entries: The volcanic lakes of the Yixian Formation captured examples of animals and plants that thrived between the volcanic disasters. In the silent sediments of these lakes, carcasses of non-avian dinosaurs, birds, pterosaurs, mammals, insects, and plants were all preserved from the surrounding forests. There are also fossils of fish, crustaceans, and molluscs. Many are remarkably well-preserved, largely by the addition of volcanic sediments to the calm water setting. Some authors hypothesise that limnic eruptions (carbon dioxide bubbling) from the lakes may have released clouds of toxic gas that suffocated animals surrounding them, leading to their immediate death and deposition into the lake. In the following pages, we have provided stat blocks for some of these animals; {@creature Beipiaosaurus|PartneredDDDoD}, {@creature Bolong|PartneredDDDoD}, {@creature Microraptor|PartneredDDDoD}, {@creature Psittacosaurus|PartneredDDDoD}, and {@creature Yutyrannus|PartneredDDDoD}.

entries.name: As a roleplaying environment
entries: The Yixian Formation should primarily represent a high-altitude cold and mountainous conifer forest with scattered pools of volcanically-heated water. These can act as hot springs or could be frozen mountain ponds. Seasonal snow may cover the landscape on colder years, but otherwise this forest can be full of life–cawing birds, swarming insects, and bellowing predatory dinosaurs.

Being volcanic, the Yixian comes with a variety of serious dangers beyond the usual dinosaur threats. Below, are two tables that provide some volcanic hazards. Depending on how capable your party is, you may want to include both, one, or none of these tables. You may roll on the tables when your players encounter or trigger one of the events or select which is most appropriate for your setting. However, be warned, that volcanos are serious threats and an overly-curious party could easily be TPK'd.

entries.name: Volcanic Lake
entries: {@i (low- to medium-level parties)}
When the party comes across a lake in this environment, roll for or select one of the options below to determine the type of lake.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: Give your players little clues as to the type of lake this may be. Acidic lakes might have a sickly smell or the remains of partially dissolved carcasses around it. Toxic pools may have no audible birdlife nearby.

rows: {@b Acidic volcanic lake.} Water from this lake causes {@damage 1d4} Acid damage. A creature submerged in it takes {@damage 2d4} Acid damage per round.

{@b Limnic eruption.} If the waters are disturbed, a gaseous cloud 15 ft. in diameter erupts and drifts 5 ft. per round in a random (or wind blown) direction. It causes {@damage 1d6} Acid damage and {@damage 2d4} Poison damage per round to any creature inside of it. The cloud can be dissipated by a powerful continuous wind.

entries.name: Volcanic Event
entries: {@i (medium- to high-level parties)}
When the party first completes a {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB} in this environment, roll for or select one of the options below to determine the volcanic event that is occurring.

rows: {@b The volcano stirs.} Mild tremors rock the land and the sky darkens from ash. Re-roll on this table in {@dice 3d6} hours' time.
{@b Falling ash.} The sky darkens as burning cinders ignite fires throughout the forest. All native creatures begin to flee the area. Re-roll on this table in {@dice 3d6} hours' time.

{@b Eruption!} Slow flowing lava erupts, travailing at 10 ft. per round from the volcano's peak, igniting everything it touches. It flows downhill up to 900 ft., dealing {@damage 4d8} Fire damage per round to creatures in contact with it. It deals a further {@damage 4d8} Fire damage and {@damage 8d8} Bludgeoning damage per round to creatures smothered by it. Creatures native to the Elemental Plane of Fire are unaffected.
{@b Explosive eruption!} Heavy tremors rock the land as a large explosion occurs at the peak. All nearby lakes undergo a Limnic Eruption (see Volcanic Lake table).

{@b Cataclysm!} The volcano blows its peak cataclysmically. Fire and rock rains down in all directions. Every minute spent unsheltered and within 1 mile of the volcano, a creature must succeed a DC 12 Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|XPHB}, or take {@damage 2d8} Fire damage and {@damage 2d8} Bludgeoning damage. The eruption lasts 1 hour.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: Give your players warning that a volcanic event may be brewing. Have little tremors rock the landscape periodically for hours or days beforehand. If your party members are absent-minded (or curious) enough to be at the peak when it erupts, the consequences should be appropriately deadly. If you wish to use 6. Cataclysm! for a lower-level party, we recommend changing the damage to {@dice 1d8} Fire and {@dice 1d8} Bludgeoning. We also recommend rewarding ingenuity. If players take shelter or protect themselves away from the main lava flow, they should avoid the majority of the damage.

entries.name: Yixian Formation Flora
entries: The Yixian Flora has been described as a mesophytic to semi-xerophytic forest, meaning that it is a subtropical humid and sub-humid (somewhat dry) high-altitude woodland environment.

entries.name: Khitania columnispicata

entries.altText: Leaves of the woody vine Khitania, with small thin cone-like reproductive strobiles.

entries: {@i Khitania columnispicata} is closely related to modern {@i Gentum} and would have grown as a woody vine that climbed the trunks of other plants, dangling from their branches (a liana). They produced a long thin cone-like strobile and female plants would have also produced spikes with clusters of red or orange 'fruits' (not true fruits) once pollinated. The flesh of modern {@i Gentum} 'fruits' is edible but isn't generally eaten. However, its seeds are often eaten once dried, and its leaves can be eaten once boiled in oil. It is likely that {@i Khitania columnispicata} shared some of these traits and could have made for a nourishing source of food in warmer months. Its fibrous bark would have also been useful for making rope for nets and bags.

entries.name: Hyper-thermo-genetic
entries: If the strobile of this plant is crushed into a {@item Khitania columnispicata Paste|PartneredDDDoD|paste} and smeared on a creature's body, that creature gains {@variantrule Resistance|XPHB} to Cold damage for 24 hours. Consuming the {@item Khitania columnispicata Seed|PartneredDDDoD|seeds} of this plant provide {@variantrule Immunity|XPHB} to Cold damage for 1 minute.

entries.name: Ginkgo apodes
entries: {@i Ginkgo apodes} is a large tree with distinctive fan-like leaves that arose in the Jurassic, and whose relatives persist to the modern day. These trees can survive in regions with polluted air that would kill off less resistant plants and also live for an exceptionally long time, reportedly for over a thousand years. During this time, they can even develop stalactite-like structures of wood and are sometimes given the name "Maidenhair Trees" as a result. Female trees develop clusters of small yellow fruit-like fleshy structures that coat their seeds and give off an odour of cat urine. However, once dried, the seeds themselves are edible and have a rich sweet nutty flavour. {@i Ginkgo apodes} would have shared all of these characteristics.

entries.altText: A large ginkgo tree with the fruit-like yellow berries highlighted.

entries.name: Feline Warding
entries: If a humanoid creature touches the fruit-like berries from this tree, an oily residue coats them that smells strongly of cat urine. For the next 1 hour, herbivorous and omnivorous beasts will avoid that humanoid where possible, and the humanoid has {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on {@skill Intimidation|XPHB} checks against them. However, for the next 1 hour, carnivorous beasts will be more aggressive towards that humanoid, favouring attacking them in combat, and they will have {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on {@skill Perception|XPHB} and {@skill Survival|XPHB} checks to find them.

entries.name: Resistant
entries: {@i Ginkgo apodes} is immune to Necrotic and Poison damage, and it can survive in soiled, polluted, or otherwise contaminated land.

entries.name: Siphonospermum simplex
entries: {@i Siphonospermum simplex} grew as a wiry bush and preferred dryer soils. Modern relatives of this plant can be used for medicinal purposes, particularly to treat allergies, coughs, and circulation issues, and some components can even be brewed into a psychoactive tea. It is possible that {@i Siphonospermum simplex} could have been used in similar ways. Interestingly, some plants of this group with flower-like cones only bloom during a full moon and are pollinated by nocturnal insects.

entries.title: Siphonospermum simplex bush
entries.altText: The small bushy plant Siphonospermum.

entries.name: Psychoactive
entries: This plant is used as a key ingredient in spiced ales and is highly valued by some merchants. It can also be brewed into a delicious {@item Siphonospermum simplex Brew|PartneredDDDoD|potion} that provides {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on Wisdom Saving Throws for 1 hour when consumed.

entries.name: Lunar Ritual
entries: During a full moon at night, this plant's flowers bloom and radiate magical energies. If a creature takes a {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB} within 10 ft. of this plant during that night, they awaken with one of the affects below (DM's choice):

items: They awaken with an additional temporary spell slot of their highest level. This spell slot lasts until they cast a spell at that level or complete a {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB}.

They awaken with additional {@variantrule Temporary Hit Points|XPHB} equal to twice their level. These {@variantrule Temporary Hit Points|XPHB} are lost when they complete a {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB}.

entries.name: Sinocarpus decussatus
entries: {@i Sinocarpus decussatus} was a small herb that grew in the shaded understory of the Yixian forests. It had tiny flowers that developed four peapod-like seed cases after pollination. Aside from these characteristics, little is known about the biology of this plant, as there are no close modern relatives of it.

entries.name: Ultra-Pigmented
entries: The pollen of this plant is a bright yellow pigment that is extremely difficult to remove from clothing and skin. If a creature touches this plant's flowers, it becomes covered in a bright dusty yellow stain that persists for 3{@dice  + 1d4} days. Anything else that touches the stain on that creature also becomes covered in a bright dusty yellow stain that persists for {@dice 1d4} days. The stain is magical in nature and washing does not remove it.

entries.altText: The small mostly green herb Sinocarpus with a single purple leaf and pink bases to tiny green flowers.

entries.name: Liaoningocladus boii
entries: {@i Liaoningocladus boii} was a coniferous tree with red berry-like pseudofruits. The flesh of these pseudofruits was probably edible, but the seeds would have been poisonous to humans. This tree was regularly parasitised by insects, forming large swollen galls on the leaves. In fact, when these leaves were first discovered as fossils, they were misinterpreted as a part of the plant's intended anatomy and representative of a carnivorous pitcher. Modern relatives of this tree are frequently used to make longbows, as their wood is particularly suitable for them, and were historically planted around ancient burial grounds in some druidic traditions.

entries.altText: A tall conifer tree with red berry-like fruits highlighted.

entries.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: Each time the party encounters a new plant of this species, choose (or roll for) one of the options below and apply the corresponding Trait. If a player examines the tree before touching it, they can determine which of the two it is by succeeding on a DC 12 {@skill Nature|XPHB} check.

1. {@b {@i Anaesthetic.}} This tree will yield {@dice 1d20} red {@item Liaoningocladus boii Pseudofruit|PartneredDDDoD|pseudofruits}. These can be eaten and restore 1 hit point each, but also contain a large central seed. If a creature swallows one of these seeds it must succeed a DC 12 Constitution {@variantrule Saving Throw|XPHB} or become {@condition Poisoned|XPHB} for 24 hours and fall asleep for 1 minute. The creature awakens if it takes damage.

2. {@b {@i Galled.}} This plant has concealed bulbous galls on its leaves that harbour vicious parasitic insects. The first time a creature touches the leaves of this plant, the galls burst, and the creature takes {@damage 1d4 + 1} Poison damage.

entries.altText: A flock of Beipiaosaurus stand in a snow-covered glade. Some of these fluffy theropods feed on lichen growing on dead trees as others continue to search for food. One is crying out loudly, its hot breath condensing in the cold air.

entries.title: {@i Lytoceras}
entries.altText: A side-view of the shell of the ammonite Lytoceras.

entries.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, change {@creature Beipiaosaurus|PartneredDDDoD|Beipiaosaurus'} CR to 3 and increase its XP to 700 accordingly.

entries.name: Predatory Ancestors
entries: {@creature Beipiaosaurus|PartneredDDDoD} retains the nocturnal hunter-killer instincts of its predatory theropod ancestors. At night, {@i Beipiaosaurus} gains the following temporary changes:

items: It has {@sense Darkvision|XPHB} 60 ft.
Its movement speed is 35 ft. and its climb speed is 20 ft.
It has {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on {@skill Perception|XPHB} checks.
It has {@variantrule Resistance|XPHB} to Bludgeoning, Piercing, and Slashing damage.
It has {@variantrule Vulnerability|XPHB} to Radiant damage.
It has an aversion to {@variantrule Bright Light|XPHB}.
It loses its "Peaceful Aura, Fearsome Presence" Trait.

entries.altText: Bolong, a medium sized herbivorous dinosaur, walks on two legs through a shallow rocky stream. Its forelimbs are held up, and each hand has a prominent thumb spike.

entries.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, you do not need to change {@creature Bolong|PartneredDDDoD|Bolong's} CR.

entries.name: Dragon's Legacy
entries: Bolong has {@variantrule Resistance|XPHB} to Fire damage.

entries.name: Actions
Bo's Dragon (Recharge 4-6)
entries: Bolong spits a ball of burning ash at a point within 20 ft. of it. The ground within a 10 ft. {@variantrule Emanation [Area of Effect]|XPHB|Emanation} from that point is engulfed in burning embers and flame.

For the next minute, any creature that starts its turn within or moves into the embers suffers the following: {@i Constitution Saving Throw:} DC 12. {@i Failure:} 13 ({@damage 3d6 + 3}) Fire damage. {@i Success:} Half damage.

entries.altText: Two black and iridescent Microraptor squabble in the branches of a tree.

entries.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, you do not need to change {@creature Microraptor|PartneredDDDoD|Microraptor's} CR.

entries.name: Familiar
entries: Microraptor may be used as a familiar via the {@spell Find Familiar|XPHB} spell or any similar effect.

entries.name: Shimmering Feathers (2/day)
entries: {@i Trigger:} Microraptor is hit by a Melee {@variantrule Attack Roll|XPHB}. {@i Response:} Microraptor uses its iridescent feathers to misdirect and confuse attackers. Increase its AC by 2 until the end of the turn.

entries.altText: A brown, beaked Psittacosaurus stands clutching a conifer branch with some simple cones on it, as it looks upwards at the snow slowly falling around it.

entries.name: Optional Magical Rules
entries: If you choose to use the optional magical rules listed below, you do not need to change {@creature Psittacosaurus|PartneredDDDoD|Psittacosaurus'} CR.

Two enormous Yutyrannus play during heavy snowfall, with one leaping up in front of the other, kicking snow around.

entries.name: Legendary Action: Frost Bellow (Recharge 5-6)

entries.altText: The landscape of the Bahariya Formation, a heavily vegetated muggy mangrove swamp splays out before you, with the silhouettes of two sauropods in the distance wading through the water. The waterways are flanked by tall, thin trees with mangrove-like roots.

entries: We had sailed down that river for three days, but eventually found ourselves unable to continue. The waterways fanned out into an expansive delta, stretchin' as far as the eye could see. Lush vegetation and mangroves filled the area, along with the silhouettes of some pretty big dinos in the mornin' sun. The stretchin' of the river made it pretty shallow and the mangroves encroached on almost all of the waterways. They were far too shallow and narrow for our boat to get through quickly, and we knew that the ship off the coast would only wait for us a few more days. There wasn't time to carry the boat around, and the smoke on the horizon suggested that it ain't safe anyway. So, we had only one option: ditch the boat, wade through the delta, and flag down the ship with a fire from the coast. I knew this was gunna be a dangerous few days.

entries.name: Background
entries: The Bahariya Formation is located in the Western Desert of Egypt and is Early Cretaceous, specifically Cenomanian (93.5-99 million years ago), in age. Its sedimentology and stratigraphy are well-studied, in part due to the region's rich iron deposits making it a focal point of geological research. The Bahariya Formation itself was deposited over a period of 3 to 6 million years and forms a consistent succession of rock between 295 and 330 ft. thick.

Early excavations of the Bahariya Formation were undertaken by German palaeontologist Ernst Freiherr Stromer von Reichenbach (1871-1952) and his expedition team. They discovered the first {@i Spinosaurus} fossils, along with many other animals from the Bahariya Formation. Unfortunately, the vast majority of their collection was destroyed in the bombing of Munich Museum in 1944 during World War II.

entries.name: Description
entries: The lowermost part of Bahariya Formation yields most of its dinosaur fossils. This portion of the formation was deposited in a fluviatile-deltaic (river-delta) setting, which was a major component of the Bahariya palaeoenvironment. Plant fossils indicate that Bahariya was a colossal mangrove swamp (sometimes called the Bahariya Bight), possibly up to 115 mi2 and is hypothesised to be similar to the "Ten Thousand Islands" in modern Florida, USA.

The Bahariya Formation had regular dry and monsoonal seasons. The monsoons were likely violent and devastating during the wet season, whereas the dry season would have been very hot and calm, leading to low-energy waters for most of the year and the retention of nutrients within the sediments. This made the mangroves among the most productive non-marine biomes from the Mesozoic (measured in tonnes of carbon produced by photosynthesis per unit area), meaning abundant plant growth within organic and nutrient-rich sediments that were not washed away by high-energy waters for most of the year. This provided a lush and nourishing environment. Rare traces of charcoal indicate that wildfires ripped through the surrounding arid scrub during the hottest periods.

entries.name: Geology
entries: The Bahariya Formation is an excellent example of a complete stratigraphic sequence. It has unconformities at its base and top, which means that there was a period of erosion before it was deposited, and deposition stopped after it (but it wasn't eroded entirely away). This means that the Bahariya Formation provides a single snapshot of one basin that we can be sure represents continuous deposition over 3-6 million years. This, in turn, allows us to understand how environments in a single location change over time. For Bahariya, the lowermost rocks were deposited in river and delta settings, which then transitioned to costal, shoreface, shelf, and finally outer shelf in the uppermost rocks. This shows that the environment changed from river, to coastal, then to open sea as the basin level changed.

The rocks themselves consist of interbedded siltstones and sandstones, followed by cross-bedded amalgamated sandstones, then dark coloured ferruginous (iron-rich) sandstones in the uppermost unit. The different stages of the environmental change correspond to different rock types and colours.

entries.title: {@i Dapedium}
entries.altText: Two deep bodied Dapedium fish swim in open water.

entries.name: Fossils
entries: The formation yields a mixture of aquatic and terrestrial animals, with lots of molluscs (specifically oysters and clams), crabs, and fish, as well as turtles, sea snakes, plesiosaurs, crocodiles, and pterosaurs. Dinosaurs are not uncommon but, despite the abundance of lush plant-life, the fossils indicate that herbivores were relatively under-represented within the formation, generally restricted to gigantic titanosaurian sauropods (with lots of offspring, but few large adults). On the other hand, carnivores were present in their normal numbers and were probably sustained by the abundant fish and crustaceans that thrived in the nutrient-rich waters. This would have led to an environment that is substantially more carnivore-dominated than other Cretaceous settings. In the following pages, we have included the rules for the {@creature Bahariyan Polycotylid|PartneredDDDoD}, {@creature Carcharodontosaurus|PartneredDDDoD}, {@creature Paralititan|PartneredDDDoD}, {@creature Spinosaurus|PartneredDDDoD}, and {@creature Stomatosuchus|PartneredDDDoD}.

entries.name: As a roleplaying environment
entries: The Bahariya delta is a region of extremes. In the dry season, the weather should be beautifully calm and sunny with overwhelmingly lush mangroves and waters abundant with life. Giant dinosaurs should roam the sandbanks, most of which are predators, making it a treacherous place for humanoids. Players can be directed into the mangroves by fires in the surrounding scrub, pushing all manner of creatures into the confines of the waterways for safety.

In the monsoon season, the region should be battered by heavy rains, strong winds, and blackened skies. Many of the animals will persist in the region, but may be seeking shelter within the densest mangroves, or fleeing rising waters by moving into the soaked scrubland.

entries.name: Predatory Population
entries: Players have an increased chance of encountering carnivores. If you roll on a table to determine encounters for the party, the first time you roll, re-roll any result that isn't a carnivore (do not re-roll a second time). If you do not use an encounter table, the first time the party encounters a large carnivore, they instead encounter two fighting in a titanic battle.

entries.name: Over-productivity
entries: When foraging for food, you can find triple the amount of food that you would normally be able to find in the same amount of time (particularly fish, fruits, and shellfish).

entries.name: Soupy Sediment
entries: Any creature that takes the {@action Dash|XPHB} action while moving across the mangrove sediment (touching the ground) must roll a {@dice d6} and consult the table below.

rows: Its speed becomes 0 until its next turn. It may use a {@variantrule Bonus Action|XPHB} to make a Strength or Intelligence check with a DC of 14. On a success, it is instead considered to be moving through {@variantrule Difficult Terrain|XPHB} until its next turn.
It treats the ground as {@variantrule Difficult Terrain|XPHB}.

entries.name: Bahariya Formation Flora
entries: The Bahariya forest was fundamentally a mangrove forest with mixed salinity waters. However, muddy banks and margins would have allowed other plants to flourish as well. Further upstream from the delta's mouth, the fresh waters would have fed more diverse forests.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: The use of "sp." indicates that the specimen belongs to a species within that genus, but the scientists describing it cannot determine which one.

entries.name: Weichselia reticulata

entries.altText: The tall, thin tree fern Weichselia growing in swampy waters.

entries: {@i Weichselia reticulata} was a tree fern that formed much of the Bahariya mangrove forest. Its long, slender, and light trunks would have been useful for simple raft building, but lacked the structural integrity to be used in larger constructions. Their leaves may have contained an irritant, and caused mild rashes when touched, however the submerged part of the stem would likely have been edible, although not very tasty and difficult to harvest.

entries.name: Congestant
entries: The thick {@item Weichselia reticulata Stem|PartneredDDDoD|stem} of this plant causes a creature's sinuses and ear canals to swell if chewed, dulling their hearing. A creature that chews this stem gains {@variantrule Resistance|XPHB} to Thunder damage for 24 hours, but also has {@variantrule Disadvantage|XPHB} on {@skill Perception|XPHB} checks that involve sound for 24 hours.

entries.name: Mild Irritant
entries: If a humanoid creature touches the leaves of this plant, they break out in a mild rash. This causes no damage and does not affect any of their abilities, but is itchy and uncomfortable.

entries.name: Marsilea sp.
entries: {@i Marsilea} sp. was a small aquatic fern with clover-like leaves. These leaves would have floated on the surface of shallow water around the Bahariya delta. Both the leaves and sporocarps (small growths at the base of the leaf) would have been edible. In fact, the sporocarps could have been ground into flour if enough were harvested. However, other components of the plant would have been highly toxic and modern relatives of this genus are known to cause brain damage to livestock that eat it.

entries.name: Neurotoxic Stimulant
entries: The leaves of this plant are a powerful stimulant. They can be crushed to create a {@item Marsilea sp. Potion|PartneredDDDoD|potion} that, if consumed, gives {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on Dexterity Saving Throws for 24 hours. However, if the wrong parts of the plant are included in the {@item Marsilea sp. Potion (Incorrectly Harvested)|PartneredDDDoD|potion}, it also inflicts {@damage 2d4} Psychic damage when consumed. When harvesting the plant as an ingredient, a DC 14 {@skill Nature|XPHB} check is required to ensure that only the correct parts are harvested.

entries.altText: The aquatic plant Marsilea has pale green clover-like leaves and thin stems.

entries.name: Agathis sp.

entries.altText: The huge and broad conifer tree Agathis has clusters of leaves towards its top and a fat trunk.

entries: {@i Agathis} sp. was an exceptionally tall evergreen coniferous tree that stood more than twice the height of the tallest sauropods. This genus persists today and its trees (sometimes called Kauri or Dammara trees) can be found in Southeast Asia, Australia, and many of the surrounding island regions. The hard wood and wide trunks of this tree make it an exceptional building material and Polynesian cultures have historically used it in ship construction. The trees themselves can live for a very long time, reportedly well over a thousand years.

entries.name: Ancient Soul
entries: Certain trees of this species harbour an old druidic soul (DM's choice). A humanoid who knows the spell {@spell Speak with Plants|XPHB} feels a strange spiritual connection to this tree when they first come within 30 ft. of one possessing such a soul. They instinctively know that they can commune with it in a 10 minute meditation ritual. If they do so, they gain {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on all Saving Throws for the next 24 hours.

entries.name: Cladophlebis sp.
entries: {@i Cladophlebis} was a genus of fern that grew in clusters within moist ground. It grew along the margins and sandy banks of the Bahariya delta as a low-lying plant. Despite its generic appearance, some components of this plant would have been edible. Young fiddleheads (the curled up developing leaves) could have been cooked and eaten, and the rhizome (underground stem) could have been processed to make a butter-like substance.

entries.name: Optional Magical Rules
Flammable Oils
entries: The oils in this plant's rhizome ignite and detonate when compressed rapidly. If a Medium or larger creature falls onto or steps on this plant, it suffers {@damage 1d4} Bludgeoning damage and {@damage 1d4} Fire damage as the plant detonates. The plant is destroyed by this process.
Alternatively, the rhizome can be carefully extracted with a DC 10 {@skill Sleight of Hand|XPHB} check and then may function like a {@item Cladophlebis Rhizome Grenade|PartneredDDDoD|grenade}:

entries.name: Rhizome grenade
entries: As an {@variantrule Action|XPHB}, a humanoid creature can throw the grenade (20/60 ft.). Any creature within 5 ft. {@variantrule Emanation [Area of Effect]|XPHB|Emanation} of where it lands must succeed a DC 12 Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|XPHB}, or take {@damage 1d4} Bludgeoning damage and {@damage 1d4} Fire damage.

entries.altText: The typical fern Cladophlebis has several fronds of both green and brown colour.

entries.name: Nelumbites
entries: {@i Nelumbites} was a small aquatic lotus that grew in still water. The close modern relative Nelumbo (lotuses) is grown as a food crop, as it produces nutritious tubers buried in the wet sediment. Unusually, this plant is also able to generate its own heat through a thermoregulatory alternative oxidase pathway (AOX). It is probable that {@i Nelumbites} also produced such edible structures, and would have been an excellent source of food, and may have even had the same heat-generating properties as Nelumbo. Lotus flowers also carry cultural significance as symbols of beauty, purity, faithfulness, and spirituality.

entries.altText: The aquatic Nelumbites is a lotus with a thick root and very long and thin stems.

entries.name: Daucunoid-like Tuber
entries: Each plant yields a thick tuber that can provide one day's ration and grants a {@sense Darkvision|XPHB} of 60 ft. for 24 hours when consumed.

entries.name: Spiritual Warmth
entries: Rarely, this plant will produce a single large magical flower. This flower radiates warming spiritual energies and can be carefully harvested by completing a DC 15 {@skill Nature|XPHB} check. On a success, the harvested plant becomes the magical item described below. On a failure, it instead crumbles to ash.

entries.altText: The landscape of Haţeg Island shows tropical forest on a large island, with open ocean spanning in the distance. The giant pterosaur Hatzegopteryx swoops down on the mini-sauropod Magyarosaurus in a clearing.

entries: We'd been told of a mysterious island 30 miles off the coast that was, apparently, filled with all manner of strange creatures. After a few hours of sailin', we arrived. This island was quite large, covered in dense forest and jungle. The tales were indeed true, as it was largely populated by miniature dinosaurs–a remarkable sight to behold. I had read about such a phenomenon, called "insular dwarfism" in the literature. A term I found interestin' as a dwarf meself. Several other adventuring parties had also warned us not to go though, sayin' it was unsafe. Looked perfectly fine when we arrived and most of the lil' beasts posed no threat at all. However, we soon found out that the warnin's were to be heeded.

entries.name: Background
entries: Hațeg Island isn't a single geological formation, but rather a landmass that we can determine existed by the characteristics of the sediments that were deposited in its surrounding basins. Located in modern day Romania, Hațeg Island was a landmass that persisted for a very long time, but the sediments that we study to learn about it are of Late Cretaceous age.

Hațeg Island first drew the attention of palaeontologists in the early 1900s, after the discovery of dinosaur bones in the region. It quickly became apparent that many of the examples found appeared to be adult specimens, but were significantly smaller than their close relatives found elsewhere. It soon became apparent that Hațeg Island was the first example of insular dwarfism in the fossil record. This is a process whereby large animal communities isolated on islands for thousands or millions of years adapt to the limited resources by significantly reducing their body size over many generations.

entries.name: Description
entries: Hațeg Island was either a single island, archipelago, or (at the very least) an isolated spit of land. Current data suggests that it was most likely a very large island (30,000 mi2), with the nearest mainland over 125 mi away, and had at least one volcano.

It was in the warm sub-tropical part of the Tethys Sea, about 27° North of the equator. This gave it a hot climate with a mean annual temperature of 20–25 °C (68–77 °F), as the Cretaceous was warmer than the world today. This climate supported a sub-tropical flora, with a mix of ferns and flowering plants.

entries.name: Geology
entries: As there are many geological formations that allow us to reconstruct Hațeg Island, describing the combined geology of all of these strata is rather complex. Nevertheless, the two main Late Cretaceous successions are the Densuş–Ciula and Sânpetru formations. These are generally molasse-type deposits, which in geology means a combination of sandstones, shales, and conglomerates (rounded coarse-grains cemented together) deposited in non-marine aquatic settings, such as lakes, rivers, and streams. Deposits of volcanic tuffs, tuffities, and volcanic agglomerates indicate infrequent periods of volcanic activity from at least one volcano on the island. Most of the fossils are preserved in these molasse-type deposits, but our information about Hațeg Island is also supplemented by an array of shallow marine basin deposits that were formed in the surrounding Tethys Sea.

entries.name: Fossils
entries: Hațeg Island has been described as having a diversity so large that it must have been from a large island (>30,000 mi2). These encompass a wide variety of animals, including fish, frogs, turtles, and crocodiles in the island's waterways and coastal waters, as well as lizards, snakes, pterosaurs, dinosaurs, and mammals throughout the island. This fauna is generally reflective of the typical Euramerican Early Cretaceous fauna. As mentioned above, the flora was dominated by ferns and angiosperms (flowering plants), forming a hot dry sub-tropical woodland setting.

entries.name: As a roleplaying environment
entries: Hațeg Island can be run one of two ways: either as a giant mysterious island, or as dozens of small islands, each populated with their own unique creatures. In either case, the creatures found on Hațeg should be visually distinct from their mainland relatives, displaying unusual colours and patterns in addition to their reduced size.

Hațeg borderlines on a tropical island setting (albeit a bit cooler) and can be populated by lush forests and jungles. The isolation of the island(s) makes it a great setting for forgotten temples and lost civilisations, and including Hațeg as a 'lost island' in a nautical-themed setting can add a sense of realism to this standard fantasy trope. In the following pages, we have provided stats for {@creature Balaur|PartneredDDDoD}, {@creature Hatzegopteryx|PartneredDDDoD}, {@creature Magyarosaurus|PartneredDDDoD}, {@creature Struthiosaurus|PartneredDDDoD}, and {@creature Zalmoxes|PartneredDDDoD}.

entries.name: Designers' Note
entries: We ran an adventure to Hațeg Island with a level 4 party and it worked exceptionally well. In this, we had {@i Hatzegopteryx} be a looming deadly presence that the party had to avoid, rather than fight. They travelled throughout the island, encountering other dinosaurs and the ruins of a civilisation that worshipped {@i Hatzegopteryx}. This was interspersed with chase scenes through narrow forests and caves, fleeing from {@i Hatzegopteryx} itself.

entries.title: {@i Sphenopteris}
entries.altText: A fossil of the fern Sphenopteris

entries.name: Insular dwarfism
entries: Any creature (excluding {@creature Hatzegopteryx|PartneredDDDoD}, {@creature Balaur|PartneredDDDoD}, {@creature Zalmoxes|PartneredDDDoD}, {@creature Magyarosaurus|PartneredDDDoD}, and {@creature Struthiosaurus|PartneredDDDoD}) that makes landfall on Hațeg Island is affected by {@b Insular Dwarfism}. If the affected creature remains on the island, it will shrink by one size category after its next {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB}. A creature can only ever be reduced by one size category from this effect. The affect dissipates after 24 hours if the creature leaves Hațeg Island within the next two days. If it does not, the affect becomes permanent and can only be removed by a {@spell Greater Restoration|XPHB} spell or effect.

entries.name: Island Isolation
entries: Non-humanoid creatures on this island do not see humanoids as a threat and are instead highly curious of them. These creatures may still see humanoids as prey.
